For each byte array configuration, call a helper assertion method that performs the core decoding operation by invoking the codec's decode method with the expected binary string representation (such as "00000000", "00000001", "00000011", up to "1111111111111111" for two-byte combinations), then validates that the decoded result matches the original byte array by comparing their string representations. The helper method tests multiple decode method overloads including string input, byte array input, and character array input to ensure consistent behavior across different input types. Additionally, test the edge case of decoding an empty byte array with a null input to verify proper null handling. After test completion, clean up by nullifying the codec instance. This test uses the standard JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of extracting option properties from command line arguments that use value separators, specifically testing the getOptionProperties method of the CommandLine class when provided with a specific Option instance. Initialize a string array containing command line arguments with various formats including system property-style arguments with the -D flag such as -Dparam1=value1, -Dparam2=value2, a standalone -Dparam3 flag, -Dparam4=value4, a standalone -D, and a long option --property with foo=bar. Create a new Options instance and construct two Option objects using the Option builder pattern: first, build optionD with the short name D, configure it with a value separator, set numberOfArgs to 2, and enable optionalArg; second, build optionProperty with a value separator, numberOfArgs set to 2, and longOpt set to property. Add both options to the Options instance using addOption. Instantiate a GnuParser and call its parse method with the options and arguments array to obtain a CommandLine instance. Invoke getOptionProperties on the CommandLine instance, passing optionD as the parameter, to retrieve a Properties object. Assert that the returned Properties object is not null with the message null properties. Assert that the Properties size equals 4 with a descriptive message including the properties content. Verify individual property values by asserting that param1 maps to value1, param2 maps to value2, param3 maps to true, and param4 maps to value4, each with descriptive assertion messages. Finally, assert that calling getOptionProperties with optionProperty and then getProperty with foo returns bar, validating the long format property handling. The test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that a command line parser can correctly process a short option that accepts a value argument. Initialize a command line parser and configure it with several options including one short option that can accept an optional argument with a specific parameter name. Create an input array containing a short option flag followed by a file path value. Parse the input array using the configured parser and options to generate a parsed command line result. Assert that the parsed result correctly retrieves the expected file path value when queried for the specific option, and verify that an unrelated option is not present in the parsed results. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions.

This test validates the consistency of the MurmurHash3 128-bit hash function when processing string data through different input pathways. Initialize a fixed seed value and define parameters for generating random Unicode strings with lengths between 1 and 10 characters, drawing from the full Unicode character set of approximately 112,956 code points. Execute a loop one thousand times, where each iteration generates a random string by selecting random Unicode code points and converting them to characters using the appropriate character encoding methods. For each generated string, obtain its UTF-8 byte representation using string utilities, then compute the 128-bit hash using the MurmurHash3 algorithm with both the byte array representation (including offset, length, and seed parameters) and the string representation directly. Assert that both hash computations produce identical results by comparing the resulting long arrays element-wise. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that hash computation produces consistent results when processing the same string data through different input formats. Initialize a fixed seed value and define parameters for generating random Unicode strings with lengths between one and ten characters, drawing from the full Unicode character set. Execute a loop one thousand times, where each iteration generates a random string by selecting random Unicode code points and converting them to characters. For each generated string, obtain its byte representation using UTF-8 encoding, then compute a 128-bit hash using both the byte array format and the string format directly. Assert that both hash computations produce identical results, ensuring the hashing algorithm maintains consistency regardless of the input data format. This validation spans multiple randomly generated inputs to verify robustness across diverse string content. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions.

This test validates that the Crypt class uses the SHA-512 algorithm variant by default when no salt is provided or when a null salt is explicitly passed. Initialize a test method annotated with @Test that exercises the default cryptographic behavior of the Crypt utility class. Call the crypt method from the Crypt class with the string literal "secret" as the only parameter, then assert that the returned encrypted string starts with the prefix "$6$" using assertTrue, which indicates the SHA-512 crypt algorithm variant is being used. Next, call the same crypt method again with "secret" as the first parameter and null as the second parameter representing an explicitly null salt, then assert using assertTrue that this result also starts with "$6$" to verify that both scenarios produce the same default algorithm selection. The test ensures that when salt generation is left to the implementation, the system consistently defaults to the SHA-512 variant rather than other available crypt algorithms like MD5 or SHA-256, providing predictable cryptographic behavior for applications that rely on default salt generation. This testing approach uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the command-line usage formatting functionality when a custom long option separator is configured, specifically testing how the HelpFormatter class generates usage strings with equals signs separating long options from their argument placeholders. Initialize a new Options instance and add three command-line options: first, add a short option "f" with argument requirement set to true and description "the file" using the addOption method; second, create an option using Option builder with short option "s", long option "size", description "the size", argument requirement enabled, and argument name "SIZE", then add it to the options; third, build another option with only long option "age", description "the age", and argument requirement, adding it to the options as well. Create a new HelpFormatter instance and configure it by calling setLongOptSeparator with the string "=" to specify that long options should be separated from their arguments using equals signs instead of the default space. Initialize a StringWriter to capture the formatted output, then call the printUsage method on the formatter, passing a new PrintWriter wrapping the StringWriter, width of 80 characters, command name "create", and the configured options. Assert that the trimmed string representation of the StringWriter output equals exactly "usage: create [--age=<arg>] [-f <arg>] [-s <SIZE>]", validating that the formatter correctly applies the custom separator to long options while maintaining proper formatting for short options and argument placeholders. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the hexadecimal encoding functionality when processing empty byte buffers. Initialize an empty byte buffer with zero capacity using a buffer allocation helper method. Call the static hex encoding method on this empty buffer and assert that it returns an empty character array. Next, create a new hex encoder instance and invoke its encode method on the same empty buffer, asserting that it produces an empty byte array. Both assertions verify that the encoding operations correctly handle edge cases with no input data by returning appropriately empty results. This test uses JUnit as the testing framework.

This test validates that hexadecimal encoding functionality correctly handles empty input data by producing empty output. Initialize an empty byte buffer with zero capacity, then invoke the static hexadecimal encoding method to convert the empty buffer and assert that it returns an empty character array. Next, create a new hexadecimal encoder instance and call its encoding method on the same empty buffer, asserting that it produces an empty byte array. The test confirms that both encoding approaches consistently handle edge cases where no data is provided for conversion. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the command line parsing functionality for short options with values by initializing a default parser and creating an options configuration with various option definitions including a short option that accepts arguments. Initialize a command line parser and configure it with options where one option accepts a single argument with an optional value, and several boolean flag options. Create a string array containing a short option flag followed by a file path value as separate elements. Parse the command line arguments using the parser with the configured options to produce a command line object. Assert that the parsed command line correctly retrieves the file path value when queried for the specific option, and verify that an unrelated boolean option is not present in the parsed results. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the parsing and retrieval of command line options with various data types using a pattern-based option configuration. Initialize a command line options configuration using a pattern string that defines multiple option types including strings, objects, booleans, files, classes, numbers, URLs, and dates. Create an expected date value and format it using a standard date formatter to ensure consistent time zone handling. Construct a command line argument array containing flags and their corresponding values, including a string value, a class name, a file path, another class name, a numeric value, a URL, and the formatted date string. Parse the command line arguments using a parser to generate a command line representation. Verify that each option can be retrieved correctly by asserting that string options return their expected values, object options are properly instantiated as the correct types, boolean flags reflect their presence or absence, file options create appropriate file objects, class options resolve to the correct class types, numeric options parse to the expected numeric values, and URL options construct valid URL objects. Additionally, validate that the same options can be accessed using character-based method calls to ensure API consistency. Confirm that date options are parsed back to the original expected date value, and verify that unsupported operations throw the appropriate exceptions. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the performance and reliability of phonetic encoding when processing progressively longer text segments. Initialize a phonetic encoder configured for generic name processing with approximate matching rules. Define a lengthy text phrase containing concatenated words without spaces. Iteratively encode substrings of increasing length, starting from the first character and extending one character at a time until the entire phrase is processed, ensuring the encoding functionality handles varying input sizes without errors or performance degradation. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the hexadecimal encoding functionality when processing empty byte buffers, specifically testing that both static and instance methods of the Hex class correctly handle zero-capacity buffers and return empty arrays. Initialize the test by using a helper method allocate that creates a ByteBuffer with zero capacity by calling ByteBuffer.allocate with a parameter of 0, which returns an empty ByteBuffer instance. Call the static method encodeHex on the Hex class, passing the empty ByteBuffer as an argument, and assert using assertArrayEquals that the result equals a new character array of length 0, validating that the static encoding method properly handles empty input by returning an empty character array. Next, create a new instance of the Hex class and call its instance method encode with the same empty ByteBuffer created by the allocate helper method, then assert using assertArrayEquals that the returned result equals a new byte array of length 0, confirming that the instance encoding method also correctly processes empty buffers by returning an empty byte array. The test uses the @Test annotation and employs JUnit testing framework for the assertion methods.

This test validates the performance and stability of the Beider-Morse encoder when processing progressively longer string inputs. Initialize a Beider-Morse encoder configured with generic name type and approximate rule type settings through the helper method. Define a test phrase containing a long concatenated string of words without spaces. Execute a loop that iterates from 1 to the full length of the phrase, where each iteration calls the encode method on a substring starting from the beginning and extending to the current loop index, effectively testing the encoder with inputs of increasing length from single characters up to the complete phrase. The test ensures that the encoder can handle variable-length inputs without throwing exceptions during the encoding process, particularly focusing on performance characteristics as input size grows. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the binary-to-string decoding functionality of a binary codec system, specifically testing the decode method's ability to convert byte arrays into their corresponding binary string representations and verifying the accuracy through multiple assertion mechanisms. Initialize a byte array with a single element and systematically test decoding scenarios by creating byte arrays with progressively more bits set using bitwise OR operations with the test class fields BIT_0 through BIT_7, which are static final int fields representing individual bit positions. Begin with an empty byte array and call the helper method assertDecodeObject with the expected binary string representation "00000000", then progressively set individual bits by assigning combinations like BIT_0 for "00000001", BIT_0 OR BIT_1 for "00000011", continuing through all eight possible bit combinations up to all bits set requiring a byte cast for "11111111". Expand testing to two-byte arrays by creating byte arrays of length two and setting various bit combinations across both bytes, with the second byte representing higher-order bits and the first byte representing lower-order bits, testing combinations from "0000000011111111" through "1111111111111111". The helper method assertDecodeObject performs three distinct validation approaches: first calling the instance decode method with the expected string and comparing the decoded byte array result using assertEquals after converting both arrays to strings, second calling decode with the string converted to bytes using CHARSET_UTF8 (a static final Charset field of the test class), and third calling decode with the string converted to a character array, with special null handling for each approach. Complete the test by calling assertDecodeObject with an empty byte array and null expected value to validate null input handling. In the teardown method tearDown, set the instance field to null for cleanup. This test uses the Test annotation and employs standard assertion mechanisms for validation.

This test validates the performance and stability of phonetic encoding when processing progressively longer input strings. Initialize a phonetic encoder configured for generic name types with approximate matching rules. Create a test phrase containing the full alphabet repeated twice. Iteratively encode substrings of increasing length, starting from a single character and extending one character at a time until the entire phrase is processed, ensuring the encoding functionality handles varying input lengths without errors or performance degradation. The test uses JUnit framework.

This test validates that the MurmurHash3 hash algorithm produces consistent 128-bit hash values when processing the same string data through different input methods, specifically comparing byte array input versus direct string input to ensure hash computation equivalence. The test iterates one thousand times, each time generating a random Unicode string and computing its hash through both pathways to assert that the results are identical. Initialize a seed value of 104729 for the hash function, set minimum string size to 1 and maximum size to 11 characters, and define the Unicode code point range as 112956 to cover Unicode Standard Version 7.0 characters. Create a character array with capacity for the maximum possible string length accounting for surrogate pairs. For each iteration, use ThreadLocalRandom to generate a random string size between the minimum and maximum bounds, then populate the character array by generating random Unicode code points and converting them to characters using the Character toChars method, tracking the position as characters are added to handle variable-width Unicode encoding. Create a string from the populated character array using String copyValueOf with the actual character count. Convert the generated string to a UTF-8 byte array using StringUtils getBytesUtf8 method. Compute the 128-bit hash of the byte array using MurmurHash3 hash128 method with the byte array, starting offset of 0, the full byte array length, and the predefined seed. Compute the 128-bit hash of the original string directly using the overloaded MurmurHash3 hash128 method that accepts a string parameter. Assert that both hash results are equal using assertArrayEquals to validate that the hash128 method produces identical output regardless of whether the input is provided as a byte array or string. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates the parsing functionality of command line arguments where a short option is provided with an associated value, specifically testing the DefaultParser's ability to correctly extract and store option values from command line input. Initialize a DefaultParser instance and configure an Options object with four distinct options: create option "t1" using Option.builder with hasArg set to true, numberOfArgs set to 1, optionalArg set to true, and argName set to "t1_path", then create three additional boolean options "a", "b", and "last" using Option.builder with hasArg set to false, and add all four options to the Options instance. Create a string array containing two elements: "-t1" as the option flag and "path/to/my/db" as the option value. Call the parse method on the DefaultParser instance, passing the configured Options object and the string array as arguments, which returns a CommandLine object representing the parsed command line arguments. Assert that calling getOptionValue with argument "t1" on the CommandLine object returns exactly "path/to/my/db" to verify the option value was correctly parsed and stored. Assert that calling hasOption with argument "last" on the CommandLine object returns false to confirm that the "last" option was not present in the input arguments. This test uses the JUnit testing framework, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the text column formatting functionality that breaks text into properly aligned segments based on styling configurations. Initialize a text help formatting component with a string builder, then create a style configuration builder with a maximum width of ten characters, zero indentation, and zero left padding. Using a sample text phrase, call the column queue generation method with left alignment styling and verify the resulting queue contains the expected text segments broken at appropriate word boundaries. Clear the expected results and reconfigure the style for right alignment, then validate the queue generation produces right-aligned text segments with proper spacing. Reset again and test center alignment to ensure the text segments are appropriately centered within the specified width constraints. Finally, modify the style configuration to include right alignment with additional left padding and indentation values, then verify the column queue generation correctly applies these combined formatting rules to produce the expected padded and indented text segments. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the pattern option builder and command line parsing functionality by creating options from a pattern string and verifying that various option types are correctly parsed and converted. Initialize a pattern option builder with the pattern string "a:b@cde>f+n%t/m*z#" to create an options configuration that defines multiple option types including strings, objects, booleans, files, classes, numbers, URLs, and dates. Create an expected date object using the timestamp 1023400137000L and format it using a simple date format with pattern "EEE MMM dd HH:mm:ss zzz yyyy". Construct a command line arguments array containing flags and values such as "-c", "-a", "foo", "-b", "java.util.Vector", "-e", "build.xml", "-f", "java.util.Calendar", "-n", "4.5", "-t", "https://commons.apache.org", "-z" with the formatted date string, and "-m", "test*". Initialize a POSIX parser and parse the options with the arguments array to produce a command line object. Assert that option "a" returns the string value "foo" using both string and object retrieval methods, option "b" returns an empty Vector object, option "c" is present as a boolean flag while option "d" is not present, option "e" returns a File object for "build.xml", option "f" returns the Calendar class object, option "n" returns the Double value 4.5, option "t" returns a URL object for "https://commons.apache.org", and option "z" returns the expected date object. Repeat all assertions using character-based option access methods to verify the character delegation functionality works identically to string-based access. Verify that accessing option "m" throws an UnsupportedOperationException since file patterns are not yet supported. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the syntax formatting functionality for command-line option groups by verifying how grouped options are rendered into user-friendly syntax strings. Initialize a help formatter using a builder pattern, then create an option group containing multiple command-line options with various configurations including short options, long options, required flags, and argument specifications. Add seven different options to the group with combinations of single-character flags, long-form names, argument requirements, and custom argument names. Call the syntax formatting method on the formatter with the populated option group and assert that the returned string matches the expected bracketed format showing all available options with their argument placeholders. Modify the option group to mark it as required, then call the formatting method again and verify the output now displays the options without surrounding brackets to indicate the group is mandatory. Finally, test the edge case by calling the formatting method with an empty option group and confirm it returns an empty string. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the performance characteristics of the Beider-Morse encoder when processing progressively longer string inputs. Initialize a Beider-Morse encoder configured with generic name type and approximate rule type settings. Create a test phrase containing the complete lowercase alphabet repeated twice, totaling 52 characters. Execute a loop that iterates from 1 to the full length of the phrase, where each iteration calls the encode method on a substring starting from the beginning and extending to the current loop index, effectively testing encoding performance on strings of incrementally increasing length from 1 character up to the full 52-character phrase. The test exercises the encoder's ability to handle variable-length inputs and ensures no exceptions are thrown during the encoding process, particularly validating that the encoder can process both short single-character inputs and longer multi-character sequences without performance degradation or errors. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the text help appendable's column queue generation functionality across different text alignment configurations. Initialize a string builder and create a text help appendable instance using the builder. Define a sample text string containing "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" and create a text style builder with a maximum width of 10, zero indent, and zero left padding. Create an expected queue containing the anticipated text segments for left alignment, then call the column queue generation method with the sample text and the built text style, asserting that the result matches the expected left-aligned segments. Clear the expected queue and populate it with right-aligned text segments, modify the style builder to use right alignment, generate a new column queue, and assert the result matches the right-aligned expectations. Repeat this process for center alignment by clearing the expected queue, adding center-aligned segments, setting the style builder to center alignment, and asserting the generated queue matches the expected center-aligned output. Finally, test a more complex configuration by creating a new expected queue with right-aligned segments that include additional left padding and indentation, configure the style builder with right alignment, left padding of 5, and indent of 2, then generate the column queue and assert it matches the expected padded and indented segments. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the command line parsing functionality for options defined using pattern-based configuration, specifically testing how PatternOptionBuilder creates typed options and how CommandLineParser processes arguments with type conversion and validation. Initialize an Options instance by calling PatternOptionBuilder parsePattern method with the pattern string "a:b@cde>f+n%t/m*z#" which defines various option types including string, object, boolean, file, class, number, URL, and date options. Create a Date object with the timestamp 1023400137000L and format it using SimpleDateFormat with pattern "EEE MMM dd HH:mm:ss zzz yyyy" to ensure consistent date string representation across different environments. Construct a string array containing command line arguments with flags and values: "-c", "-a", "foo", "-b", "java.util.Vector", "-e", "build.xml", "-f", "java.util.Calendar", "-n", "4.5", "-t", "https://commons.apache.org", "-z" followed by the formatted date string, and "-m", "test*". Initialize a PosixParser instance and call its parse method with the options and arguments array to produce a CommandLine object. Assert that getOptionValue method with argument "a" returns "foo" with message "flag a", then assert getOptionObject method with "a" also returns "foo" with message "string flag a". Verify getOptionObject with "b" returns a new empty Vector with message "object flag b". Assert hasOption method returns true for "c" with message "boolean true flag c" and false for "d" with message "boolean false flag d". Confirm getOptionObject with "e" returns a File object for "build.xml" with message "file flag e", and getOptionObject with "f" returns Calendar.class with message "class flag f". Validate getOptionObject with "n" returns Double.valueOf(4.5) with message "number flag n" and getOptionObject with "t" returns a URL object for "https://commons.apache.org" with message "url flag t". Repeat all the same assertions using character-based method calls instead of string-based calls to test the character delegate methods of CommandLine. Assert that calling getOptionObject with 'm' throws UnsupportedOperationException since file patterns are not yet supported. Finally, assert that getOptionObject with 'z' returns the expectedDate object with message "date flag z". The test uses JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the encoding of byte arrays to string representations using various encoding methods and input scenarios. Initialize a base encoder with no line chunking, then prepare test data including a UTF-8 encoded text string, an empty byte array, a null reference, and a hexadecimal-decoded byte sequence representing binary data. Execute encoding operations using both instance methods and static utility methods to convert each byte array into its string representation, verifying that the standard encoding produces the expected base64 output for the text data, returns empty strings for empty input, returns null for null input, and correctly encodes the binary data with proper padding. Additionally, validate that the URL-safe encoding variant produces the expected output with modified characters for the binary data, replacing standard base64 characters with URL-safe alternatives and omitting padding. Assert that all encoding results match their expected string values across both standard and URL-safe encoding modes. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that encoding and decoding operations maintain data integrity across a range of small input sizes. Decode the encoded data back to its original form and assert that the decoded result exactly matches the original input data, ensuring the encoding and decoding process is reversible without data loss.
