This test validates the syntax option formatting functionality of a help formatter component when processing option groups containing command-line options with various configurations. Initialize a help formatter using its builder pattern, then create an option group and populate it with multiple options that have different characteristics including short options like "o" and "t", long options such as "one", "two", "three", "five", "six", and "sevem", some requiring arguments with custom argument names like "other", and some marked as required. Call the syntax options method on the help formatter with the populated option group and assert that the returned string matches the expected format "[-f | --five <other> | -o <arg> | -s <arg> | --six <other> | -t <other> | -th]" which represents the bracketed, pipe-separated list of formatted options. Modify the option group by setting its required flag to true, then call the syntax options method again and verify the output now excludes the outer brackets, producing "-f | --five <other> | -o <arg> | -s <arg> | --six <other> | -t <other> | -th". Finally, test the edge case by calling the syntax options method with an empty option group and assert that it returns an empty string. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the Base64 encoding and decoding functionality by performing round-trip conversions on randomly generated byte arrays of varying small sizes. Initialize a loop that iterates twelve times, creating byte arrays of incrementally increasing lengths from zero to eleven bytes. For each iteration, populate the byte array with random bytes using a random number generator, then encode the data using Base64 encoding functionality. Assert that the encoded result is valid Base64 data by checking its format compliance. Decode the Base64-encoded data back to its original byte array format and assert that the decoded result exactly matches the original input data using array equality comparison. The test uses a helper method to convert byte arrays to comma-separated string representations for assertion failure messages. This test uses standard JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the performance and functionality of the BeiderMorseEncoder when processing progressively longer substrings of a fixed input phrase to ensure the encoding mechanism can handle varying input lengths without errors. The test exercises the BeiderMorseEncoder's encode method with incremental substring inputs and verifies that no exceptions are thrown during the encoding process. Initialize a BeiderMorseEncoder instance using the helper method createGenericApproxEncoder, which creates a new BeiderMorseEncoder, calls setNameType with NameType.GENERIC to configure it for general name processing, calls setRuleType with RuleType.APPROX to enable approximate phonetic matching rules, and returns the configured encoder. Define a string phrase with the literal value "ItstheendoftheworldasweknowitandIfeelfine" to serve as the test input. Execute a for loop starting from index 1 and continuing through the full length of the phrase, where each iteration calls the encode method on the encoder with a substring of the phrase from index 0 to the current loop index i, effectively testing the encoder with progressively longer portions of the input string from single characters up to the complete phrase. The encode method processes the input string through the internal PhoneticEngine to generate Beider-Morse phonetic encodings, returning null for null inputs or delegating to the engine's encode method for valid string inputs. No explicit assertions are present in this test method, as it primarily serves as a performance and stability check to ensure the encoder can process various substring lengths without throwing exceptions, particularly the EncoderException that the method signature declares it may throw. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the bidirectional encoding and decoding functionality of Base64 operations for small data arrays ranging from zero to eleven bytes in length. The test iterates through twelve iterations where each iteration creates a byte array of increasing size starting from zero bytes, populates the array with random bytes using the getRandom method which accesses the random field of type Random from the test class, encodes the data using the Base64 encodeBase64 method, validates that the encoded result is proper Base64 format using the Base64 isBase64 method with a assertTrue assertion that includes the encoded string representation in the failure message, decodes the encoded data back to bytes using the Base64 decodeBase64 method, and finally asserts that the original and decoded byte arrays are identical using assertArrayEquals with a custom message that displays both arrays in comma-separated format via the toString helper method which iterates through byte array elements and concatenates them with commas between values. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation and assertion methods.

This test validates the performance and stability of the Beider-Morse phonetic encoding algorithm when processing progressively longer input strings, specifically testing the encode method of the BeiderMorseEncoder class to ensure it can handle varying input lengths without performance degradation or errors. Initialize a BeiderMorseEncoder instance using the helper method createGenericApproxEncoder, which creates a new BeiderMorseEncoder, sets its NameType to GENERIC via setNameType, sets its RuleType to APPROX via setRuleType, and returns the configured encoder optimized for general-purpose approximate phonetic matching. Define a test phrase containing the string "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz" which represents a doubled alphabet sequence of 52 characters total. Execute a loop that iterates from 1 to the full length of the phrase, where each iteration calls the encode method on the BeiderMorseEncoder with a substring of the phrase starting from index 0 and extending to the current loop index, effectively testing encoding performance on strings of incrementally increasing length from 1 character up to the full 52-character phrase. The encode method processes each input string through the Beider-Morse phonetic encoding algorithm, which analyzes the input for language patterns, converts it to phonetic representations, and applies cross-linguistic phonetic rules to produce encoded output, with the APPROX rule type allowing for broader phonetic interpretations and the GENERIC name type providing general-purpose encoding rather than optimization for specific ethnic naming patterns. This test method is annotated with @Test and uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the text column formatting functionality of a help system that breaks text into properly aligned and padded column segments for display purposes. The test exercises the TextHelpAppendable class's makeColumnQueue method across multiple text alignment scenarios and verifies that text is correctly segmented, padded, and aligned according to specified style configurations. Initialize a StringBuilder and create a TextHelpAppendable instance with the StringBuilder as its underlying appendable target. Define the input text as "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" and create a TextStyle Builder configured with a maximum width of 10, indent of 0, and left padding of 0. Construct a LinkedList queue containing the expected left-aligned segments: "The quick ", "brown fox ", "jumps over", "the lazy ", and "dog ". Call the makeColumnQueue method on the TextHelpAppendable instance with the input text and the built TextStyle, then assert that the returned queue equals the expected queue with the message "left aligned failed". Clear the expected queue and populate it with right-aligned segments: " The quick", " brown fox", "jumps over", " the lazy", and " dog". Configure the style builder to use RIGHT alignment by calling setAlignment with TextStyle.Alignment.RIGHT, then call makeColumnQueue again and assert equality with the message "right aligned failed". Clear the expected queue once more and add center-aligned segments: "The quick ", "brown fox ", "jumps over", " the lazy ", and " dog ". Set the style builder alignment to CENTER using TextStyle.Alignment.CENTER, invoke makeColumnQueue, and assert the result matches the expected queue with the message "center aligned failed". Create a new LinkedList with segments for a more complex configuration: " The quick", " brown", " fox", " jumps", " over the", and " lazy dog". Configure the style builder with RIGHT alignment, left padding of 5, and indent of 2 using chained calls to setAlignment, setLeftPad, and setIndent, then call makeColumnQueue and assert the result equals the expected queue with the message "right aligned failed". This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the Base64 encoder's string conversion functionality by initializing a Base64 instance with zero line length and preparing four different byte arrays: a UTF-8 encoded "Hello World" string, an empty byte array, a null reference, and a hexadecimal-decoded UUID byte sequence. The test exercises both instance and static encoding methods by calling the encoder's string conversion method on each byte array and comparing the results with expected Base64-encoded strings using equality assertions. For the "Hello World" bytes, it verifies the output matches "SGVsbG8gV29ybGQ=" for both instance and static methods, confirms empty arrays produce empty strings, validates null inputs return null values, and checks the UUID bytes encode to "K/fMJwH+Q5e0nr7tWsxwkA==" in standard format and "K_fMJwH-Q5e0nr7tWsxwkA" in URL-safe format. The assertions verify that the encoding produces consistent results between instance and static method calls, handles edge cases like null and empty inputs appropriately, and correctly applies URL-safe character substitutions when requested. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality for extracting property-style key-value pairs from command line options that use value separators. Initialize a command line argument array containing various property-style options including short options with parameters, options without values, standalone separator flags, and long options with property syntax. Create an options configuration that defines two options: one short option that accepts optional arguments with a value separator and supports multiple arguments, and one long option with similar capabilities. Use a command line parser to process the arguments against the defined options configuration. Retrieve the properties associated with the short option and verify that the returned properties collection is not null and contains exactly four key-value pairs. Assert that each property key maps to its expected value, including cases where missing values default to true for boolean flags. Additionally, verify that the long option property extraction works correctly by checking that its property collection contains the expected key-value mapping. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the command line parser's ability to extract option properties from parsed arguments that use value separators. Initialize a string array containing command line arguments with various property-style options including "-Dparam1=value1", "-Dparam2=value2", "-Dparam3", "-Dparam4=value4", "-D", "--property", and "foo=bar". Create an options configuration object and add two option definitions: one for the short option "D" with value separator enabled, optional arguments, and accepting two arguments, and another for the long option "property" with similar configuration but no short name. Instantiate a GNU parser and parse the arguments against the options configuration to produce a command line object. Call the get option properties method on the command line object with the option name "D" to retrieve a properties object containing the parsed key-value pairs. Assert that the returned properties object is not null, contains exactly four properties, and verify each individual property value: "param1" should equal "value1", "param2" should equal "value2", "param3" should equal "true" (indicating a boolean flag), and "param4" should equal "value4". Additionally, verify that calling get option properties with "property" returns a properties object where the key "foo" maps to the value "bar". This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the syntax option formatting functionality for command-line option groups, specifically testing how the HelpFormatter class converts OptionGroup instances into properly formatted syntax strings that represent mutually exclusive command-line options. Initialize a HelpFormatter instance using the builder method to get a default formatter configuration, then create an OptionGroup and populate it with seven distinct Option instances using the Option builder pattern, where the first option has short option "o", long option "one", and accepts an argument, the second has short option "t", long option "two", is required, accepts an argument with argument name "other", the third has short option "th", long option "three", is required with argument name "other", the fourth has short option "f" with argument name "other", the fifth has only long option "five" with an argument and argument name "other", the sixth has only long option "six", is required, accepts an argument with argument name "other", and the seventh has short option "s", long option "sevem", and accepts an argument. Call the toSyntaxOptions method on the HelpFormatter instance with the populated OptionGroup and assert that it equals the expected string "[-f | --five <other> | -o <arg> | -s <arg> | --six <other> | -t <other> | -th]" which represents the options in square brackets indicating they are mutually exclusive. Modify the OptionGroup by calling setRequired with true to make the entire group required, then call toSyntaxOptions again and assert that it equals "-f | --five <other> | -o <arg> | -s <arg> | --six <other> | -t <other> | -th" without the square brackets since required option groups are not enclosed in brackets. Finally, call toSyntaxOptions with a new empty OptionGroup instance and assert that it returns an empty string with the assertion message "empty group should return empty string" to verify that empty option groups produce no syntax output. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that a phonetic encoding system correctly generates sound-alike variations for Ashkenazi names under different configuration scenarios. Initialize a configuration map and set the name type to Ashkenazi, then call the encoding functionality with concatenation enabled on a sample name and assert that the output contains the expected pipe-delimited phonetic variations. Modify the configuration to use exact rule matching and verify that the encoding produces a more restrictive set of variations for both simple and apostrophe-containing names. Further constrain the configuration by specifying a limited language set and confirm that the output is filtered to only relevant phonetic matches, while also verifying that numeric input produces empty results. Repeat the entire validation sequence with concatenation disabled to ensure consistent behavior regardless of this setting. Switch the rule type to approximate matching and validate that the encoding generates broader phonetic variations, again testing with both concatenation settings, language constraints, and numeric input edge cases. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions.

This test validates the functionality of deprecated command line option handling and notification mechanisms. Initialize a command line parser with a custom deprecated option handler that collects deprecated options into a set. Create three command line options: two that are marked as deprecated with different deprecation attributes including removal flags and version information, and one regular non-deprecated option. Configure an options collection with all three options and parse a command line containing flags for all three options. Verify that the parser correctly identifies and processes all three options as present in the parsed command line. Assert that the deprecated option handler was triggered only for the two deprecated options and not for the regular option, confirming that the deprecation detection and notification system works properly. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that hexadecimal encoding of byte data produces uppercase output when configured appropriately. Convert a simple text string into its byte representation using UTF-8 encoding, then define the expected uppercase hexadecimal representation of that byte data. Perform hexadecimal encoding on the byte array using the default configuration and verify that the result does not match the expected uppercase format. Execute the encoding again with an explicit flag set to true and confirm it still does not produce the expected uppercase output. Finally, perform the encoding with the flag set to false and assert that the resulting hexadecimal string exactly matches the expected uppercase format, demonstrating that the false flag parameter enables uppercase hexadecimal output. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a command line parser can correctly handle concatenated short options where multiple single-character flags are combined into a single argument. Initialize a parser and configure it with several command line options including one that accepts an optional argument and several boolean flags. Parse a command line input containing a short option with an optional argument followed by a concatenated string of multiple boolean flags. Verify that the parser correctly identifies the presence of the individual options from the concatenated string, confirms that the optional argument option is recognized but has no value assigned, and ensures that options not present in the input are correctly reported as absent. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the phonetic encoding functionality of a Beider-Morse phonetic engine specifically configured for Ashkenazi name processing across different rule types and concatenation settings. Initialize a map to hold configuration parameters and set the name type to Ashkenazi, then call the encode method with concatenation enabled and the input "Angelo" to assert that the output matches a pipe-delimited string of phonetic variants. Configure the rule type to exact matching and verify that encoding "Angelo" produces a more restricted set of phonetic alternatives, then test encoding "D'Angelo" to confirm proper handling of names with apostrophes. Add a language set restriction to Italian, Greek, and Spanish languages and assert that the phonetic output is further filtered to only relevant variants for those languages, then verify that encoding a numeric string returns an empty result. Repeat the entire sequence of assertions with concatenation disabled to ensure consistent behavior regardless of the concatenation setting. Execute another complete test cycle using approximate rule matching instead of exact matching, verifying that the approximate rules produce the expected broader set of phonetic variants for both simple and apostrophe-containing names, and confirm that language set filtering and numeric input handling work consistently across all configuration combinations. The testing is performed using JUnit framework.

This test validates that phonetic encoding can handle exceptionally long English surnames within reasonable time constraints. Initialize a phonetic encoder configured for generic name processing with approximate matching rules. Execute the encoding operation on a very long Scottish surname and assert that the operation completes within a ten-second timeout period. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a command line parser with a deprecated option handler that collects deprecated options into a hash set, then create three option instances where the first option is marked as deprecated with basic deprecation, the second option is deprecated with detailed attributes including removal flag set to true, version "1.0", and description "Do this instead.", and the third option is a regular non-deprecated option with identifier "a". Parse a command line containing all three options using arguments "-d1", "-d2", and "-a", then verify that all options are present in the parsed command line by asserting that each option exists. Additionally, confirm that the deprecated handler was properly triggered by asserting that the handler's collection contains the first two deprecated options but does not contain the third non-deprecated option. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the Base64 encoding functionality for converting byte arrays to their string representations using both instance and static methods across various input scenarios. Initialize a Base64 instance with a line length of 0 to disable chunking, then create four test byte arrays: convert the string "Hello World" to UTF-8 bytes using StringUtils getBytesUtf8 method, create an empty byte array, set a null byte array reference, and decode the hexadecimal string "2bf7cc2701fe4397b49ebeed5acc7090" into bytes using Hex decodeHex method. Call the Base64 instance's encodeToString method on the "Hello World" bytes and assert it equals "SGVsbG8gV29ybGQ=" with the message "byteToString Hello World", then call the static Base64 encodeBase64String method on the same bytes and assert it produces the identical result with message "byteToString static Hello World". Call encodeToString on the empty byte array and assert it returns an empty string with message "byteToString \"\"", then verify the static encodeBase64String method produces the same empty string result with message "byteToString static \"\"". Call encodeToString on the null byte array and assert it returns null with message "byteToString null", then verify the static encodeBase64String method also returns null with message "byteToString static null". Call encodeToString on the decoded hex bytes and assert it equals "K/fMJwH+Q5e0nr7tWsxwkA==" with message "byteToString UUID", then verify the static encodeBase64String method produces the identical result with message "byteToString static UUID". Finally, call the static Base64 encodeBase64URLSafeString method on the same decoded hex bytes and assert it equals "K_fMJwH-Q5e0nr7tWsxwkA" with message "byteToString static-url-safe UUID", demonstrating the URL-safe encoding variant that replaces plus and slash characters with dash and underscore respectively while omitting padding. The test uses JUnit 5 testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the functionality of parsing command-line arguments with property-style options and extracting them as Properties objects from a CommandLine instance. Initialize a string array named args containing seven elements: "-Dparam1=value1", "-Dparam2=value2", "-Dparam3", "-Dparam4=value4", "-D", "--property", and "foo=bar". Create a new Options instance and add two options to it using the Option builder pattern - first, build an option with short name "D" that has a value separator, optional arguments set to true, and accepts up to 2 arguments, then add a second option with a value separator, 2 arguments, and long option name "property". Instantiate a GnuParser and call its parse method with the options and args array to produce a CommandLine instance. Call the getOptionProperties method on the CommandLine with argument "D" to retrieve a Properties object, then assert that the returned properties object is not null with message "null properties". Assert that the properties size equals 4 with message "number of properties in " plus the properties string representation. Verify individual property values by asserting that getProperty with "param1" returns "value1" with message "property 1", getProperty with "param2" returns "value2" with message "property 2", getProperty with "param3" returns "true" with message "property 3", and getProperty with "param4" returns "value4" with message "property 4". Finally, assert that calling getOptionProperties on the CommandLine with "property" and then getProperty with "foo" returns "bar" with message "property with long format". This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the performance characteristics of a Beider-Morse phonetic encoder when processing a particularly long English surname. Initialize a Beider-Morse encoder configured with generic name type and approximate rule type settings through a helper method that creates and configures the encoder instance. Execute the encode method on the encoder using the lengthy Scottish surname "MacGhilleseatheanaich" as input, ensuring that this phonetic encoding operation completes within a timeout constraint of 10 seconds. Assert that the encoding process finishes within the specified time limit to verify that the encoder can handle exceptionally long surnames without experiencing performance degradation or hanging. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the hexadecimal encoding functionality of a utility class by converting a UTF-8 byte array representation of a text string into hexadecimal format with different case options. Initialize a byte array by converting the string "Hello World" to UTF-8 encoding using a string utility method, then define the expected uppercase hexadecimal representation as "48656C6C6F20576F726C64". Call the hex encoding method three times with different parameters: first with only the byte array (using default case), then with the byte array and a true boolean parameter for uppercase, and finally with the byte array and a false boolean parameter for lowercase. Convert each resulting character array to a string and assert that the first two calls do not equal the expected uppercase string, while the third call with the false parameter does equal the expected uppercase string, confirming that the false parameter produces uppercase hexadecimal output. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a command line parser and create an options configuration with four distinct options: a "t1" option that accepts an optional argument with the argument name "t1_path", and three boolean options "a", "b", and "last" that do not accept arguments. Parse a string array containing the concatenated short options "-t1" and "-ab" using the parser's parse method with the configured options. Verify that the resulting command line object correctly identifies the presence of options "t1", "a", and "b" by asserting that each returns true when checked for existence, confirm that the "t1" option has no associated value by asserting its option value is null, and ensure that the "last" option is not present by asserting it returns false when checked. This test validates the parser's ability to handle concatenated short options where multiple single-character flags are combined in a single argument string while maintaining proper option recognition and value assignment. The test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the hexadecimal encoding functionality for byte arrays, specifically testing that the Hex class can properly encode UTF-8 byte data into uppercase hexadecimal representation with correct case sensitivity control. Initialize a byte array by calling StringUtils getBytesUtf8 method with the string literal "Hello World" to convert the text into UTF-8 encoded bytes, then define the expected uppercase hexadecimal string as "48656C6C6F20576F726C64" which represents the hexadecimal encoding of "Hello World" in uppercase format. Call the Hex encodeHex method with the byte array using the default parameters and store the resulting character array, then assert that the string representation of this character array does not equal the expected uppercase string using assertNotEquals to verify that the default behavior produces lowercase hexadecimal. Next, call Hex encodeHex again with the byte array and a boolean parameter set to true, then assert that this result also does not equal the expected uppercase string using assertNotEquals to confirm that the true parameter still produces lowercase output. Finally, call Hex encodeHex with the byte array and a boolean parameter set to false, then assert that the string representation of this character array equals the expected uppercase hexadecimal string using assertEquals to validate that the false parameter produces the desired uppercase hexadecimal encoding. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation and assertion methods.

This test validates the encoding and decoding behavior of quoted-printable text processing when handling space characters with different configuration settings. Initialize a codec for quoted-printable encoding and set the blank encoding configuration to false, then encode a plain text string containing spaces and assert that the encoded result preserves spaces in their original form. Next, change the blank encoding configuration to true and encode the same plain text again, asserting that the encoded result now transforms spaces into underscores. Proceed to decode both encoded versions back to their original form and assert that both decoding operations successfully restore the original plain text string, demonstrating that the codec can properly handle both encoding formats during decoding regardless of the current configuration setting. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the deprecated option handling functionality in command-line parsing by ensuring that deprecated options trigger a handler when parsed and that the handler correctly identifies which options are deprecated. Initialize a HashSet to serve as a handler collection, then create a DefaultParser instance using the builder pattern with setDeprecatedHandler configured to add deprecated options to the handler set. Create three Option instances using the Option builder: first, build an option with option name "d1" and mark it as deprecated using the deprecated method; second, build an option with option name "d2" and configure it as deprecated with detailed DeprecatedAttributes including setForRemoval set to true, setSince set to "1.0", and setDescription set to "Do this instead."; third, build a non-deprecated option with option name "a". Parse the command line arguments using the parser's parse method, passing a new Options instance with all three options added and a String array containing the arguments "-d1", "-d2", and "-a". After parsing, assert that the CommandLine contains all three options by calling hasOption with each option's getOpt method and verifying each returns true using assertTrue. Validate the deprecated handler functionality by asserting that the handler set contains the first deprecated option using assertTrue with handler.contains, assert that it contains the second deprecated option using assertTrue with handler.contains, and confirm that it does not contain the non-deprecated option using assertFalse with handler.contains. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the sorting functionality for command-line options within a help formatting system. Initialize a collection of command-line options with various short and long names, including options with identifiers "a", "b", and one with only a long option "COpt", each configured to accept arguments and include descriptive text. Create a help formatter using the default builder configuration, then establish an expected ordering list by retrieving the options in a specific sequence. Verify that the formatter's sort method returns the options in the expected default alphabetical order by comparing the sorted result against the predefined expected list. Modify the expected ordering by swapping the first and last elements to reflect reverse alphabetical sorting, then create a new help formatter configured with a reversed comparator. Assert that this reversed formatter produces the modified expected ordering when sorting the same options. Additionally, validate edge cases by confirming that sorting empty collections returns empty results, and that sorting null iterables or null option collections also returns empty lists rather than throwing exceptions. The test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the Q codec's encoding and decoding functionality with different blank space handling configurations. Initialize a plain text string containing spaces, along with two expected encoded representations - one with spaces preserved and another with spaces converted to underscores. Create a Q codec instance and configure it to not encode blanks, then encode the plain text and assert that the result matches the first expected encoded string with preserved spaces. Reconfigure the codec to encode blanks as underscores, encode the same plain text again, and verify the output matches the second expected encoded string with underscores replacing spaces. Decode both encoded representations back to plain text and assert that each decoding operation correctly recovers the original string, demonstrating bidirectional conversion capability regardless of the blank encoding setting. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions and test execution.

This test validates the command line parser's ability to correctly handle concatenated short options where multiple single-character flags are combined into a single argument. Initialize a DefaultParser instance as the parser field of the test class, then create four Option objects using the Option builder pattern: option t1 with argument name t1_path that has one argument, is optional, and accepts arguments; option a without arguments; option b without arguments; and option last without arguments, then add all four options to an Options instance as the options field of the test class. Create a string array containing two elements: -t1 and -ab, where -ab represents the concatenated short options a and b. Call the parse method on the parser with the options and the concatenated short options array to produce a CommandLine instance. Assert that the CommandLine has option t1 using assertTrue with hasOption method, then assert that the option value for t1 is null using assertNull with getOptionValue method to verify the optional argument was not provided. Assert that the CommandLine has option a using assertTrue with hasOption method, then assert that the CommandLine has option b using assertTrue with hasOption method to confirm both concatenated options were parsed correctly. Finally, assert that the CommandLine does not have option last using assertFalse with hasOption method to verify only the specified options were processed. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the phonetic encoding functionality of the Beider-Morse algorithm specifically for Ashkenazi Jewish names, ensuring that various combinations of rule types, concatenation settings, and language sets produce the expected encoded outputs. The test exercises the encode helper method with different parameter configurations and asserts that the resulting phonetic encodings match predetermined expected values for specific input names. Initialize a TreeMap to store configuration arguments and set the nameType parameter to ASHKENAZI, then call the encode helper method with concatenation enabled and the input Angelo, asserting that the result equals the pipe-delimited string containing multiple phonetic variations like YngYlo, Yngilo, angYlo, and others. Add the ruleType parameter with value EXACT and verify that encode produces a more restricted set of variations including andZelo, angelo, anhelo, and anxelo for the same input, then test the name D'Angelo which should yield dandZelo, dangelo, danhelo, and danxelo. Configure the languageSet parameter to italian,greek,spanish and assert that the encoding becomes further refined to only angelo and anxelo for Angelo, while also verifying that numeric input 1234 returns an empty string. Repeat the entire sequence with concatenation disabled by calling encode with false as the second parameter, confirming identical results for all test cases. Reset the configuration map and test the APPROX rule type with concatenation enabled, verifying that Angelo produces the same comprehensive set of variations as the initial test, while D'Angelo generates an expanded set prefixed with d including dYngYlo, dYngilo, dangYlo, and others. Apply the language set restriction again and confirm the filtered results of angilo, anxilo, ongilo, and onxilo for Angelo. Execute the final test sequence with APPROX rule type and concatenation disabled, validating identical outputs to the concatenation-enabled APPROX tests. The encode helper method constructs a PhoneticEngine using the specified NameType and RuleType from the arguments map with GENERIC and APPROX as defaults, processes the languageSet parameter by splitting comma-separated values using the COMMA_PATTERN field of the test class, and returns the phonetic encoding either with or without language set constraints depending on the configuration. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a command line options container and add three options: a short option with argument requirement, a builder-constructed option with both short and long forms plus argument specifications, and a long-only option with argument capability. Create a help formatter instance and verify its default long option separator matches the expected default value. Modify the formatter's long option separator to an equals sign and confirm the change took effect. Initialize a string writer to capture output, then invoke the formatter's help printing method with specific parameters including line width of 80, command name "create", header text, the options container, padding values of 2, and footer text. Assert that the generated help output matches the expected format showing the modified separator being used between long options and their argument placeholders. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a base32 hexadecimal encoder properly rejects invalid input strings by throwing exceptions when encountering impossible character sequences. Initialize a base32 encoder configured for hexadecimal encoding with strict decoding policy, then attempt to decode each string from a predefined collection of impossible test cases, asserting that each decode operation throws an illegal argument exception. Repeat this validation process using alternative encoder configurations created through a builder pattern, including scenarios where encoding and decoding table settings are overridden multiple times with the final settings taking precedence. The test ensures that the encoder maintains data integrity by refusing to process malformed input rather than producing incorrect output. This test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates that base64 decoding correctly handles trailing bits when exactly 12 bits are encoded in the final characters. Initialize a strict base64 decoder that enforces proper encoding standards and verify its strict decoding policy, then create a lenient decoder for comparison that allows invalid encodings. Construct encoded byte arrays representing 12-bit trailing scenarios by filling initial positions with valid base64 characters and padding the remainder, then calculate the number of bits that would be discarded and determine which trailing character combinations are invalid. Iterate through all possible final characters in the encoded sequence, and for invalid combinations where lower bits are improperly set, assert that the strict decoder throws an illegal argument exception while the lenient decoder successfully processes the data but produces different output when re-encoded. For valid trailing character combinations, verify that the strict decoder successfully decodes the data, confirm that the final decoded byte matches the expected bit pattern after accounting for discarded bits, and validate that re-encoding the decoded result produces the original encoded array. This testing uses JUnit framework.

This test validates the sorting functionality of a help formatter component used for command-line option processing. Initialize an options collection and add three option instances using the option builder pattern, where the first option has short name "a" and long name "optA" with an argument and description "The description of A", the second has short name "b" and long name "BOpt" with an argument and description "B description", and the third has only long name "COpt" with an argument and description "A COpt description". Create a help formatter instance using the builder pattern with default settings. Construct an expected list containing the options retrieved from the options collection in the order "a", "b", "COpt". Call the sort method on the help formatter with the options collection and assert that the returned list equals the expected list, verifying default alphabetical sorting behavior. Modify the expected list by swapping the first and third elements so the order becomes "COpt", "b", "a". Create a new help formatter instance using the builder pattern but configure it with a reversed default comparator. Call the sort method again with the options collection and assert that the returned list matches the modified expected list, confirming reversed sorting functionality. Finally, test edge cases by calling the sort method with an empty collection, a null iterable, and null options, asserting that each returns an empty list with size zero. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the performance of the Beider-Morse phonetic encoding algorithm when processing the longest English surname, specifically ensuring that encoding operations complete within acceptable time limits for complex linguistic inputs. The test creates a BeiderMorseEncoder instance configured for generic name types and approximate rule matching, then verifies that the encode method can process the string "MacGhilleseatheanaich" within a 10-second timeout constraint. Initialize a BeiderMorseEncoder using the helper method createGenericApproxEncoder, which constructs a new BeiderMorseEncoder instance, calls setNameType with NameType.GENERIC to configure it for general name processing rather than specific Jewish surname optimization, and calls setRuleType with RuleType.APPROX to enable approximate phonetic matching that considers a wider range of possible pronunciations. Execute an assertTimeout assertion with a Duration of 10000 milliseconds that wraps a lambda expression calling the encode method on the configured encoder with the input string "MacGhilleseatheanaich", which represents one of the longest documented English surnames. The encode method processes the input string through the Beider-Morse phonetic algorithm, first determining the likely language origin, then converting it to phonetic representations, and finally producing a standardized phonetic encoding that may include multiple possible pronunciations separated by pipe characters. The timeout assertion validates that this complex phonetic encoding operation completes within the specified time limit, ensuring the algorithm performs adequately even with exceptionally long and complex surname inputs. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the customization of long option separators in help text formatting. Initialize a command line options configuration and add three options: a short option with an argument, a long option with both short and long forms that accepts a size argument, and a long-only option that accepts an age argument. Create a help formatter and verify that it initially uses the default long option separator by checking its current value. Modify the formatter to use an equals sign as the separator instead of the default, then confirm this change by retrieving and verifying the new separator value. Generate help text by writing it to a string output stream using the formatter with specified width, command name, header text, the configured options, padding values, and footer text. Assert that the generated help output correctly displays the long options with the custom equals sign separator format, showing the age option as "--age=<arg>" and the size option as "-s,--size=<SIZE>" while maintaining proper formatting for all option descriptions and layout. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the syntax formatting capability for command-line options across various configurations. Initialize an option formatter from an option builder that creates options with different combinations of short names, long names, argument requirements, and custom argument names. For each configuration, create the option using the builder pattern with methods to set the short option, long option, argument requirements, required status, and argument names, then construct a formatter from that option and call the syntax formatting method to generate the display string. Assert that the output matches expected syntax patterns, verifying that optional options are wrapped in brackets, required options appear without brackets, argument placeholders use angle brackets with either default or custom names, multi-character short options are handled correctly, and long-only options display with double-dash prefixes. The test covers scenarios including optional arguments with default names, optional arguments with custom names, required arguments with custom names, required options without arguments, optional options without arguments, long-only options with arguments, required long options with arguments, and multi-character short options with arguments. This testing uses the JUnit framework.

This test validates the Base32 hexadecimal codec's ability to properly reject invalid input strings by throwing exceptions. Initialize a Base32 codec instance configured with hexadecimal encoding tables and strict decoding policy, then call a helper method that iterates through a predefined array of impossible Base32 hexadecimal test cases. For each impossible case string in the array, attempt to decode the invalid input using the codec's decode method and assert that an IllegalArgumentException is thrown. Repeat this validation process with additional Base32 codec instances created using a builder pattern, where the builder is configured with hexadecimal encoding enabled and strict decoding policy, including scenarios where conflicting settings are applied with the last configuration taking precedence. The test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the string representation functionality for command-line options with various deprecation states. Initialize an options container and add four different options: a standard option, a basic deprecated option, a deprecated option marked for removal with version and description details, and a deprecated option with long name and argument capabilities. Verify that the standard string representation for each option starts with the expected format prefix. Assert that the non-deprecated option does not produce a deprecation-specific string representation, while confirming that the basic deprecated option generates a simple deprecation message and the fully-detailed deprecated option produces a comprehensive removal notice including version and description information. Validate that all options can successfully generate both standard and deprecation-specific string representations without throwing exceptions and return non-null values. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the sorting functionality of the HelpFormatter class by testing how it orders command-line options and handles edge cases with null or empty collections. Initialize an Options instance and add three Option objects using the Option builder pattern: create option "a" with long option "optA", argument capability, and description "The description of A"; create option "b" with long option "BOpt", argument capability, and description "B description"; and create an option with only long option "COpt", argument capability, and description "A COpt description". Create a HelpFormatter instance using the HelpFormatter builder with default settings. Construct an expected list containing the options in the order they were added by retrieving each option from the Options instance using getOption with the respective option keys "a", "b", and "COpt". Call the sort method on the HelpFormatter instance passing the Options object and assert that the returned list equals the expected list, verifying that the default sorting maintains the original order. Modify the expected list by swapping the first and third elements so that "COpt" comes first and "a" comes last. Create a new HelpFormatter instance using the builder with a reversed comparator by calling setComparator with AbstractHelpFormatter.DEFAULT_COMPARATOR.reversed(). Call sort again with the same Options object and assert that the result matches the modified expected list, confirming that the reversed comparator properly reorders the options. Test edge cases by calling sort with an empty Collections list and asserting the returned list has size 0 with the message "empty colleciton should return empty list". Call sort with a null Iterable of Option type and assert the returned list has size 0 with the message "null iterable should return empty list". Call sort with a null Options object and assert the returned list has size 0 with the message "null Options should return empty list". This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that Base32 hex encoding properly rejects invalid input strings by throwing IllegalArgumentException exceptions when attempting to decode impossible cases. Initialize a Base32 codec instance using the constructor with parameters zero for line length, null for line separator, true for hex encoding, PAD_DEFAULT for padding, and STRICT for the CodecPolicy, then call the helper method testImpossibleCases with this codec and the BASE32HEX_IMPOSSIBLE_CASES array. The helper method iterates through each impossible case string in the provided array and asserts that calling the decode method on the codec with each impossible string throws an IllegalArgumentException using assertThrows. Additionally, create two more Base32 instances using the builder pattern: first by setting setHexEncodeTable to true and setDecodingPolicy to STRICT, then calling get to build the codec; second by demonstrating override behavior where setHexDecodeTable is called with false then true, setHexEncodeTable is called with false then true, and setDecodingPolicy is set to STRICT before calling get, with both builder-created codecs also being tested against the same impossible cases array using the same helper method that validates IllegalArgumentException is thrown for each decode attempt. The testing framework used is JUnit 5, identified by the @Test annotation and assertThrows method.

This test validates that base32 decoding behavior can be configured to either accept or reject invalid input data through different policy settings. Initialize a collection of problematic base32 encoded strings that represent impossible or invalid cases, then convert each string to its byte representation for processing. Create an output stream and configure a base32 decoder with default lenient settings, verify that strict decoding is disabled, then attempt to write the invalid encoded data and confirm that the operation completes successfully with output generated. Next, create a second output stream and configure another base32 decoder with strict policy enforcement, verify that strict decoding is enabled, then attempt to write the same invalid encoded data and assert that an illegal argument exception is thrown due to the strict validation rules rejecting the malformed input. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the help formatter's ability to customize the separator character used between long options and their argument values when generating help text for command-line applications. Initialize a new Options instance and configure it with three command-line options: add a short option "f" that accepts an argument with description "the file", create a complex option using Option builder with short name "s", long name "size", description "the size", argument requirement, and argument name "SIZE", and build another option with only long name "age", description "the age", and argument requirement. Create a new HelpFormatter instance and verify its initial long option separator matches the DEFAULT_LONG_OPT_SEPARATOR constant by calling getLongOptSeparator and asserting equality. Modify the formatter's separator to an equals sign by calling setLongOptSeparator with "=" as the parameter, then confirm this change by calling getLongOptSeparator again and asserting it equals "=". Initialize a StringWriter to capture the formatted output and invoke the printHelp method on the formatter with parameters including the StringWriter wrapped in a PrintWriter, width of 80 characters, command name "create", header text "header", the configured options, left padding of 2, description padding of 2, and footer text "footer". Assert that the generated help text in the StringWriter matches the expected format where long options use the equals separator, specifically verifying the output contains the usage line, header, option descriptions with "--age=<arg> the age", "-f <arg> the file", "-s,--size=<SIZE> the size", and footer, all separated by end-of-line characters. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the availability tracking functionality of a Base16 decoding stream when processing encoded data. Initialize a Base16 decoding stream with an input source containing encoded Base16 data, then verify that the stream correctly reports one byte as available for reading. Skip a large number of bytes from the stream and confirm that exactly six bytes were actually skipped, indicating the decoded content length. Assert that the stream now reports zero bytes available since the end has been reached. Attempt to read from the exhausted stream twice and verify that both read operations return the end-of-stream indicator. Finally, confirm that the stream continues to report zero bytes available after reaching the end. The test uses JUnit for assertions and validation.

This test validates the strict decoding behavior of a Base32 output stream when processing invalid Base32 encoded data. Initialize a loop that iterates through a collection of impossible Base32 test cases, converting each string case to UTF-8 bytes. For each test case, create a byte array output stream and instantiate a Base32 output stream in decoding mode with default lenient policy. Assert that strict decoding is disabled by default, then write the encoded bytes to the stream and close it. Verify that the output stream produced some data by asserting the byte array size is greater than zero. Next, create a new byte array output stream and instantiate another Base32 output stream in decoding mode but with strict codec policy enabled. Assert that strict decoding is now enabled, then verify that writing the same encoded bytes throws an IllegalArgumentException due to the invalid Base32 data being rejected under strict decoding rules. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the Base64 decoder's handling of trailing 12-bit sequences in encoded data. Initialize a strict Base64 codec with zero line length, no line separator, URL-safe mode disabled, and strict decoding policy, then verify its strict decoding configuration and codec policy. Create a default lenient Base64 codec and confirm its lenient policy settings. Construct a 4-byte encoded array representing 12 bits by filling the first two positions with the standard encoding table's zero character and padding the remaining positions with equals signs. Calculate the number of bits that would be discarded from 8-bit alignment and create a bitmask for empty bits, noting that single trailing characters represent an invalid case. Iterate through all 64 possible final characters from the standard encoding table, placing each in the last valid position of the encoded array. For invalid cases where lower bits are set or the sequence is impossible, assert that the strict codec throws an IllegalArgumentException during decoding, while verifying the lenient codec successfully decodes the data and produces different output when re-encoded. For valid cases, decode the array with the strict codec, verify the final decoded byte matches the expected bit-shifted value, and confirm that re-encoding produces an array identical to the original input. This test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the Q codec's ability to encode and decode strings containing blank spaces with configurable blank space handling behavior. The test verifies that the QCodec class correctly encodes and decodes text with spaces using two different encoding strategies and ensures bidirectional conversion accuracy through multiple assertion checks. Initialize a plain text string with the value "Mind those pesky blanks" and two expected encoded string values representing the same text encoded with different blank space handling approaches, where the first encoded string preserves spaces as literal spaces and the second replaces spaces with underscores. Create a new QCodec instance and configure it to not encode blanks by calling setEncodeBlanks with false, then invoke the encode method with the plain text string and assert that the result equals the first encoded string using assertEquals with the message "Blanks encoding with the Q codec test" to validate that spaces remain unencoded. Reconfigure the same QCodec instance to encode blanks by calling setEncodeBlanks with true, then call encode again with the plain text and assert that the result equals the second encoded string using assertEquals with the same message to verify that spaces are converted to underscores during encoding. Test the decoding functionality by calling decode on the first encoded string and asserting that the result equals the original plain text using assertEquals with the message "Blanks decoding with the Q codec test" to confirm proper decoding of space-preserved encoding. Finally, call decode on the second encoded string and assert that the result also equals the original plain text using assertEquals with the message "Blanks decoding with the Q codec test" to validate that underscore-encoded spaces are correctly converted back to the original text. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

Initialize an option formatter and create multiple option configurations to test the syntax option formatting behavior. Build an option with short name "o", long name "opt", and argument capability, then create an option formatter from it and assert that the syntax option output equals "[-o <arg>]" for the optional argument case. Create another option with the same short and long names but with a custom argument name "other", format it, and verify the output is "[-o <other>]". Build a required option with short name "o", long name "opt", argument capability, and argument name "other", then assert the syntax output is "-o <other>" without optional brackets. Create a required option with short name "o", long name "opt", and argument name "other" but without argument capability, and verify it produces "-o" as the syntax output. Build an optional option with only short name "o" and argument name "other", then assert it generates "[-o]" as the syntax format. Create an option with only long name "opt", argument capability, and argument name "other", and verify the syntax output is "[--opt <other>]" for the optional long option case. Build a required option with long name "opt", argument capability, and argument name "other", then assert it produces "--opt <other>" without optional delimiters. Finally, create an option with multi-character short name "ot", long name "opt", and argument capability, and verify the syntax output is "[-ot <arg>]" for the optional multi-character option. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the available byte counting and stream positioning behavior of a Base16 input stream during decoding operations. Initialize a byte array input stream containing ISO-8859-1 encoded Base16 data, then wrap it with a Base16 input stream configured for decoding. Assert that the stream initially reports one available byte, then skip ten bytes and verify that six bytes were actually skipped. Assert that the stream has reached its end by confirming zero available bytes, and validate end-of-stream behavior by reading twice and confirming both operations return negative one to indicate no more data. Finally, assert that the available byte count remains zero after reaching the end of the stream. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the strict decoding functionality of Base32OutputStream by ensuring that invalid Base32 input is handled differently under lenient versus strict decoding policies. Initialize a loop that iterates through each string in the BASE32_IMPOSSIBLE_CASES array from Base32Test, which contains Base32 strings that cannot be validly decoded. For each impossible case string, convert it to a UTF-8 byte array using StringUtils getBytesUtf8 method, then create a ByteArrayOutputStream and instantiate a Base32OutputStream with decoding mode enabled by passing false as the second parameter, which uses the default lenient decoding policy. Assert that isStrictDecoding returns false to confirm lenient mode is active, then write the encoded byte array to the output stream and close it. Assert that the output stream size is greater than zero to verify that lenient decoding processed the invalid input without throwing an exception. Create a new ByteArrayOutputStream and instantiate another Base32OutputStream with decoding mode enabled, but this time pass CodecPolicy.STRICT as the fifth parameter to enable strict decoding. Assert that isStrictDecoding returns true to confirm strict mode is active, then use assertThrows to verify that writing the same encoded byte array throws an IllegalArgumentException, demonstrating that strict decoding properly rejects invalid Base32 input that lenient decoding would otherwise process. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the Base64 decoding behavior when handling trailing 12-bit encoded sequences, specifically ensuring that strict decoding policies properly reject invalid trailing characters while lenient policies accept them. Initialize a helper method that creates two Base64 codec instances: one with strict decoding policy using Base64 constructor with parameters 0, null, false, and CodecPolicy.STRICT, and another default Base64 instance with lenient policy. Assert that the strict codec returns true for isStrictDecoding and has CodecPolicy.STRICT, while the default codec returns false for isStrictDecoding and has CodecPolicy.LENIENT. Calculate the encoded byte array length as 12 divided by 6, then create a 4-byte encoded array filled with the first character from the STANDARD_ENCODE_TABLE field (a private static final byte array field of the test class) for valid positions and padding characters for remaining positions. Compute the number of discarded bits as 12 modulo 8 and create an empty bits mask using bit shifting operations. Determine if the sequence is invalid when length equals 1, then iterate through all 64 possible final characters from STANDARD_ENCODE_TABLE. For each character, set it as the last valid position in the encoded array, then check if the character has invalid lower bits set by performing bitwise AND with the empty bits mask. When invalid trailing bits are detected, assert that IllegalArgumentException is thrown when calling decode on the strict codec, decode the same input with the lenient codec, and assert that re-encoding the decoded result with encode does not match the original invalid array using assertFalse with Arrays.equals. For valid trailing characters, decode the input with the strict codec, calculate the expected bits by right-shifting the character index by the discard amount, assert that the last byte of the decoded result equals the expected bits using assertEquals, and verify that re-encoding the decoded result matches the original array using assertArrayEquals with the encode method. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the string representation and deprecation functionality of command line options within an options collection. Initialize an options container and add four different option configurations using an option builder: a standard option with identifier "a", a deprecated option "b" without additional attributes, a deprecated option "c" marked for removal since version "2.0" with a descriptive message "Use X.", and a deprecated option "d" with a long option name and argument support. Verify that the standard string representation of each option begins with the expected format by calling the string conversion method on options "a", "b", and "c" and asserting they start with "[ Option" followed by their respective identifiers. Test the specialized deprecation string method by confirming that the non-deprecated option "a" does not start with "Option a", while the basic deprecated option "b" returns exactly "Option 'b': Deprecated", and the fully-attributed deprecated option "c" returns "Option 'c': Deprecated for removal since 2.0: Use X.". Finally, invoke a helper method on each option to ensure both the standard and deprecation string methods return non-null values without throwing exceptions. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of deprecated command-line options by verifying both their standard string representation and specialized deprecation messaging. Initialize a new Options instance and add four Option objects using the Option builder pattern: create option "a" as a standard non-deprecated option, option "b" as a deprecated option without additional attributes, option "c" as a deprecated option with detailed DeprecatedAttributes including forRemoval set to true, since version "2.0", and description "Use X.", and option "d" as a deprecated option with long option "longD" and argument support enabled. Call the getOption method on the Options instance to retrieve each option by its short name, then invoke toString on options "a", "b", and "c" and assert that each result starts with the expected "[ Option" prefix using assertTrue. Next, call toDeprecatedString on option "a" and assert using assertFalse that the result does not start with "Option a", then call toDeprecatedString on option "b" and assert using assertEquals that it returns exactly "Option 'b': Deprecated", and call toDeprecatedString on option "c" and assert using assertEquals that it returns exactly "Option 'c': Deprecated for removal since 2.0: Use X.". Finally, invoke a helper method for each of the four options that calls both toString and toDeprecatedString methods and asserts using assertNotNull that neither method returns null, ensuring the string generation methods never throw exceptions and always produce valid string outputs. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that the cloning functionality creates an independent copy of a configuration option while preserving its initial state. Initialize a test option with a short name, a boolean flag, and an empty description, then create a clone of this option and verify that the clone equals the original but represents a distinct instance in memory. Modify the original option's description to a non-empty value and confirm that the cloned option retains its original empty description, demonstrating independence between the two instances. Configure the cloned option to accept multiple arguments and add two string values to it, then assert that the original option maintains its single argument configuration and empty values collection while the clone correctly holds the two added values. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the cloning functionality of a test option object to ensure deep copying behavior works correctly. Initialize a test option instance with a string identifier "a", a boolean flag set to true, and an empty string description. Clone the original test option object and assert that the cloned instance equals the original while confirming they are not the same object reference. Modify the original option's description to "a" and verify that the cloned option's description remains an empty string, demonstrating independence between the objects. Update the cloned option by setting its argument count to 2 and adding two string values "b1" and "b2". Assert that the original option retains its initial argument count of 1 and has zero values in its values list, while the cloned option contains exactly 2 values, confirming that modifications to either object do not affect the other. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the available method functionality of a Base16InputStream when decoding Base16-encoded data, specifically testing that the stream correctly reports the number of bytes available for reading and handles end-of-stream conditions. Initialize a ByteArrayInputStream using StringUtils.getBytesIso8859_1 method with the ENCODED_B16 constant as input, then wrap this input stream in a Base16InputStream using a try-with-resources block for automatic resource management. Assert that the available method returns 1, indicating one byte is available for reading from the decoded stream. Call the skip method with an argument of 10 to attempt skipping 10 bytes and assert that it returns 6, confirming that only 6 bytes were actually skipped before reaching the end of the available data. Assert that available now returns 0, indicating no more bytes are available for reading. Call the read method twice consecutively and assert that both calls return -1, confirming that the end of stream has been reached and no more data can be read. Finally, assert that available still returns 0 after the read attempts, validating that the stream consistently reports no available bytes once the end is reached. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the syntax option formatting functionality of the OptionFormatter class, which converts command-line option configurations into standardized syntax representations for help documentation and usage displays. The test systematically exercises the toSyntaxOption method across eight different option configurations, asserting that each produces the correct syntax string format with proper bracketing for optional options, argument placeholders, and prefix handling. Initialize an OptionFormatter instance using the from factory method with an Option created through the Option builder pattern, then call toSyntaxOption to generate the syntax representation and assert the result matches the expected format string. Begin by creating an Option with builder method calls to option with value "o", longOpt with value "opt", and hasArg, then build the Option and pass it to OptionFormatter from method to create the formatter instance, call toSyntaxOption, and assert the result equals "[-o <arg>]" with message "optional arg failed". Create a second Option using the same pattern but adding argName with value "other", format it with OptionFormatter from, call toSyntaxOption, and assert the result equals "[-o <other>]" with message "optional 'other' arg failed". Build a third Option with option "o", longOpt "opt", hasArg, required, and argName "other", format it, call toSyntaxOption, and assert it equals "-o <other>" with message "required 'other' arg failed". Construct a fourth Option with option "o", longOpt "opt", required, and argName "other" but without hasArg, format it, call toSyntaxOption, and assert it equals "-o" with message "required no arg failed". Create a fifth Option with only option "o" and argName "other", format it, call toSyntaxOption, and assert it equals "[-o]" with message "optional no arg arg failed". Build a sixth Option with longOpt "opt", hasArg, and argName "other" but no short option, format it, call toSyntaxOption, and assert it equals "[--opt <other>]" with message "optional longOpt 'other' arg failed". Create a seventh Option with longOpt "opt", required, hasArg, and argName "other", format it, call toSyntaxOption, and assert it equals "--opt <other>" with message "required longOpt 'other' arg failed". Finally, build an eighth Option with option "ot", longOpt "opt", and hasArg, format it, call toSyntaxOption, and assert it equals "[-ot <arg>]" with message "optional multi char opt arg failed". The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the Test annotation.

This test validates the MD2 hash algorithm's hexadecimal string output functionality across various input scenarios. Initialize test data with random bytes and create temporary files containing this data for comprehensive validation. Execute the MD2 hexadecimal hashing function against a series of predefined string inputs including an empty string, single characters, common phrases, alphabetic sequences, and alphanumeric combinations, asserting that each produces the expected hexadecimal hash value as specified in the RFC 1319 standard. Additionally, verify that the hashing function produces identical results when processing the same data from both byte array and input stream sources by comparing the hash of the test data bytes with the hash generated from a byte array input stream containing the same data. Clean up by closing file resources and removing temporary files after test completion. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the MD2 hexadecimal digest utility functionality by verifying hash computations against known reference values from RFC 1319. Initialize a byte array with random test data and create temporary file paths with corresponding file streams and random access file wrappers during setup. Execute the MD2 hex digest method with a series of string inputs including an empty string, single character "a", "abc", "message digest", the full lowercase alphabet, a mixed case alphanumeric string, and a repeated numeric sequence, asserting that each produces the expected hexadecimal hash value as specified in the RFC standard. Additionally, verify that the digest utility produces identical results when processing the random test data directly versus when reading it from a byte array input stream. Clean up by closing the random access file wrapper and deleting the temporary files during teardown. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the deep cloning functionality of the TestOption class to ensure that cloned instances are independent copies that do not share mutable state. The test creates a TestOption instance with constructor arguments "a", true, and an empty string, then invokes the clone method to create a second TestOption instance, casting the result to TestOption type. Assert that the original and cloned instances are equal using assertEquals, then verify they are distinct objects in memory using assertNotSame. Modify the original instance by calling setDescription with argument "a", then assert that the cloned instance's description remains an empty string by calling getDescription and comparing with assertEquals. Further demonstrate independence by calling setArgs on the cloned instance with argument 2, then calling addValue twice on the cloned instance with arguments "b1" and "b2". Validate that the original instance retains its initial state by asserting getArgs returns 1 and getValuesList returns a collection of size 0 using assertEquals. Finally, confirm the cloned instance has been properly modified by asserting getValues returns an array of length 2 using assertEquals. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the SHA-1 hexadecimal digest functionality of a digest utility component. Initialize a byte array with random test data and create two temporary files on the filesystem, writing the test data to both files and establishing a random access file wrapper for one of them. Execute the SHA-1 hex digest method with various string inputs including simple ASCII text like "abc" and longer alphanumeric sequences, converting UTF-8 encoded bytes where necessary. Assert that the computed digest matches expected SHA-1 hash values from FIPS 180-1 examples, verifying that identical results are produced when processing the same data as both byte arrays and input streams. Clean up by closing the random access file wrapper and deleting the temporary files from the filesystem. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the behavior of command line option value retrieval when no deprecation handler is configured, spanning multiple input combinations. Initialize a command line options configuration by adding the provided option group, then parse the given command line arguments using a default parser to create a command line representation. Set up string suppliers for default values including a functional supplier that returns a default string and a null supplier, and redirect system output to capture any deprecation messages during testing. Systematically retrieve option values using various accessor methods that accept different parameter types including character representations, short option names, long option names, and option objects themselves, testing both with and without default value fallbacks using string literals and supplier functions. For each retrieval operation, verify that the returned value matches the expected option value or falls back to the default when the option value is null, and confirm that deprecation warnings are only written to output when the option is marked as deprecated. Additionally test option group value retrieval using the same pattern of accessor methods and default value handling, ensuring that group values are properly returned when the group is selected. Test retrieval attempts on unrelated option groups and null groups to verify they return null values without triggering deprecation warnings, and test non-existent option names to confirm they also return null without warnings. After each value retrieval operation, validate whether deprecation messages were written to the captured output stream based on the deprecation status of the accessed option, then reset the output stream for the next test iteration. Restore the original system output stream in the finally block to ensure proper cleanup. This test uses JUnit 5 with parameterized testing.
