The test exercises the JexlContext interface and JexlExpression evaluation capabilities, specifically testing greater than, greater than or equal, less than, and less than or equal operators with mixed string and integer operands, using boolean assertions to verify the expected comparison outcomes. Initialize a JexlContext instance using MapContext as the implementation, then use the helper method assertExpression to evaluate twelve different comparison expressions that test type coercion behavior between strings and integers. Call assertExpression with the context, the string expression "'2' > 1", and Boolean.TRUE as the expected result to verify that the string '2' is coerced to integer 2 and correctly compared as greater than 1. Continue with assertExpression using "'2' >= 1" expecting Boolean.TRUE, "'2' >= 2" expecting Boolean.TRUE, "'2' < 1" expecting Boolean.FALSE, "'2' <= 1" expecting Boolean.FALSE, and "'2' <= 2" expecting Boolean.TRUE to test all comparison operators with string-to-integer coercion. Then reverse the operand types by calling assertExpression with "2 > '1'" expecting Boolean.TRUE, "2 >= '1'" expecting Boolean.TRUE, "2 >= '2'" expecting Boolean.TRUE, "2 < '1'" expecting Boolean.FALSE, "2 <= '1'" expecting Boolean.FALSE, and "2 <= '2'" expecting Boolean.TRUE to verify integer-to-string coercion works identically. The helper method assertExpression creates a JexlExpression using the JEXL engine's createExpression method with the provided string expression, evaluates it against the given context using the evaluate method, and asserts that the actual result equals the expected value using assertEquals with the expression string as the assertion message. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the execution behavior of do-while loop constructs in JEXL script expressions, specifically verifying that the loop body executes at least once and continues while the condition remains true, with proper variable modification and return value handling. Initialize a JexlScript by calling createScript on the JEXL engine with the expression "do x = x + 1 while (x < 10)", then create a MapContext instance and set the variable "x" to the integer value 1 using the set method. Execute the script by calling the execute method on the JexlScript with the context, then assert that the returned object equals 10 and that the context variable "x" also equals 10 using assertEquals. Create another JexlScript with the multi-line expression "var x = 0; do x += 1; while (x < 23)" and execute it with the same context, asserting that the result equals 23. Reset the context variable "x" to 1, then create a third JexlScript containing "do x += 1; while (x < 23); return 42;" and execute it with the context. Assert that the context variable "x" equals 23 and that the script execution result equals 42, validating that the do-while loop modifies variables correctly and that explicit return statements override the loop's final value. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the execution behavior of JEXL scripts containing do-while loops with false conditions. Initialize a JEXL engine and create a script containing a do-while loop with an empty body and a false condition, then create a map-based context for variable storage. Execute the script with the context and assert that the result is null, verifying that an empty do-while false loop returns no value. Create a second script that contains the same do-while false loop structure followed by the integer value 23, then execute this script with the same context. Assert that the execution result equals 23, confirming that statements following a do-while false loop are properly executed and their values returned. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that script creation properly enforces feature restrictions when using a script-configured feature set. Initialize a script feature configuration that enables lexical scoping, lexical shading, and constant capture while disabling pragma-anywhere and comparator names support. Verify that the feature set correctly reports the enabled and disabled capabilities through assertion checks. Create a script engine using these configured features and retrieve the collection of reserved variable names from the feature set. For each reserved name, attempt to create a script that declares a variable with that reserved name and assert that a feature exception is thrown, confirming that reserved names are properly protected. Additionally, test a series of comparison operator scripts using legacy comparator names like equality, inequality, and relational operators, and verify that each script creation attempt throws an ambiguous exception since comparator names are disabled in this feature configuration. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the cancellation functionality of JEXL scripts running in executor threads, specifically testing that a script containing an infinite loop can be properly cancelled and that the executor handles the cancellation gracefully. Initialize a Semaphore with zero permits to serve as a synchronization mechanism, create a TestContext instance as the JEXL execution context, and set the semaphore in the context using the key "latch". Create a JexlScript using the JEXL engine with script content that calls release on the latch followed by an infinite runForever method call. Convert the script to a Callable using the callable method with the prepared context, then create a single-threaded ExecutorService using newFixedThreadPool with a pool size of one. Submit the callable to the executor and capture the returned Future object. Assert that calling get on the future with a timeout of 100 milliseconds throws a TimeoutException using assertThrows, confirming the script is running indefinitely. Invoke cancel on the future with the interrupt flag set to true to forcibly cancel the running script. In the finally block, call shutdownNow on the executor to immediately terminate all running tasks and capture the list of tasks that were waiting to be executed. After the executor cleanup, assert that isCancelled on the future returns true to verify the cancellation was successful, and assert that the returned task list isEmpty to confirm no tasks were pending execution when the executor was shut down. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the ternary conditional operator functionality when evaluating expressions with variables that have assigned values. Initialize a script engine and create a variable context that maps a test variable name to a corresponding test value. Set up the context by associating the variable name with its value, then create and execute a script that uses the ternary conditional operator to check if the variable exists and return its value or null as a fallback. Execute the script within the prepared context and assert that the returned result matches the originally assigned variable value, confirming that the ternary operator correctly evaluates the variable's presence and returns its value rather than the null fallback. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the JEXL engine's feature enforcement for script parsing with specific language restrictions enabled. Initialize a script features configuration using the script creation factory method, then verify that lexical scoping, lexical shading, and constant capture features are enabled while pragma-anywhere and comparator names features are disabled through boolean assertion calls. Create a JEXL engine instance using a builder pattern with the configured features, then retrieve the collection of reserved variable names from the features object. Iterate through each reserved name in the collection and construct a variable declaration script string by concatenating "var " with each reserved name, then assert that attempting to create a script from this source throws a feature exception using the engine's script creation method. Define an array of comparator name script strings containing expressions like "1 eq 1", "2 ne 3", "1 lt 2", "3 le 3", "4 gt 2", and "3 ge 2", then iterate through each script string and assert that attempting to create a script from each source throws an ambiguous exception using the engine's script creation method. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a JEXL engine configured with script features properly enforces restrictions on reserved variable names and comparator operator names by throwing appropriate exceptions when these disabled features are used. Initialize a JexlFeatures instance using the createScript factory method, then assert that the features instance has lexical scoping enabled by calling isLexical, lexical shading enabled by calling isLexicalShade, and constant capture support enabled by calling supportsConstCapture, while confirming that pragma anywhere support is disabled by calling supportsPragmaAnywhere and comparator names support is disabled by calling supportsComparatorNames. Create a JexlEngine instance using a JexlBuilder configured with the features instance by calling the features method followed by create. Retrieve the collection of reserved names from the features instance using getReservedNames and iterate through each reserved name, constructing a script source string by concatenating "var " with each reserved variable name, then assert that calling createScript on the engine with this source throws a JexlException.Feature exception using assertThrows. Define an array of comparator name script strings containing "1 eq 1", "2 ne 3", "1 lt 2", "3 le 3", "4 gt 2", and "3 ge 2", then iterate through each script string and assert that calling createScript on the engine with each source throws a JexlException.Ambiguous exception using assertThrows. This test uses the JUnit testing framework with the @Test annotation.

This test validates the execution of a script engine with multiple annotations applied to a code block. Initialize an annotation context object that tracks annotation processing and create a script containing two annotations - one parameterized annotation with a numeric argument and one synchronization annotation - applied to a block that returns the integer 42. Execute the script using the annotation context and assert that the returned result equals 42. Verify that the annotation context processed exactly 2 annotations by checking its count, then confirm that the context's name collection contains the synchronization annotation name, the parameterized annotation name, and the string representation of the numeric argument passed to the parameterized annotation. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the proper evaluation of a ternary conditional operator expression when the condition variable exists and has a non-null value in the context. Initialize a string variable with the value "Test.Name" to serve as both the variable name and part of the expression, and create another string variable with the value "Test.Value" to represent the expected result. Instantiate a new Engine object, which is an implementation of the JexlEngine abstract class, to serve as the expression evaluation engine. Create a MapContext instance to hold variable bindings during expression evaluation. Use the set method on the MapContext to bind the variable name to the test value, establishing the context for expression evaluation. Construct a ternary conditional expression by concatenating the variable name with the operator "?:null", creating an expression that returns the variable's value if it exists and is truthy, or null otherwise. Call the createScript method on the JexlEngine with the constructed expression string to parse and compile it into an executable script. Execute the script by calling the execute method with the MapContext as the evaluation context, which will resolve the variable and evaluate the ternary conditional. Assert that the returned object equals the original test value using assertEquals, validating that the ternary operator correctly returned the variable's value rather than the null fallback. The test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the execution behavior of do-while loop constructs in JEXL scripts when the condition evaluates to false, ensuring that the loop body executes once and that subsequent statements are properly evaluated. Initialize a JexlScript instance by calling createScript on the JEXL engine with a do-while loop script containing an empty body and a false condition, then create a MapContext instance to serve as the execution context. Execute the script using the execute method with the context and assert that the returned object is null using assertNull, verifying that an empty do-while false loop returns no value. Create a second JexlScript instance using createScript with a script that contains the same do-while false loop structure followed by the integer literal 23 on a separate line. Execute this second script with the same context using the execute method and assert that the returned object equals 23 using assertEquals, confirming that statements following a do-while false loop are properly executed and their values returned. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the functionality of JEXL script execution with multiple annotations by verifying that annotation processing correctly handles both parameterized and non-parameterized annotations while maintaining accurate counts and name tracking. Initialize an AnnotationContext instance which serves as the execution context for annotation processing, then create a JexlScript using the JEXL engine's createScript method with a script string containing two annotations: "@one(1)" with a parameter and "@synchronized" without parameters, followed by a code block that returns the integer value 42. Execute the script by calling the execute method on the JexlScript instance, passing the AnnotationContext as the execution context, which triggers the processAnnotation method within AnnotationContext that increments the count field and adds annotation names to the names Set field based on the annotation type encountered. Assert that the script execution returns exactly 42 as the result value, then verify that the AnnotationContext count field equals 2 indicating both annotations were processed, and confirm that the names Set contains the strings "synchronized", "one", and "1" to validate that both the annotation names and the parameter value from the "@one(1)" annotation were properly captured during execution. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that arithmetic and bitwise shift operations follow correct operator precedence rules in expression evaluation. Initialize an assertion utility for testing expression evaluation capabilities. Execute a series of expression evaluations that combine addition and left bitshift operations with varying parentheses groupings, using both integer and long numeric literals to verify that the expression parser correctly handles operator precedence across different numeric types. Assert that each expression string evaluates to the same result as the equivalent mathematical operation performed directly in code, ensuring that addition operations are performed before bitshift operations when no parentheses alter the natural precedence, and that explicit parentheses can override the default precedence as expected. The testing uses JUnit framework.

This test validates operator precedence in mathematical expressions involving addition, bit shift, and long integer operations using an expression assertion utility. Initialize an asserter component to evaluate mathematical expressions and compare their results against expected Java computations. Execute a series of assertion calls that test various combinations of arithmetic and bitwise operations with different operator precedence scenarios, using expressions like "40 + 2 << 1 + 1" with integer values, "40 + 2L << 1 + 1" with mixed long and integer values, and "40L + 2 << 1 + 1" with long integer values, along with parenthesized variations that explicitly control evaluation order such as "(40 + 2) << (1 + 1)" and "40 + (2 << 1) + 1". Each assertion validates that the expression evaluator correctly handles operator precedence by comparing the parsed expression result against the equivalent Java arithmetic computation, ensuring that addition, bit shift left operations, and type promotions between integers and longs follow proper mathematical precedence rules. The testing framework used is JUnit.

This test validates that a script execution engine can properly handle and process multiple annotations applied to a code block. Initialize an annotation processing context that tracks annotation usage, then create a script containing a code block annotated with both a parameterized annotation and a synchronization annotation that returns a numeric value. Execute the script using the annotation context and verify that the execution returns the expected numeric result. Assert that the annotation processor was invoked the correct number of times to handle both annotations, and confirm that the processor's tracking mechanism captured all relevant annotation names including the synchronization directive, the parameterized annotation name, and the parameter value. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the execution behavior of a JEXL script engine when processing a try-finally block construct. Initialize a string containing JEXL source code that represents a try-finally block where the try section contains the integer value 42 and the finally section contains the integer value 169. Create a JEXL script object from this source code using the script engine's creation method. Assert that the resulting script object is not null to verify successful script compilation. Execute the script with a null context parameter to run the compiled JEXL code. Assert that the execution result equals the integer value 42, confirming that the try-finally block correctly returns the value from the try section while still executing the finally block. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string concatenation functionality within the JEXL expression evaluation engine by verifying that string variables can be properly combined using the plus operator. The test creates a MapContext instance to serve as the variable container, then populates it with two string variables by calling the set method to assign "Hello" to a variable named "first" and "World" to a variable named "second". The test then uses a helper method called assertExpression which takes the context, the expression string "first + ' ' + second", and the expected result "Hello World" as parameters. Within the helper method, the JEXL engine creates a JexlExpression from the provided expression string, evaluates it against the given context using the evaluate method, and validates that the actual result matches the expected value "Hello World" through an assertEquals assertion that includes the original expression string as a message parameter. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that a JEXL script correctly executes a try-finally block and returns the value from the try block as the overall result. Initialize a string containing JEXL source code that defines a try-finally block where the try section contains the literal value 42 and the finally section contains the literal value 169. Create a JexlScript instance by calling the createScript method on the JEXL engine with the source string as the argument. Assert that the created script is not null using assertNotNull to verify successful script compilation. Execute the script by calling the execute method on the JexlScript instance with a null context parameter, which programmatically interprets the try-finally construct and evaluates both blocks while ensuring the finally block runs regardless of the try block's completion. Assert that the execution result equals the integer 42 using assertEquals, validating that the script correctly returns the value from the try block rather than the finally block value, demonstrating proper try-finally semantics where the try block's value becomes the overall expression result when no exception occurs. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates that a script engine can properly execute a try-finally block structure and return the correct result from the try section. Create a script containing a try block with a numeric expression followed by a finally block with a different numeric expression, then use the script engine to parse this source code into an executable script. Verify that the script creation was successful, then execute the script without providing any context variables. Assert that the execution returns the value from the try block rather than the finally block, confirming that try-finally control flow behaves correctly where the try block's result is preserved as the overall return value. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a JEXL expression evaluator properly handles undefined variable references by verifying error detection capabilities. Initialize a test asserter component that can evaluate JEXL expressions and validate expected failure conditions. Execute a failure assertion test by providing the expression "objects[1].status" to the asserter's fail expression method, which should attempt to evaluate the expression and expect it to fail with a specific error pattern. Assert that the evaluation fails with an error message matching the regular expression pattern indicating that the variable 'objects' is undefined, confirming that the expression evaluator correctly identifies and reports undefined variable access attempts. The test uses JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates that the JEXL expression engine properly detects and reports undefined variable errors when attempting to access properties of non-existent variables. The test specifically verifies that accessing a property on an undefined array variable triggers the appropriate error handling mechanism within the expression evaluation system. Initialize the test by utilizing the asserter field of type Asserter from the test class, which serves as the primary validation mechanism for expression evaluation failures. Execute the failExpression method on the asserter instance, passing the expression string "objects[1].status" as the first parameter and the regular expression pattern ".*variable 'objects' is undefined.*" as the second parameter to validate the expected error message format. The failExpression method attempts to evaluate the provided JEXL expression and asserts that the evaluation fails with an error message matching the specified pattern, confirming that the expression engine correctly identifies that the variable 'objects' has not been defined in the current evaluation context before attempting to access its indexed element and subsequent status property. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that expression evaluation properly detects and reports undefined variable references. Initialize an assertion utility that can evaluate expressions and verify expected failure conditions. Execute an expression that attempts to access a property on an undefined variable, specifically trying to reference a status field on an element within an undefined collection. Assert that the evaluation fails with an error message indicating that the referenced variable is undefined, confirming that the expression engine correctly identifies and reports undefined variable usage rather than silently failing or producing unexpected results. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that expression evaluation can access both properties and methods of objects through a scripting context. Initialize a test object that provides a count property and a square calculation method, then verify the square method works correctly by calling it with positive and negative integer inputs and confirming both return the expected squared result. Create an expression context and register the test object within it under a variable name. Use the expression evaluation system to access the object's count property through the context and verify it returns the expected integer value, then evaluate expressions that call the square method with the same positive and negative inputs used earlier, confirming the expression evaluation produces the same squared results as the direct method calls. This test uses JUnit for test execution.

This test validates that arithmetic and bitwise shift operator precedence is correctly evaluated in expression parsing, specifically testing that addition operations are performed before left shift operations according to standard operator precedence rules. Initialize a test method annotated with @Test that accesses the a360 field, which is a private final Asserter type field of the test class. Call the assertExpression method nine times with different combinations of arithmetic and bitwise shift expressions, comparing the parsed expression results against the expected Java evaluation results. The first assertion validates "40 + 2 << 1 + 1" against the computed value of 40 + 2 << 1 + 1, testing basic precedence without parentheses. The second assertion tests "40 + (2 << 1) + 1" against 40 + (2 << 1) + 1, explicitly grouping the shift operation. The third assertion validates "(40 + 2) << (1 + 1)" against 40 + 2 << 1 + 1, demonstrating that explicit parentheses around additions produce the same result as natural precedence. The fourth through sixth assertions repeat the same pattern using long literal 2L instead of integer 2, testing "40 + 2L << 1 + 1", "40 + (2L << 1) + 1", and "(40 + 2L) << (1 + 1)" against their respective computed values. The seventh through ninth assertions use long literal 40L, testing "40L + 2 << 1 + 1" against 40L + 2L << 1 + 1, "40L + (2 << 1) + 1" against 40L + (2L << 1) + 1, and "(40L + 2) << (1 + 1)" against 40L + 2L << 1 + 1, ensuring consistent precedence behavior across different numeric types. Each assertExpression call validates that the expression parser correctly interprets operator precedence by comparing the parsed result with the expected Java computation result. The testing framework used is JUnit, as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the evaluation of comparison and equality expressions within an expression language engine. Initialize a context and populate it with various data types including boolean values, numeric types like integers and big decimals, date values from different time periods, and a custom object. Execute a comprehensive series of expression evaluations that test equality comparisons between boolean values and literals, less-than comparisons involving numeric values against literals and null values, less-than-or-equal comparisons with the same variety of operands, greater-than-or-equal comparisons across different numeric types and date values, and greater-than comparisons between various data types including big integers and big decimals. Assert that each expression evaluation returns the expected boolean result, verifying that the expression engine correctly handles type coercion and comparison logic across different data types including proper null handling and cross-type numeric comparisons. The testing uses JUnit framework.

This test validates that script execution properly handles variable scoping and null reference behavior when accessing nested properties. Initialize a context for script execution, then create a script that declares a local variable and attempts to access a nested property on that null variable, expecting this to throw an exception and verifying the exception message is present. Next, create a second script that accesses the same nested property path without the local variable declaration, execute it within the same context, and assert that it returns the expected numeric value, demonstrating that the variable is treated as a global reference in this case. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of integer property access and method invocation through JEXL expression evaluation by testing both direct method calls and expression-based evaluation of a Foo object's square method and count property. Initialize a new Foo instance, then directly call the square method with the integer value 2 and assert that it returns the Integer value 4, followed by calling square with the integer value -2 and asserting it also returns the Integer value 4, verifying that the square method correctly computes the square of both positive and negative integers by multiplying the input value by itself. Create a new MapContext instance as a JexlContext, then use the set method to bind the Foo instance to the string key "foo" within the context. Execute a helper method three times to validate JEXL expression evaluation: first call assertExpression with the context, the string expression "foo.count", and the expected Integer value 5 to verify property access returns the correct count value, then call assertExpression with the context, the string expression "foo.square(2)", and the expected Integer value 4 to validate method invocation through expression evaluation, and finally call assertExpression with the context, the string expression "foo.square(-2)", and the expected Integer value 4 to confirm negative input handling through expression evaluation. The helper method assertExpression creates a JexlExpression using JEXL.createExpression with the provided expression string, evaluates it against the given context using the evaluate method, and asserts that the actual result equals the expected value using assertEquals with the expression string as the assertion message. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates that static field access through class references works correctly in script execution. Initialize a context with a structure and set a class reference that contains a static field with a specific constant value. Create a script that assigns the static field value from the referenced class to a variable, then execute the script with the prepared context. Assert that the script execution returns the expected static field value and verify that the variable was properly set in the context with the same value. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the JEXL script engine's handling of null variable access and global variable behavior. Initialize a map-based JEXL context to serve as the variable environment. Create a first JEXL script that declares a local variable as null and attempts to access a nested property on it, such as setting a value on a null object's property chain. Execute this script within the context and assert that a JEXL exception is thrown, verifying that the exception message is not null. Create a second JEXL script that performs the same property assignment operation but without the local variable declaration, treating the variable as a global antish variable. Execute this second script in the same context and assert that the returned result equals the assigned integer value, demonstrating that global variables can be successfully created and assigned through property chains. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the ability of a JEXL script engine to access static fields from Java classes through expression evaluation. Initialize a struct object and a map-based context, then register the struct in the context under a key and associate an inner class with a namespace identifier in the context. Create a JEXL script from a source string that assigns a static field value from the namespaced class to a variable, then execute the script against the prepared context. Assert that the script execution result equals the expected static field value, and verify that the assigned variable in the context also contains the same static field value. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the integration between a Foo object and JEXL expression evaluation capabilities. Initialize a new Foo instance and directly verify its square method functionality by asserting that calling square with the value 2 returns 4, and calling square with the value -2 also returns 4. Create a JEXL context using a map-based implementation and register the Foo instance within it using the key "foo". Evaluate three JEXL expressions through the context: first assert that accessing the "foo.count" property returns the integer value 5, then assert that the expression "foo.square(2)" evaluates to the integer value 4, and finally assert that the expression "foo.square(-2)" evaluates to the integer value 4. Each JEXL expression evaluation creates a JEXL expression object, evaluates it against the context, and compares the actual result with the expected value using equality assertions. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates JEXL script execution behavior when attempting to access properties on null variables, specifically testing the difference between local variable declaration with null assignment versus accessing undefined global variables. Initialize a MapContext as the execution context for the JEXL scripts. Create the first JexlScript using the createScript method with the source text "var quux = null; quux.froboz.value = 10" which declares a local variable quux as null and then attempts to access nested properties on it. Execute this script with the context and assert that a JexlException is thrown using assertThrows, then verify the exception's string representation is not null using assertNotNull. Create a second JexlScript with the source text "quux.froboz.value = 10" which attempts to access the same nested property path on quux but without the local variable declaration, treating quux as a global antish variable. Execute this second script with the same context and capture the returned object. Assert that the execution result equals the integer value 10 using assertEquals, demonstrating that accessing undefined global variables in antish form succeeds while accessing null local variables fails. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation and assertion methods.

This test validates that a script engine can properly parse and represent a complex script containing nested scopes with variable shadowing and control flow structures. Initialize a script engine with strict mode enabled, then create a script from source text that defines a local variable, contains an immediately-invoked lambda function with a for-loop that iterates over null, declares another local variable within a nested block, and returns the loop variable from an inner scope. Verify that the script creation succeeds by asserting the script is not null. Convert the script's internal representation to a string format and retrieve the original source text from the script. Finally, assert that the regenerated string representation matches the original source text when whitespace differences are ignored, confirming that the parser correctly handles the complex nested scope structure and can accurately reconstruct the script's syntax. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the ability to access static fields from Java classes through JEXL script execution, specifically testing that static field references are properly resolved and their values correctly retrieved and assigned to variables within the script context. Initialize a Struct object and assign it to a MapContext under the key "pub", then configure the context by setting the key "com.jexl" to reference the Inner class, which provides access to its static members through the JEXL scripting environment. Create a JEXL script with the source text "x = com.jexl.NOT42" that assigns the static field NOT42 from the Inner class to a variable named x within the script. Execute the script using the execute method of JexlScript with the configured context, which processes the script and returns the result of the assignment operation. Assert that the returned result equals the static field value Inner.NOT42 to verify the script correctly accessed and returned the static field value. Additionally, assert that the context variable "x" also equals Inner.NOT42 to confirm that the assignment within the script properly stored the static field value in the script's variable context. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the exception handling behavior when a script throws a value, catches it, and then throws a modified version of that value. Initialize a script engine and create a script containing a try-catch block that declares a variable with a numeric value, throws that value in the try block, catches the thrown value in a catch block, and then throws the negated value of the caught exception. Execute the script without any context variables, expecting it to throw a specific type of exception that wraps thrown values. Assert that the script creation succeeds and that executing the script produces the expected exception type. Verify that the final thrown value matches the negated version of the originally thrown value, confirming that the exception propagation and value transformation occurred correctly through the try-catch-throw sequence. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the evaluation of comparison and equality expressions in the JEXL expression language engine by verifying that various relational operators produce correct boolean results when applied to different data types. Initialize a MapContext instance as the JEXL context and populate it with variables including a Foo object, boolean values for variables a and b set to true and false respectively, an integer variable num with value 5, a current date from Calendar.getInstance for variable now, a future date from a GregorianCalendar set to year 5000 month 11 day 20 for variable now2, a BigDecimal with value 7 for variable bdec, and a BigInteger with value 7 for variable bint. Execute a series of expression evaluations using the helper method assertExpression which creates a JexlExpression from the provided string, evaluates it against the context, and asserts the result equals the expected value. Validate equality operations by asserting that "a == b" returns false, "a==true" returns true, "a==false" returns false, and "true==false" returns false. Test less-than comparisons by asserting "2 < 3" returns true, "num < 5" returns false, "num < num" returns false, "num < null" returns false, "num < 2.5" returns false, and "now2 < now" returns false. Verify less-than-or-equal operations by asserting "num <= 5" returns true, "num <= num" returns true, "num <= null" returns false, "num <= 2.5" returns false, and "now2 <= now" returns false. Test greater-than-or-equal comparisons by asserting "num >= 5" returns true, "num >= num" returns true, "num >= null" returns false, "num >= 2.5" returns true, and "now2 >= now" returns true. Validate greater-than operations by asserting "num > 4" returns true, "num > num" returns false, "num > null" returns false, "num > 2.5" returns true, and "now2 > now" returns true. Test BigDecimal and BigInteger comparisons by asserting "bdec > num" returns true, "bdec >= num" returns true, "num <= bdec" returns true, "num < bdec" returns true, "bint > num" returns true, "bint == bdec" returns true, "bint >= num" returns true, "num <= bint" returns true, and "num < bint" returns true. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the expression evaluation capabilities of a JEXL expression engine by testing various comparison and equality operators across different data types. Initialize a map-based JEXL context and populate it with diverse test data including a custom Foo object, boolean values true and false, an integer value of 5, the current date, a future date from year 5000, and numeric types BigDecimal and BigInteger both set to 7. Execute a comprehensive series of expression evaluations using a helper method that creates JEXL expressions from string representations and compares their evaluated results against expected boolean outcomes. Test equality operations between boolean variables and literals, comparison operations (less than, less than or equal, greater than or equal, greater than) between integers, nulls, decimals, and date objects, and cross-type comparisons between BigDecimal, BigInteger, and regular integer values. Assert that each expression evaluation returns the correct boolean result, verifying that the JEXL engine properly handles type coercion, null comparisons, and numeric precision across different data types. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a JEXL engine with strict mode enabled, then create a script containing a complex nested structure with variable declarations, lambda expressions, for loops, and block scoping that includes a let statement declaring a variable, an immediately invoked lambda function containing a for-each loop iterating over null with its own local variable declaration, and nested blocks with return statements. Assert that the created script is not null, then retrieve the script's debug string representation and source text to verify that the parsed representation matches the original source when whitespace differences are ignored. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the ternary conditional operator behavior in the JEXL expression engine by setting up a logging configuration to suppress warnings, then creating a JEXL engine instance and a map context for variable storage. Initialize a string variable name "Test.Name" and a corresponding string value "Test.Value", then populate the map context by setting the name-value pair. Create a JEXL script using the engine that contains a ternary conditional expression combining the variable name with the "?:null" operator syntax, then execute this script against the populated context to evaluate the conditional expression. Assert that the returned object from the script execution equals the original test value, verifying that the ternary operator correctly returns the variable's value when it exists rather than the null fallback. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the edge case behavior of modulo operations when handling null operands and division by zero scenarios. Initialize two arithmetic computation engines with different null handling configurations, where one strictly enforces null operand validation and the other provides lenient null handling. Verify that performing modulo operations with null operands either throws appropriate null operand exceptions or returns expected default values depending on the engine configuration. Assert that division by zero scenarios consistently trigger arithmetic exceptions across various numeric types including integers, longs, floats, doubles, and big number representations. Confirm that the strict arithmetic engine properly validates null operands in division operations as well. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the behavior of variable scoping in JEXL script execution when lexical scoping is disabled, specifically testing that variables declared in one block scope remain accessible in subsequent block scopes. Initialize a JexlEngine using JexlBuilder with strict mode enabled and lexical scoping set to false, then create a MapContext as the execution context. Create a JexlScript containing two sequential block statements where the first block declares and assigns the value 42 to variable x, and the second block declares variable x without initialization and returns its value. Execute the script with the context and capture the result. Assert that the returned result equals 42, which validates that when lexical scoping is disabled, the variable x retains its value from the first block scope and is accessible in the second block scope, demonstrating non-lexical variable scoping behavior where variables persist across block boundaries. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the behavior of a JEXL expression engine when lexical scoping is disabled for variable declarations across code blocks. Initialize a JEXL engine builder with strict mode enabled and lexical scoping set to false, then create the engine instance. Prepare an empty map-based execution context for the script. Create a script containing two sequential code blocks where the first block declares and assigns a variable with the value 42, and the second block redeclares the same variable without assignment and returns its value. Execute the script within the provided context and capture the returned result. Assert that the result equals 42, demonstrating that with lexical scoping disabled, the variable retains its value from the first block despite being redeclared in the second block. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the exception handling behavior when a JEXL script throws a value within a try-catch block that subsequently re-throws a modified version of that value. The test creates a JexlScript from source code that uses a try-catch construct where the try block throws the integer value 42, the catch block captures this value and throws its negation, and asserts that the final thrown exception contains the expected modified value. Initialize a string variable containing JEXL source code that declares a try block with a let statement assigning 42 to variable x followed by a throw statement that throws x, and a catch block with a const parameter y that throws the negated value of y.value. Create a JexlScript instance by calling the createScript method on the JEXL engine with the source string as the argument. Assert that the created script is not null using assertNotNull. Execute the script by calling the execute method with a null context parameter, expecting this to throw a JexlException.Throw, and capture this exception using assertThrows with JexlException.Throw.class as the expected exception type. Assert that the thrown value retrieved from the exception using the getValue method equals -42, validating that the catch block successfully caught the original thrown value of 42 and re-threw its negation. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation and assertion methods.

This test validates the behavior of a JEXL script engine when executing a script that throws an exception within a try-catch block and then re-throws a modified value from the catch handler. Initialize a string containing JEXL source code that defines a try block with a resource declaration binding a variable to the value 42, throws that variable as an exception, catches it with a constant parameter, and then throws the negated value of the caught exception. Create a JEXL script object from this source code using the script engine's creation method. Assert that the script object is not null to verify successful parsing. Execute the script with a null context, expecting it to throw a JEXL Throw exception, and capture this exception using an assertion that validates the specific exception type is thrown. Finally, assert that the thrown exception's value equals -42, confirming that the catch block successfully negated the original thrown value of 42. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the edge case behavior of modulo operations in JEXL arithmetic components when handling null operands and division by zero scenarios. Initialize two JEXL arithmetic instances with different null handling configurations, where one throws exceptions for null operands and the other returns zero. Execute a series of modulo operations starting with null operand combinations, asserting that the first arithmetic instance either returns null or throws a null operand exception while the second instance returns zero for null inputs. Proceed to test division by zero conditions using various numeric types including integers, longs, floats, doubles, big integers, and big decimals with values like 1 and 0, verifying that arithmetic exceptions are thrown for each division by zero attempt. Conclude by testing a divide operation with null operands to ensure consistent null handling behavior. The assertions validate null operand handling, arithmetic exception throwing for division by zero, and proper return values, using JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the creation and parsing of a JEXL script containing nested scopes with variable shadowing and lambda expressions to ensure proper source text reconstruction. Initialize a JexlEngine using a JexlBuilder with strict mode enabled set to true, then call the create method to instantiate the engine. Create a JexlScript by calling the createScript method on the engine with a multi-line string containing JEXL syntax that declares a variable x with value 32, defines an immediately-invoked lambda expression that contains a for-each loop iterating over null with a local variable x that shadows the outer x, declares a local variable c with value 0 within the loop body, and returns the local x variable from within a nested block scope. Assert that the created script is not null using assertNotNull. Convert the script to its string representation by calling the toString method from JexlTestCase, passing the script as an argument, and store the result. Retrieve the original source text of the script by calling the getSourceText method on the script object. Validate that the original source text and the reconstructed debug representation are equivalent by calling the equalsIgnoreWhiteSpace method from JexlTestCase with the source text and debug string as arguments, then assert the result is true using assertTrue. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates script execution behavior when lexical scoping is disabled in the expression engine. Initialize an expression engine with strict mode enabled and lexical scoping turned off, then create an empty execution context. Construct a script containing two separate code blocks where the first block declares and assigns a variable with a numeric value, and the second block redeclares the same variable without assignment before returning its value. Execute the script within the prepared context and assert that the returned result equals the numeric value from the first block, demonstrating that without lexical scoping, variable declarations from different blocks share the same scope. This test uses JUnit as the testing framework.

This test validates the JEXL permissions system's ability to parse and compose permission configurations that selectively allow specific methods within restricted classes. Initialize a string containing a permission configuration that grants access to the getName and getSimpleName methods of the java.lang.Class class, then compose this configuration with a restricted permissions base to create a new permissions object. Retrieve method references for getName and getSimpleName from the Class class using reflection, and assert that both methods are not null and are allowed by the composed permissions object while being denied by the original restricted permissions. Additionally, retrieve method references for getMethod from the Class class and exit from the Runtime class, asserting that both are not null but are not allowed by the composed permissions, demonstrating that only explicitly granted methods are permitted while others remain restricted. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that pragma directives with null values are correctly parsed and stored in script metadata. Initialize a script engine using the builder pattern, then create a script containing a pragma directive that explicitly assigns a null value to a custom pragma key. Retrieve the pragma metadata from the compiled script and verify that the pragma key exists in the metadata collection. Assert that the stored value for the pragma key is indeed null, confirming that the engine properly handles null value assignments in pragma directives rather than treating them as undefined or missing entries. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that permission composition functionality correctly extends a restricted permission set by parsing a textual configuration to selectively allow specific methods on a class. Initialize a string configuration that defines permissions for the java.lang package, specifically allowing the getName and getSimpleName methods on the Class type. Use the restricted permission set to compose with this configuration string, creating a new permission set that extends the base restrictions. Retrieve method references for getName and getSimpleName from the Class type, then verify that the composed permissions allow both of these methods while confirming that the original restricted permissions still deny them. Additionally, retrieve method references for getMethod from Class and exit from Runtime, then assert that the composed permissions correctly deny access to these methods that were not explicitly allowed in the configuration. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the edge case behavior of the modulo operation in JEXL arithmetic, specifically testing how the JexlArithmetic class handles null operands and division by zero scenarios across different numeric types. Initialize the test by calling the setUp method to configure the test class fields including two JexlArithmetic instances named jexla and jexlb. Execute a series of assertions to verify proper exception handling, beginning with a call to the assertNullOperand helper method that passes a lambda expression invoking the mod method on jexla with null arguments, which should either return null or throw a NullOperand exception. Follow this with an assertEquals assertion that calls mod on jexlb with null arguments and expects a return value of 0. Next, invoke the assertArithmeticException helper method multiple times, each time passing lambda expressions that call the mod method on jexla with various numeric types and zero divisors: first with integer values 1 and 0, then with long values 1L and 0L, followed by float values 1f and 0f, then double values 1d and 0d, next with BigInteger.ONE and BigInteger.ZERO, and finally with BigInteger.ONE and BigDecimal.ZERO, where each call should throw an ArithmeticException. Conclude the test with another call to assertNullOperand passing a lambda that invokes the divide method on jexla with null arguments. The assertNullOperand helper method attempts to call the supplied function and either asserts the result is null or catches a NullOperand exception and asserts it is not null, while the assertArithmeticException helper method uses assertThrows to verify that an ArithmeticException is thrown when the supplied function executes. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation and assertion methods.

Initialize a JEXL engine using the default builder configuration, then create a script from a string containing a pragma directive that assigns a null value to a custom pragma key named "myNull". Retrieve the pragmas map from the created script and verify that it contains the expected pragma key by asserting its presence in the map. Finally, confirm that the pragma value associated with the key is indeed null by asserting that retrieving the value returns null. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that CSV format configurations with different header record skipping settings are properly recognized as unequal. Initialize a CSV format configuration with a single quote delimiter, carriage return record separator, hash comment marker, plus escape character, and enable options for ignoring empty lines, ignoring surrounding spaces, double quote character, quote-all mode, null string representation, and header record skipping. Create a second format by modifying the first to disable header record skipping. Assert that the two format configurations are not equal to each other, verifying that the equality comparison correctly identifies the difference in the skip header record setting. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a JexlEngine instance using a JexlBuilder with default configuration by calling create method, then create a JexlScript by calling createScript method on the engine with a string literal containing "#pragma myNull null\n" which defines a pragma directive that sets a null value for the myNull key. Call getPragmas method on the script to retrieve a Map containing the pragma key-value pairs defined in the script source. Assert that the returned pragmas map contains the key "myNull" using assertTrue with the message "pragma key present?" to verify the pragma was properly parsed and stored. Assert that the value associated with the "myNull" key in the pragmas map is null using assertNull with the message "expected null value" to confirm that the pragma directive correctly assigned a null value to the specified key. This test validates that the JEXL engine can parse pragma directives that explicitly set null values and properly store them in the script's pragma metadata, ensuring that pragma parsing handles null value assignments correctly as part of the script compilation process. The testing framework used is JUnit.

This test validates the functionality of JEXL permission composition by verifying that a restricted permission set can be extended to allow specific methods while maintaining overall security constraints. The test exercises the JexlPermissions compose method and the allow method to ensure that permission parsing and method access control work correctly, using assertions to validate both positive and negative permission checks. Initialize a string variable containing a permission configuration that specifies allowing the Class class from the java.lang package with explicit permissions for the getName and getSimpleName methods. Call the compose method on the RESTRICTED field of type JexlPermissions from the test class, passing the permission configuration string to create a new JexlPermissions instance. Use the helper method getMethod to retrieve the getName method from the java.lang.Class class and assert that the returned Method object is not null using assertNotNull. Call the allow method on the composed permissions instance with the getName method and assert that it returns true using assertTrue, then call allow on the RESTRICTED field with the same method and assert that it returns false using assertFalse to verify the base restrictions are still in place. Retrieve the getSimpleName method from java.lang.Class using the helper method, assert it is not null with assertNotNull, verify the composed permissions allow this method with assertTrue on the allow call, and confirm the RESTRICTED permissions deny it with assertFalse on the allow call. Obtain the getMethod method from java.lang.Class through the helper method, assert it is not null, then verify that both the composed permissions and RESTRICTED permissions deny access to this method by asserting false for both allow method calls, demonstrating that methods not explicitly listed in the permission configuration remain restricted. Finally, retrieve the exit method from java.lang.Runtime class, assert it is not null, and confirm that both permission sets deny access to this method by asserting false for both allow calls, validating that methods from classes outside the permission scope remain blocked. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates the evaluation and manipulation of self-referencing array structures through expression parsing and variable access. Initialize a self-referencing array where the first element points to the array itself, along with integer and string values in subsequent positions, then register this array and numeric index variables with an expression asserter. Execute a loop that comprehensively tests array access patterns using both literal numeric indices and variable-based indices, verifying that direct array access, nested self-referential access, and deep nested access all return expected values. Throughout the iterations, perform assignment operations that modify array elements and confirm the changes persist correctly, testing both integer and string value assignments and retrievals. Validate that the self-referential nature of the array allows multi-level nested access patterns to function properly, ensuring that accessing the array through its self-reference produces identical results to direct access. The assertions confirm that expression evaluation correctly handles array indexing, assignment operations, variable substitution in indices, and maintains referential integrity in self-referencing data structures. This testing uses the JUnit framework.

This test validates an expression asserter's ability to handle self-referential array structures and nested array access patterns. Initialize integer values representing 42 and 43, along with corresponding string representations "fourty-two" and "fourty-three", then create an object array where the first element references the array itself, the second element contains the integer 42, and the third element contains the string "fourty-two". Configure the asserter with this self-referential array as variable "foo" and set up index variables for zero, one, and two. Execute a loop twice to verify consistent behavior across multiple iterations, where each iteration performs a comprehensive series of expression assertions that test direct array access, nested self-referential access through the first element, assignment operations that modify array contents, and variable-based indexing using the predefined index variables. The assertions validate that expressions correctly resolve array elements, handle self-referential structures without infinite loops, properly execute assignment operations that change array values from 42 to 43 and back to 42, and similarly modify string values between "fourty-two" and "fourty-three", while ensuring that nested access patterns through the self-referential first element produce identical results to direct access. This testing uses the JUnit framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates namespace functionality with feature configuration and context setup. Initialize a specialized context for namespace testing and create a map containing a namespace mapping that associates a string key with a class reference. Configure a feature set that enables namespace testing by setting up a predicate that accepts all namespace names, then build an engine with the namespace mappings, the configured features, and safety disabled. Execute four sequential helper operations that each perform namespace-related testing scenarios, passing the configured engine and context to validate different aspects of namespace behavior and functionality. The testing uses JUnit framework.

This test validates the namespace functionality of the JEXL expression engine by creating a context instance, configuring a namespace map with a class reference, setting up engine features with namespace testing enabled, and building a JEXL engine with non-safe mode. Initialize a context of type ContextNs348 and create a HashMap to store namespace mappings, adding an entry with key "ns" mapped to the Ns348 class. Configure a JexlFeatures instance by enabling namespace testing with a predicate that accepts all namespace names. Construct a JexlEngine using a JexlBuilder, passing the namespace map, the configured features, and disabling safe mode. Execute four sequential helper method calls that test different aspects of namespace functionality, each receiving the configured engine and context along with a namespace prefix string "ns : ". The test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the capability to dynamically create and manipulate Java collection types through script execution. Initialize a context for variable storage and create an engine with default configuration settings. Configure logging to suppress warnings during execution. Create a script that instantiates a new hash set collection using the fully qualified class name, adds a numeric element to the collection, and returns the collection as the result. Execute the script within the provided context to obtain the resulting collection. Assert that the returned result is an instance of the Set interface type. Verify that the collection contains the expected numeric element that was added during script execution. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a JEXL context using a map-based implementation and create a JEXL engine using the default builder configuration. Create a script from a source string that instantiates a new Java HashSet object, adds the integer value 1 to it, and returns the set. Execute the script with the context to obtain the result object. Assert that the returned object is an instance of the Set interface, then cast it to a Set and verify that it contains the integer value 1. This test validates the JEXL engine's ability to dynamically instantiate Java objects using string-based class names and perform method calls on those objects within script execution. The test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the comprehensive namespace functionality within the JEXL expression engine by configuring and executing multiple namespace-related test scenarios. Initialize a JexlContext instance using the ContextNs348 class to provide the evaluation context, then create a HashMap to store namespace mappings and populate it with a key-value pair where the key is the string "ns" and the value is the Ns348 class. Create a JexlFeatures instance and configure it by calling the namespaceTest method with a lambda expression that returns true for all namespace names, enabling unrestricted namespace testing. Construct a JexlEngine using the JexlBuilder class by calling the namespaces method with the created namespace map, the features method with the configured JexlFeatures instance, the safe method with false to disable safe navigation, and finally the create method to instantiate the engine. Execute four helper methods sequentially: run348a, run348b, run348c, and run348d, each accepting the configured JexlEngine and JexlContext as parameters. Each helper method internally delegates to an overloaded version of itself by passing the same engine and context parameters along with the string literal "ns : " as an additional argument, which likely serves as a namespace prefix for testing various namespace resolution scenarios and validation of namespace-related expression evaluation capabilities. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that array-like objects can be accessed and manipulated through expression evaluation with proper indexing and size retrieval capabilities. Initialize an expression asserter and create a mixed-type array containing string and numeric elements, then register this array as a variable within the asserter's context. Evaluate an expression to retrieve an element at a specific index and verify it returns the expected string value, then evaluate an expression to get the array's size and confirm it matches the expected count. Execute an expression that sets a new value at an existing index position, asserting that it returns the previous value that was replaced, then evaluate another expression using bracket notation to access the same index and verify it now contains the newly set value. The testing uses JUnit framework for test execution and a custom assertion utility for expression evaluation.

This test validates array manipulation functionality within an expression evaluation framework. Initialize an object array containing mixed data types including strings and a long value, then register this array with an expression asserter component using a variable name. Execute expression evaluations to verify array access operations by asserting that retrieving an element by index returns the expected string value, and that querying the array size returns the correct integer count. Test array modification behavior by setting a new value at a specific index, asserting that the operation returns the previous value at that position, then verify the array contains the updated value by accessing the same index again. The testing utilizes JUnit framework with custom assertion utilities from Apache Commons JEXL.

This test validates the functionality of nested array access and assignment operations within an expression evaluation system, specifically testing how self-referential arrays and multi-dimensional array indexing behave when accessed through both literal indices and variable references. Initialize Integer objects with values 42 and 43, String objects with values "fourty-two" and "fourty-three", and create a three-element Object array where the first element references the array itself, the second element contains the Integer 42, and the third element contains the String "fourty-two". Use the asserter field of type Asserter from the test class to register the self-referential array as variable "foo" and register Integer values 0, 1, and 2 as variables "zero", "one", and "two" respectively. Execute a loop twice to validate consistent behavior across multiple iterations, where each iteration performs a comprehensive series of expression evaluations using the assertExpression method. Assert that accessing "foo[0]" returns the entire array, "foo[0][0]" also returns the entire array due to self-reference, "foo[1]" and "foo[0][1]" both return the Integer 42, then assign Integer 43 to "foo[0][1]" and verify the assignment succeeded, followed by reassigning Integer 42 and verifying that assignment. Validate nested self-referential access with "foo[0][0][1]" returning the current value at index 1, perform assignment operations with Integer 43 and 42, and verify each assignment. Assert that "foo[2]" and "foo[0][2]" return the String "fourty-two", assign "fourty-three" and verify the assignment, then reassign "fourty-two" and verify that assignment, followed by testing the same operations through the deeply nested path "foo[0][0][2]". Repeat all previous assertions using variable references instead of literal indices, where "foo[zero]" replaces "foo[0]", "foo[one]" replaces "foo[1]", and "foo[two]" replaces "foo[2]", ensuring that variable-based indexing produces identical results to literal indexing for all access patterns, assignments, and nested operations. The testing framework used is JUnit, as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates the functionality of creating and executing Java object instances through JEXL script evaluation, specifically testing the engine's ability to instantiate a HashSet, add elements to it, and return the populated collection. Initialize a MapContext instance to serve as the execution context, then create a JexlEngine using the default JexlBuilder configuration. Define a multi-line script string that contains JEXL syntax to create a new HashSet instance using the 'new' operator with the fully qualified class name 'java.util.HashSet', adds the integer value 1 to the set using the add method, and returns the set object as the final expression. Call the createScript method on the JexlEngine with the script string to parse and compile the JEXL code into a JexlScript object. Execute the compiled script by calling the execute method with the MapContext, which will run the JEXL code and return the resulting object. Assert that the returned object is an instance of the Set class using assertInstanceOf to verify the correct type was created. Cast the returned object to a Set and call the contains method with the value 1, then assert that the result is true using assertTrue to confirm that the HashSet was properly instantiated, the element was successfully added, and the collection contains the expected value. The test uses JUnit 5 testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation and assertInstanceOf and assertTrue assertion methods.

This test validates the basic execution and source text retrieval functionality of a JEXL script engine. Initialize a string containing a simple while loop script that increments a variable until it reaches ten, then create a JEXL script object from this code using the engine's script creation method. Set up a map-based context and populate it with an initial variable value of one. Execute the script with the context to perform the loop iteration, then assert that the execution result equals ten to verify the loop completed correctly. Finally, assert that the script's source text retrieval method returns the original code string to confirm proper source preservation. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the basic execution and source text retrieval capabilities of a script engine by creating a script from a simple loop expression, executing it within a variable context, and verifying both the computed result and source preservation. Initialize a script engine and create a script containing a while loop that increments a variable until it reaches a target value. Set up an execution context and populate it with an initial variable value of one. Execute the script within this context and assert that the returned result equals the expected final value of ten after the loop completes. Additionally, verify that the script correctly preserves and returns its original source text by comparing the retrieved source against the initial script code. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the array manipulation functionality within a JEXL expression evaluation system, specifically testing how arrays can be accessed, queried for size, and modified through expression evaluation with proper return value handling. Initialize an Object array containing three elements: the string "an", the string "array", and a Long value of 0, then use the asserter field of type Asserter from the test class to register this array as a variable named "objects" by calling the setVariable method. Execute the assertExpression method to verify that accessing index 1 of the objects array returns the string "array", then call assertExpression again to confirm that the size method on the objects array returns an Integer value of 3. Invoke assertExpression to test the set method behavior, verifying that setting index 1 to the string "dion" returns the previous value "array" as expected, and finally call assertExpression once more to assert that direct array access at index 1 now returns the updated string "dion". The testing framework used is JUnit, as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the behavior of null value comparisons and emptiness checks within an expression evaluation context. Initialize an evaluation context and configure its engine options to disable strict mode, then set a variable with an integer value. Evaluate multiple expressions to verify that undefined variables are properly identified as empty and null, while defined variables with values are correctly recognized as non-null and non-empty. Assert that emptiness checks return true for undefined variables and false for defined ones, and that null equality comparisons behave correctly for both scenarios. The validation confirms that the expression engine properly handles null semantics and variable existence checks when operating in non-strict mode. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the basic execution and source text retrieval functionality of JEXL script compilation and execution within the Apache Commons JEXL expression language framework. The test creates and executes a simple while loop script to verify that the JEXL engine can properly compile, execute, and return both the computed result and original source code of a script. Initialize a string variable containing the JEXL script code "while (x < 10) x = x + 1;" which represents a while loop that increments a variable until it reaches 10. Create a JexlScript instance by calling the createScript method on the JEXL engine with the script code string. Instantiate a new MapContext object to serve as the JexlContext for variable storage and retrieval during script execution. Set the variable "x" to the integer value 1 in the context using the set method. Execute the script by calling the execute method on the JexlScript instance, passing the context as a parameter, which will run the while loop incrementing x from 1 until it reaches 10 and return the final value. Assert that the returned execution result equals the integer 10 using assertEquals with the message "Result is wrong" to validate that the script executed correctly and produced the expected final value. Assert that calling getSourceText on the JexlScript instance returns the exact original script code string using assertEquals with the message "getText is wrong" to verify that the script properly preserves and can retrieve its source text. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that import pragma functionality can be properly disabled through feature configuration. Initialize a feature configuration that explicitly disables the import pragma capability, then create an engine using those restricted features. Attempt to create a script from source code that contains multiple import pragma statements for standard Java packages, which should be rejected due to the disabled feature. Assert that the script creation throws a parsing exception and verify that the exception message specifically mentions the import pragma restriction. The test uses JUnit for assertions.

This test validates the JEXL expression engine's null handling and empty checking functionality when strict mode is disabled. Initialize a JEXL evaluation context and retrieve its engine options, then configure the options to disable strict mode evaluation. Set a variable named "bar" with an integer value of 2 in the context. Execute a series of expression evaluations to verify null comparison and empty checking behaviors: assert that an "empty foo" expression returns true since foo is undefined, verify that "bar == null" returns false since bar has a value, confirm that "foo == null" returns true for the undefined variable, check that "bar != null" returns true for the defined variable, validate that "foo != null" returns false for the undefined variable, assert that "empty(bar)" returns false since bar contains a value, and finally confirm that "empty(foo)" returns true since foo remains undefined.
