This test validates the proper state transitions of a POP3 email client throughout a complete session lifecycle. Initialize a new POP3 client and verify its initial disconnected state, default port configuration, and internal reader components. Connect the client to a mail server host and confirm it transitions to the authorization state. Authenticate using valid user credentials and verify the client moves to the transaction state. Execute a series of mail operations including no-operation commands, status checks, message listing, and if messages are available, perform message deletion, reset operations, individual message queries, unique identifier lookups, and message retrieval with proper reader handling and network latency accommodation. Verify that the client maintains the transaction state throughout all these operations. Finally, logout from the server and confirm the client transitions to the update state. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the decrement functionality of a mutable double wrapper, specifically testing that the MutableDouble class correctly decreases its internal value by one and properly converts the result to different numeric types. Initialize a MutableDouble instance with the integer value 1, which sets the internal double field value to 1.0. Call the decrement method on the MutableDouble instance, which programmatically decreases the internal value field by one using the decrement operator, resulting in the value changing from 1.0 to 0.0. Assert that the intValue method returns 0 by comparing the result to the integer literal 0, validating that the decremented double value correctly converts to an integer. Assert that the longValue method returns 0L by comparing the result to the long literal 0L, validating that the decremented double value correctly converts to a long. The intValue method casts the internal double value to an int, while the longValue method casts the internal double value to a long, both ensuring proper type conversion after the decrement operation. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the getter and setter functionality of the FTPSClient class by creating multiple client instances with different configurations and verifying that property values are correctly stored and retrieved. Initialize a first FTPSClient instance using the constructor with protocol string "SSL" and implicit mode set to true, then assert that the isImplicit method returns true and the getProtocol method returns "SSL". Create a second FTPSClient instance with protocol "TLS" and implicit mode set to false, then assert that isImplicit returns false and getProtocol returns "TLS". Define a string array containing protocol values "123" and "456", call setEnabledProtocols on the second client with this array, and assert that getProtocols returns an array equal to the input array. Set the need client authentication flag to true using setNeedClientAuth, assert that isNeedClientAuth returns true, then set it to false and assert that isNeedClientAuth returns false. Similarly, set the want client authentication flag to true using setWantClientAuth, assert that isWantClientAuth returns true, then set it to false and assert that isWantClientAuth returns false. Create another string array with cipher suite values "abc" and "def", call setEnabledCipherSuites with this array, and assert that getSuites returns an array equal to the input array. Set the authentication value to "qwerty" using setAuthValue and assert that getAuthValue returns "qwerty". Set the client mode to true using setUseClientMode, assert that isClientMode returns true, then set it to false and assert that isClientMode returns false. Finally, set the session creation flag to true using setEnabledSessionCreation, assert that isCreation returns true, then set it to false and assert that isCreation returns false. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the state transitions of a POP3 client through its complete lifecycle from disconnection to update state. Initialize a new POP3 client instance and verify its initial disconnected state by asserting the default port is 110, the state equals the disconnected constant, the reader field is null, and the reply lines collection is not null. Connect the client to a mail host and assert the state transitions to authorization state. Authenticate using login credentials with a username and password, then verify the state changes to transaction state. Execute a series of POP3 commands including no-operation and status retrieval, asserting the state remains in transaction state after each operation. Retrieve the list of messages and if at least one message exists, perform additional operations including deleting message 1, resetting the deletion, listing individual messages and all messages, retrieving unique identifiers for individual and all messages, and retrieving both the full message content and the top 10 lines of message 1, with assertions confirming the transaction state persists throughout. For message retrieval operations, wait for the reader to become ready using a sleep loop, then close the reader resources. Finally, logout from the server and assert the state transitions to update state. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the proper state transitions of a POP3 email client throughout a complete session lifecycle, ensuring that the client maintains correct internal state as it progresses through connection, authentication, transaction operations, and logout phases. Initialize a new POP3Client instance and assert that its initial state shows a default port of 110, a DISCONNECTED_STATE status, a null reader field, and a non-null replyLines field. Connect the client to the mail host using the connect method, then assert that the state transitions to AUTHORIZATION_STATE. Authenticate with the server by calling the login method with user credentials, and verify the state changes to TRANSACTION_STATE. Execute a series of POP3 operations while confirming the state remains in TRANSACTION_STATE after each command: call noop to send a no-operation command, invoke status to retrieve mailbox statistics, call listMessages to get all message information, and if messages exist in the mailbox, perform additional operations including deleteMessage with message ID 1, reset to unmark deleted messages, listMessage with ID 1 for individual message info, listMessages again for all messages, listUniqueIdentifier with ID 1 for unique identifier retrieval, listUniqueIdentifiers for all unique identifiers, retrieveMessage with ID 1 to get a Reader for the full message content, wait for the reader to become ready using a sleep loop, close the reader, retrieveMessageTop with ID 1 and 10 lines to get partial message content, wait for reader readiness again, and close the second reader. Finally, call logout to terminate the session and assert that the state transitions to UPDATE_STATE. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance using the default constructor which creates an empty string builder with an initial capacity. Assert that the length method returns 0 to verify the builder starts empty. Call the append method with the string literal "Hello" to add content to the builder. Assert that the length method now returns 5, confirming that the append operation correctly updates the internal size field and that the length method accurately reflects the number of characters stored in the builder's internal character buffer. This test validates the basic functionality of the StrBuilder class's length tracking mechanism, ensuring that the length method properly returns the current size of the string content and that the append method correctly maintains the size counter when adding string data to the builder. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the string building functionality when appending content and handling null values with custom null text representation. Initialize a string builder and configure it to display "NULL" when null values are appended, then append a null string value and verify the output contains the custom null text. Create a fresh string builder and append a string builder containing "foo", confirming the content is correctly transferred. Append an empty string builder to verify no additional content is added and the original "foo" remains. Finally, append another string builder with "bar" content and assert the final result concatenates to "foobar". This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a StrBuilder instance with the string literal "1234567890" to create a string builder containing numeric characters, then create a String variable with the value "Test " (including a trailing space). Allocate a CharBuffer with capacity equal to the sum of the StrBuilder's size and the test string's length using CharBuffer.allocate, then put the test string into the buffer using the put method. Call the appendTo method on the StrBuilder instance, passing the CharBuffer as the argument, which appends the StrBuilder's contents to the buffer by utilizing the CharBuffer's put method to transfer the internal character array. After the appendTo operation, call flip on the CharBuffer to prepare it for reading by setting the limit to the current position and resetting the position to zero. Assert that the buffer's string representation equals "Test 1234567890" using assertEquals, validating that the appendTo method correctly appends the StrBuilder's character data to the CharBuffer and that the combined content matches the expected concatenated result. The test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality for appending multiple elements from an array to a string builder. Initialize a string builder and call the append-all method with a null array parameter, then verify the builder remains empty by converting it to a string and asserting it equals an empty string. Clear the builder and call append-all with no arguments, again verifying the result is an empty string. Clear the builder once more and call append-all with three string arguments containing sample text values, then assert the resulting string concatenates all values without separators. Finally, clear the builder and repeat the same append-all operation with the same three string arguments to confirm consistent behavior, verifying the concatenated result matches the expected combined string. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of appending string builder content with specified start and length parameters. Initialize a string builder and configure it to display a custom null text representation, then attempt to append a null string builder reference with valid start and length parameters, verifying that the null text is properly appended. Create a new string builder and append content from another string builder containing sample text using the full range parameters, confirming the complete content is transferred. Test various boundary conditions by attempting to append with invalid parameter combinations including negative start indices, out-of-bounds start positions, negative lengths, and length values that exceed the source content boundaries, ensuring that appropriate index out of bounds exceptions are thrown for each invalid scenario. Verify that appending with valid boundary parameters such as zero-length ranges produces the expected results without modifying the target content, and confirm that partial content extraction works correctly by appending a substring from a longer source string builder. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a test to verify FTP file retrieval functionality with deflate transfer mode by creating a default home directory, generating a test file named "test_download.txt" with content containing the current timestamp, and writing it to the filesystem using UTF-8 encoding. Execute a helper method that establishes a plain FTP server with test credentials, then within the server context, instantiate a new FTPClient and connect to localhost on the provided port using the supplied username and password. Call the login method on the client with the test credentials, then invoke setFileTransferMode with the parameterized transfer mode value (FTP.DEFLATE_TRANSFER_MODE from the test annotation). Assert that setFileTransferMode returns true to confirm successful mode configuration. Execute listFiles on the client to retrieve the directory contents and assert that the returned FTPFile array has exactly one element, confirming the test file is visible. Create a ByteArrayOutputStream to capture the downloaded file data, then call retrieveFile with the first file's name and the output stream, asserting that the operation returns true to indicate successful retrieval. Convert the captured bytes to a string using UTF-8 encoding and assert that it equals the original file content, validating that the file was transferred correctly through the deflate transfer mode. Finally, call logout on the client within a try-finally block to properly terminate the FTP session, and clean up by deleting the default home directory in the tearDown method using FileUtils.deleteDirectory. This test uses the ParameterizedTest and ValueSource annotations from JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the FTP client's file storage functionality using deflate transfer mode by establishing a connection to a local FTP server, authenticating with test credentials, and performing file upload operations. Initialize an FTP client instance and establish a connection to a localhost server on the provided port, then authenticate using the supplied username and password credentials. Set the file transfer mode to deflate compression mode and verify the operation succeeds. List the files in the current directory to confirm it is initially empty, asserting that zero files are present. Create test file content containing a timestamp string and upload it to the server using the store file method with a byte array input stream containing the UTF-8 encoded content. After the upload, list the files again to verify exactly one file now exists on the server. Read the uploaded file directly from the server's file system using the default home directory path and verify that the file content matches exactly what was originally uploaded by comparing the UTF-8 decoded bytes. Finally, ensure proper cleanup by logging out of the FTP client connection. The test also performs cleanup by deleting the default home directory and its contents in the teardown phase. This test uses the JUnit 5 testing framework with parameterized test support, specifically testing with the deflate transfer mode parameter.

This test validates the FTP client's passive mode reply parsing behavior when the NAT workaround strategy is disabled and the IP address usage from PASV responses is toggled. Initialize an FTP client instance with a custom passive NAT workaround local client configured with an external IP address of "8.8.8.8", then disable the passive NAT workaround strategy by setting it to null. Enable IP address extraction from PASV responses and call the internal passive mode reply parsing method with a sample PASV response string "227 Entering Passive Mode (172,16,204,138,192,22)." containing IP address components and port information. Assert that the passive host is correctly extracted as "172.16.204.138" from the response. Next, disable IP address extraction from PASV responses and parse the same PASV response again. Assert that the passive host is now null, demonstrating that the client ignores the IP address from the server response when this feature is disabled. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that type assignment compatibility checks work correctly between parameterized types and their corresponding generic array types. Initialize a parameterized type by combining a raw class with a specific type argument, then verify the parameterized type's structure by asserting that its raw type and type arguments match the expected values. Confirm that the parameterized type is not a generic array type and vice versa through class assignment checks. Create a generic array type from the parameterized type, then validate that assignment compatibility checks return false in both directions between the parameterized type and the generic array type, ensuring that these distinct type representations are properly recognized as incompatible for assignment purposes. The test uses JUnit for assertions and validation.

This test validates the type assignability behavior between generic array types and parameterized types using reflection utilities. Initialize two class references representing a constructor class and an insets class as the raw type and type argument respectively. Create a parameterized type by combining the raw class with the type argument class, then assert that the raw type matches the expected constructor class and the first type argument matches the insets class. Verify that the parameterized type is not a generic array type and that generic array types are not assignable from the parameterized type class. Generate a generic array type from the parameterized type using type utilities. Assert that the parameterized type is not assignable to the generic array type by calling the type assignability utility method, and similarly assert that the generic array type is not assignable to the parameterized type, with both assertions including formatted error messages containing the type representations. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and configure it to set the null text representation to the string "NULL" using the setNullText method, then append a null String value using the append method, which should result in the null text being appended instead of the literal null value. Assert that the string representation of the builder using toString equals "NULL" to verify the null handling behavior. Create a fresh StrBuilder instance and append a new StringBuilder object containing the string "foo" using the append method, then assert that toString returns "foo" to confirm proper StringBuilder appending. Continue with the same StrBuilder instance and append an empty StringBuilder object using append, then assert that toString still returns "foo" to verify that empty StringBuilder objects do not modify the content. Finally, append another StringBuilder containing "bar" to the existing StrBuilder and assert that toString returns "foobar" to validate that multiple StringBuilder append operations concatenate correctly. This test validates the StrBuilder class's append method behavior when handling null String values with custom null text configuration and when appending StringBuilder objects of varying content lengths, ensuring proper string concatenation and null value substitution functionality. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that generic array types and parameterized types are not assignable to each other in either direction within the TypeUtils type assignment checking system. Initialize a raw class variable with the Constructor class and a type argument class variable with the Insets class, then call the TypeUtils parameterize method with these two classes to build a ParameterizedType representing Constructor<Insets>. Assert that the parameterized type's raw type equals the Constructor class using assertEquals, and assert that the first actual type argument equals the Insets class using assertEquals. Verify that GenericArrayType is not assignable from the parameterized type's class using assertFalse with the isAssignableFrom method, and confirm the reverse relationship is also false using assertFalse with isAssignableFrom in the opposite direction. Create a GenericArrayType by calling TypeUtils genericArrayType method with the parameterized type as the argument. Assert that TypeUtils isAssignable returns false when checking if the parameterized type is assignable to the generic array type using assertFalse with a lambda supplier that formats a descriptive error message containing both type representations. Assert that TypeUtils isAssignable returns false when checking if the generic array type is assignable to the parameterized type using assertFalse with a lambda supplier that formats a descriptive error message containing both type representations. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the atomic get-and-decrement operation on a mutable numeric wrapper that returns the original value before modification. Initialize a mutable numeric container with an initial positive value, then call the get-and-decrement operation which should return the original value while simultaneously reducing the internal value by one. Assert that the returned value matches the original value, then verify that the internal state has been decremented by checking both the integer and long representations of the updated value. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the parsing behavior of passive mode server responses when no NAT workaround strategy is configured and the IP address usage setting is toggled. Initialize an FTP client with a specific external host address and disable the passive NAT workaround strategy by setting it to null. Enable the IP address extraction from passive mode responses, then parse a passive mode reply containing encoded IP and port information. Verify that the passive host is correctly extracted and matches the expected IP address from the server response. Next, disable the IP address extraction from passive mode responses and parse the same passive mode reply again. Confirm that the passive host is now null, indicating that the client ignores the server-provided IP address when this setting is disabled. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the atomic get-and-decrement operation of a mutable short wrapper class. Initialize a mutable short object with an initial value of 1, then call the get-and-decrement method which should return the original value before modification and simultaneously decrement the internal state. Assert that the returned result equals 1, confirming the method returned the pre-decrement value, then verify the object's internal state has been decremented by checking that both its integer and long value representations now equal 0. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a string builder with the text "abcbccba" and test the delete all string method's behavior with various input scenarios. Call the delete all method with a null string parameter and assert that the original content remains unchanged. Call the method with an empty string and verify the content is still "abcbccba". Test with a non-existent character "X" and confirm no changes occur. Remove all occurrences of the character "a" and assert the result is "bcbccb". Continue by deleting all "c" characters to get "bbb", then remove all "b" characters to produce an empty string. Reinitialize the builder with "abcbccba" and test removing the substring "bc", verifying the result is "acba". Finally, test the method on an empty string builder by removing "bc" and confirming it remains empty. Each assertion validates that the delete all string method correctly removes all instances of the specified string from the builder's content. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that array shuffling functionality produces a randomized arrangement while preserving all original elements. Initialize a large integer array with repeating sequential patterns to reduce the likelihood of spurious test failures due to coincidental ordering. Create a duplicate copy of this array to serve as a reference for comparison. Apply the shuffling operation to the original array, then verify that the shuffled result differs from the original arrangement by asserting the arrays are not equal. Finally, confirm that all elements from the original array are still present in the shuffled version by iterating through each element in the reference copy and asserting its existence in the shuffled array. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the atomic get-and-decrement operation functionality of a mutable short wrapper, specifically testing that the getAndDecrement method returns the original value before decrementing and properly updates the internal state. Initialize a MutableShort instance with the short value 1, then call the getAndDecrement method on this instance, which programmatically captures the current value in a local variable, decrements the internal value field by one, and returns the captured original value, providing atomic-like behavior for retrieving the pre-decrement value while simultaneously performing the decrement operation. Assert that the returned result equals 1 to validate that the method correctly returned the original value before modification. Subsequently, verify the internal state changes by calling intValue on the MutableShort instance and asserting it equals 0 to confirm the decrement operation successfully reduced the internal value from 1 to 0. Finally, call longValue on the same instance and assert it equals 0L to validate that the type conversion methods correctly reflect the updated internal state after the decrement operation. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the array shuffling functionality by creating a large integer array containing repeated sequences of digits zero through nine to ensure sufficient data for reliable randomization testing. Initialize an integer array with 130 elements following the pattern of repeated digit sequences, then create a clone of this original array using array utilities. Apply the shuffle operation to the first array while keeping the second array unchanged as a reference. Assert that the shuffled array is not equal to the original array to verify that randomization occurred. Iterate through each element in the original array and assert that every element is still present in the shuffled array to confirm that shuffling preserves all original elements without loss or duplication. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

Test the append functionality of StrBuilder when appending another StrBuilder with specified start and length parameters, validating both null handling and boundary condition enforcement through multiple assertion types. Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and call setNullText with the string "NULL", then call append with a null StrBuilder reference, start index 0, and length 1, followed by asserting that toString returns "NULL" to verify null text substitution. Create a second StrBuilder instance and call append with a new StrBuilder containing "foo", start index 0, and length 3, then assert that toString returns "foo" to confirm successful partial appending. Store the second StrBuilder in a final variable and systematically test boundary violations by calling assertIndexOutOfBoundsException with lambda expressions that invoke append with various invalid parameter combinations: negative start index -1 with length 1, start index 3 (beyond bounds) with length 1, valid start index 1 with negative length -1, start index 1 with excessive length 3 that exceeds available characters, negative start index -1 with length 3, and start index 4 (completely out of bounds) with length 0, each accompanied by descriptive error messages. Verify edge case handling by calling append with start index 3 and length 0 on a StrBuilder containing "bar", asserting the result remains "foo" since zero-length appends should have no effect. Complete testing by calling append with a StrBuilder containing "abcbardef", start index 3, and length 3 to extract "bar", then assert the final result is "foobar" to confirm proper substring extraction and concatenation. This test uses the JUnit testing framework with @Test annotation.

This test validates the random shuffling functionality for integer arrays by ensuring that the shuffle operation produces a different arrangement while preserving all original elements. Initialize a large integer array containing 130 elements with repeating sequences of digits 0 through 9 to reduce the likelihood of spurious test failures that could occur with smaller arrays. Create a clone of this original array using the ArrayUtils clone method to preserve the initial state for comparison purposes. Execute the ArrayUtils shuffle method on the original array to randomly rearrange its elements in-place. Assert that the shuffled array is not equal to the original cloned array using assertFalse with Arrays equals to verify that the shuffle operation actually modified the array arrangement. Iterate through each element in the original cloned array and assert that every element is still present in the shuffled array using assertTrue with ArrayUtils contains, providing a lambda expression that generates an error message indicating which specific element was not found if the assertion fails. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the string builder's append functionality when adding another string builder with specified start and length parameters. Initialize a new string builder instance and configure it to use "NULL" as the null text representation, then call the append method with a null string builder, start index 0, and length 1, verifying that the result equals "NULL" when converted to string. Create a second string builder and append a new string builder containing "foo" with start index 0 and length 3, asserting that the output equals "foo". Test various boundary conditions by attempting to append a string builder containing "bar" with invalid parameter combinations including negative start indices like -1, out-of-bounds start indices like 3, negative lengths like -1, and length values that exceed the available characters such as length 3 starting at index 1, expecting IndexOutOfBoundsException for each invalid case. Verify that appending with start index 3 and length 0 produces no change to the existing "foo" content, and confirm that appending from a longer string builder "abcbardef" starting at index 3 with length 3 correctly extracts and appends "bar" to result in "foobar". The test uses standard JUnit assertions including assertEquals for content validation and a custom assertIndexOutOfBoundsException helper method for exception verification, executed with the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize an integer array to track method invocation counts and create a custom string builder subclass that overrides the append method for string builders with start index and length parameters to increment the first counter, and overrides the append new line method to increment the second counter. Call the append line method on this custom string builder instance with a new string builder containing "foo", a start index of 0, and a length of 3. Assert that the resulting string builder's string representation equals "foo" concatenated with the system line separator, verify that the append method was called exactly once by checking the first counter equals 1, and confirm that the append new line method was called exactly once by checking the second counter equals 1. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the FTP client's file retrieval functionality using deflate transfer mode by creating a test file in the default home directory with timestamped content, then establishing an FTP server connection to download and verify the file. Initialize a default home directory and create a test file named "test_download.txt" containing a timestamp-based string, then start an FTP server using the helper method with test credentials. Connect an FTP client to localhost on the provided port, authenticate with the test username and password, and configure the client to use the parameterized deflate transfer mode. List the files in the current directory and assert that exactly one file is present, then retrieve the file content into a byte array output stream and verify the downloaded content matches the original file content exactly. Finally, ensure the client logs out properly and the test cleans up by deleting the default home directory. The test uses JUnit 5 with ParameterizedTest and ValueSource annotations to test specifically with deflate transfer mode.

This test validates the functionality for finding the last occurrence of a character within a string builder, starting the search from a specified position and working backwards. Initialize a string builder with the content "abab" and verify that searching for character 'a' from position -1 returns -1, from position 0 returns 0, and from position 1 returns 0. Confirm that the behavior matches the standard string implementation by comparing results for the same search parameters. Test searching for character 'b' from position 2, which should return 1, and again verify consistency with string behavior. Verify that searching for a non-existent character 'z' from position 2 returns -1. Create a new string builder with content "xyzabc" and test that searching for character 'z' from the builder's length returns 2, while searching from position 1 returns -1. The test validates both edge cases with invalid starting positions and normal search scenarios, ensuring the backward character search functionality works correctly across different string contents and search positions. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of appending a string builder with a substring and automatically adding a new line. Initialize a counter array to track method invocations, then create a custom string builder that overrides the append method for string builders with start and length parameters to increment the first counter element, and overrides the new line append method to increment the second counter element. Create a new string builder containing the text "foo" and call the append-with-newline method on the custom builder, passing the new string builder along with a start index of zero and length of three. Verify that the resulting content equals "foo" followed by the system line separator, confirm that the append method was called exactly once by checking the first counter value, and confirm that the new line append method was called exactly once by checking the second counter value. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the lastIndexOf method's behavior when searching for a character starting from a specific index position within a StrBuilder instance. Initialize a StrBuilder with the string "abab" and call the lastIndexOf method with character 'a' and starting index -1, asserting that it returns -1 since negative indices should return no match. Call lastIndexOf with character 'a' and starting index 0, asserting it returns 0 as the search finds the character at position 0. Call lastIndexOf with character 'a' and starting index 1, asserting it returns 0 since the method searches backwards from index 1 and finds 'a' at position 0. Call lastIndexOf with character 'b' and starting index 2, asserting it returns 1 as the method finds 'b' at position 1 when searching backwards from index 2. Verify the StrBuilder's lastIndexOf method behaves identically to String's lastIndexOf by asserting that both "abab".lastIndexOf('b', 2) and the StrBuilder's lastIndexOf('b', 2) return the same value. Call lastIndexOf with character 'z' and starting index 2, asserting it returns -1 since 'z' is not present in the string. Initialize a new StrBuilder with "xyzabc" and call lastIndexOf with character 'z' and the builder's length as the starting index, asserting it returns 2 since 'z' is at position 2. Call lastIndexOf with character 'z' and starting index 1, asserting it returns -1 since searching backwards from index 1 does not find 'z' which is at position 2. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the string representation functionality for map data structures when appended to a string builder with different formatting options. Initialize a string builder with a base object and append an empty map using compact formatting, then verify the output shows a size indicator rather than the map contents. Create another string builder with the same base object and append the same empty map using detailed formatting, then confirm the output displays the map structure with proper indentation and braces. Repeat this process with a single-entry map containing one key-value pair, first verifying that compact formatting shows only the size information, and then confirming that detailed formatting presents the key-value pair with appropriate formatting and indentation within the map structure. After testing, reset the default string formatting style to ensure no side effects persist. This test uses JUnit framework for assertions and test execution.

This test validates the string representation behavior of a ToStringBuilder when appending map collections with different formatting options. Initialize a ToStringBuilder with a base integer object and use the predefined base string representation for comparison. Test the append functionality by adding an empty map with the key "a" using both compact and detailed formatting modes, asserting that the compact mode produces a size indicator while the detailed mode generates a formatted block structure with braces. Similarly, test with a single-entry map containing a key-value pair like "k" and "v", verifying that the compact format shows only the size while the detailed format displays the actual key-value content within a properly indented block structure. After testing, reset the ToStringBuilder's default style to ensure no side effects persist. The testing uses JUnit framework assertions.

This test validates the string builder's append method when working with string inputs and substring parameters. Initialize a new string builder instance and configure it to display "NULL" when null values are appended, then call the append method with a null string, start index of 0, and length of 1, verifying that the builder's string representation equals "NULL". Create a fresh string builder and append the substring "foo" using start index 0 and length 3, confirming the output matches "foo". Test various boundary conditions by attempting to append substrings with invalid parameters such as negative start indices like -1, start indices beyond the string length like 3 for a 3-character string, negative lengths like -1, and length values that exceed the remaining characters, expecting IndexOutOfBoundsException for each invalid case. Verify that appending with a valid start index at the string's end with zero length produces no change to the builder content. Test successful substring appending by adding "bar" from "abcbardef" starting at index 3 with length 3, then append "ard" from the same string starting at index 4 with length 3 using a CharSequence cast, confirming the final result is "foobarard". The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of appending string content with specified start and length parameters to a string builder. Initialize a DateFormat field of the test class using SimpleDateFormat with pattern "MMM dd, yyyy H:mm:ss.SSS" and English locale, then parse multiple Date fields including targetMinuteDate set to "June 1, 2008 8:15:00.000", januaryOneDate set to "January 1, 2008 0:00:00.000", and a Calendar field januaryOneCalendar configured with the januaryOneDate. Set the calendar field constant to Calendar.MINUTE, then parse three key dates: roundedUpDate as "June 1, 2008 8:16:00.000", roundedDownDate assigned to targetMinuteDate, and lastRoundedDownDate as "June 1, 2008 8:15:29.999". Call the helper method baseRoundTest with these dates and the calendar field, which internally tests the DateUtils round method with Date, Calendar, and Object parameters, asserting that roundedDownDate equals the result of rounding itself, roundedUpDate equals the result of rounding itself, lastRoundedDownDate rounds down to roundedDownDate, and dates one millisecond after lastRoundedDownDate round up to roundedUpDate, using assertEquals for all validations across Date, Calendar, and Object type inputs. Parse minDate as "December 31, 2007 23:59:30.000" and maxDate as "January 1, 2008 0:00:29.999", then call the helper method roundToJanuaryFirst with these dates and the calendar field, which validates that januaryOneDate and januaryOneCalendar round to themselves, that minDate and maxDate both round to januaryOneDate and januaryOneCalendar respectively, and that dates one millisecond before minDate and after maxDate do not round to January 1st, using assertEquals for positive assertions and assertNotEquals for boundary exclusion validations. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the array concatenation functionality that combines two arrays into a single new array containing all elements from both input arrays. Initialize pairs of arrays containing string elements, empty arrays, and arrays with null values, then call the array concatenation utility with various combinations including null inputs, empty arrays, and populated arrays. Assert that when both inputs are null, the result is null, and when one input is null, the result matches the non-null input array but is a new array reference. Verify that concatenating two populated arrays produces a new array containing all elements from the first array followed by all elements from the second array, maintaining the correct element type. Repeat this validation process across multiple primitive data types including boolean, character, byte, short, integer, long, float, and double arrays, ensuring each concatenation operation preserves the original arrays unchanged while creating properly typed result arrays. Assert that all resulting arrays have the expected content, length, element type, and are distinct references from the input arrays. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of the appendln method when called with a StrBuilder object and integer parameters for startIndex and length, ensuring that both the append and appendNewLine methods are properly invoked during execution. Initialize an integer array named count with two elements to track method invocations, then create an anonymous subclass of StrBuilder that overrides the append method with StrBuilder, int, and int parameters to increment the first array element and call the superclass implementation, and also overrides the appendNewLine method to increment the second array element and call the superclass implementation. Create a new StrBuilder instance containing the string "foo" and call the appendln method on the anonymous StrBuilder instance, passing this new StrBuilder along with startIndex value 0 and length value 3. Assert that the resulting string representation of the anonymous StrBuilder equals "foo" concatenated with the system line separator using assertEquals. Verify that the first count array element equals 1 to confirm the append method was called exactly once, and assert that the second count array element equals 1 to confirm the appendNewLine method was called exactly once. The test uses the JUnit testing framework with the @Test annotation.

This test validates the functionality of the appendAll method when called with an Object array parameter, ensuring it correctly handles null arrays, empty arrays, and arrays containing string elements. Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and call the appendAll method with a null Object array cast, then assert that the toString method returns an empty string. Clear the StrBuilder using the clear method and call appendAll with no arguments (empty varargs), then assert that toString returns an empty string. Clear the StrBuilder again and call appendAll with three string literals "foo", "bar", and "baz", then assert that toString returns the concatenated string "foobarbaz". Clear the StrBuilder once more and repeat the same appendAll call with "foo", "bar", and "baz", asserting that toString again returns "foobarbaz". The appendAll method programmatically iterates through the provided array elements and appends each one using the append method, effectively concatenating all non-null array elements into the builder's internal character buffer. This test ensures that users can reliably append multiple objects at once to a string builder, handling edge cases like null input gracefully while properly concatenating valid string elements. The testing is performed using the JUnit framework with the @Test annotation.

This test validates the tokenization behavior when both ignored patterns and trimming are applied to input text containing delimiters. Initialize a string tokenizer with a colon delimiter and configure it to ignore all occurrences of a specific text pattern and to trim whitespace characters from tokens, while also setting it to preserve empty tokens but convert them to null values. Process an input string that contains the ignored pattern interspersed throughout, along with the delimiter and whitespace that should be trimmed. Retrieve the first token and verify it contains only the remaining characters after ignoring the specified pattern and trimming whitespace. Retrieve the second token and confirm it similarly contains the cleaned content. Retrieve the third token and assert it is null, representing an empty token after processing. Verify that no additional tokens remain in the sequence. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the array concatenation functionality of an array utility class by exercising its addAll method across multiple scenarios and data types. Initialize two string arrays containing alphabetic characters like "a", "b", "c" and numeric characters like "1", "2", "3", then call the addAll method to verify null handling by passing both null arrays and asserting the result is null. Test single-array scenarios by concatenating a populated array with null and vice versa, asserting that the result is not the same reference as the input but contains equivalent content and maintains the correct component type. Verify normal concatenation by combining both string arrays and asserting the result contains all elements in sequence. Test edge cases using empty arrays and arrays containing null elements, ensuring proper handling in all combinations. Extend testing to primitive array types including boolean arrays with true/false values, character arrays with letter values, byte arrays with small numeric values, short arrays with medium numeric values, integer arrays with positive and negative values, long arrays with large numeric values, float arrays with decimal values, and double arrays with mathematical constants, applying the same null-handling and concatenation patterns for each type. Assert array equality for content verification, reference inequality to confirm new array creation, and component type equality to validate type preservation throughout all operations. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string tokenizer's ability to handle ignored text patterns and trimming operations during token parsing. Initialize a string tokenizer with an input string containing repeated "IGNORE" text interspersed with actual token content like "a", "b", and "c", using a colon as the delimiter character. Configure the tokenizer to ignore all occurrences of the literal string "IGNORE" by setting an ignored matcher, enable trimming of whitespace characters with a trimmer matcher, disable the filtering of empty tokens, and enable the conversion of empty tokens to null values. Call the next method to retrieve the first token and assert it equals "a", then call next again to get the second token and assert it equals "bc", followed by calling next once more and asserting the result is null since the third token should be empty and converted to null. Finally, verify that the hasNext method returns false, confirming no additional tokens remain. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the array concatenation functionality provided by the ArrayUtils utility class, specifically testing the addAll method's ability to combine two arrays of various types while handling null inputs correctly. Initialize two String arrays, one containing the elements "a", "b", "c" and another containing "1", "2", "3", then call the addAll method from ArrayUtils with null as both parameters and assert that the result is null using assertNull. Call addAll with the first String array and null as the second parameter, then assert that the returned array is not the same object as the input using assertNotSame, verify the contents match the original array using assertArrayEquals with both the original array and a new array literal containing "a", "b", "c", and confirm the component type is String class using assertEquals on the array's component type. Call addAll with null as the first parameter and the second String array, then perform similar assertions to verify the result matches the second array with elements "1", "2", "3" and has String component type. Call addAll with both non-null String arrays and assert the result contains the concatenated elements "a", "b", "c", "1", "2", "3" in order, verifying the component type remains String. Test edge cases by calling addAll with ArrayUtils.EMPTY_STRING_ARRAY and null, asserting the result equals the empty array, then test with null and ArrayUtils.EMPTY_STRING_ARRAY, and finally with two empty arrays, ensuring all results maintain String component type. Create a String array containing a single null element, call addAll to concatenate it with itself, and assert the result contains two null elements with String component type. Perform comprehensive testing across primitive array types including boolean arrays with values true/false and false/true, char arrays with 'a'/'b' and 'c'/'d', byte arrays with cast values 0/1 and 2/3, short arrays with cast values 10/20 and 30/40, int arrays with 1/1000 and -1000/-1, long arrays with 1L/-1L and 1000L/-1000L, float arrays with 10.5f/10.1f and 1.6f/0.01f, and double arrays with Math.PI/-Math.PI and 0/9.99, where each primitive type test includes calling addAll with null as the first parameter and a non-null second array, then with a non-null first array and null as the second parameter, asserting in each case that the non-null array is returned unchanged. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that a utility function correctly identifies the maximum value between two timestamp inputs. Initialize the test with predefined timestamp constants representing different points in time. Call the maximum utility function with various combinations of these timestamps, including cases where the first timestamp is earlier, later, or equal to the second timestamp. Assert that the function consistently returns the later timestamp when comparing different values, and returns the same timestamp when both inputs are identical. The validation covers all permutations to ensure the comparison logic handles edge cases properly. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that the collection of initializer names returned from a multi-background initialization results container is immutable and cannot be modified. First, establish a multi-background initialization setup by adding several child initializers with unique names, start the initialization process, and retrieve the results container. From the results container, obtain the collection of initializer names and create an iterator to traverse them. Advance the iterator to the first element, then attempt to remove that element using the iterator's removal functionality. Assert that this removal operation throws an unsupported operation exception, confirming that the names collection is read-only and prevents modification attempts. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of string tokenization with ignored character filtering and trimming capabilities when empty tokens are preserved as null values. Initialize a StrTokenizer instance with the input string "IGNOREaIGNORE: IGNORE bIGNOREc IGNORE : IGNORE " and configure it to use a colon character as the delimiter by calling the constructor with the delimiter parameter. Configure the tokenizer to ignore all occurrences of the literal string "IGNORE" by calling setIgnoredMatcher with a StrMatcher created using stringMatcher method, which will remove these character sequences from the input during tokenization. Set up trimming behavior by calling setTrimmerMatcher with a StrMatcher created using trimMatcher method to remove whitespace characters from the beginning and end of each token. Configure the tokenizer to preserve empty tokens by calling setIgnoreEmptyTokens with false, ensuring that empty tokens are not discarded during processing. Enable null representation for empty tokens by calling setEmptyTokenAsNull with true, which converts empty strings to null values. Execute the tokenization process by calling next method and assert that the first token equals "a" using assertEquals, verifying that the ignored characters and trimming have been properly applied to extract the clean token. Call next method again and assert that the second token equals "bc" using assertEquals, confirming that the tokenizer correctly processes consecutive non-ignored characters as a single token. Call next method a third time and assert that the result is null using assertNull, validating that the empty token between the two colons has been converted to null as configured. Verify that no additional tokens remain by calling hasNext method and asserting false using assertFalse, confirming that the tokenization is complete and all tokens have been properly extracted and processed. This test uses the JUnit testing framework, identified by the Test annotation and assertion methods.

This test validates the maximum value determination functionality for Instant objects by exercising the max method's ability to correctly identify the later of two temporal values. The test evaluates the PoolImplUtils class's max method behavior across different comparison scenarios and asserts that the chronologically later Instant is consistently returned. Initialize the test by accessing two test class fields: INSTANT_0 and INSTANT_1, both of type Instant that are private static final fields of the test class. Call the max method from the PoolImplUtils class four times with different parameter combinations to test all possible ordering scenarios. Assert that when INSTANT_0 and INSTANT_1 are passed as arguments, the method returns INSTANT_1 using assertEquals validation. Assert that when INSTANT_1 and INSTANT_0 are passed as arguments, the method returns INSTANT_1 using assertEquals validation, confirming parameter order independence. Assert that when INSTANT_1 and INSTANT_1 are passed as arguments, the method returns INSTANT_1 using assertEquals validation, verifying identical value handling. Assert that when INSTANT_0 and INSTANT_0 are passed as arguments, the method returns INSTANT_0 using assertEquals validation, confirming consistent behavior with identical earlier values. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation and assertEquals assertion method.

This test validates the constructor and accessor methods of an eviction configuration component used in object pool management. Initialize an eviction configuration instance using a constructor that accepts three parameters: two duration values of one millisecond each for idle eviction timing and soft idle eviction timing, and an integer value of one for the minimum idle count. After construction, verify that the idle eviction duration accessor returns exactly one millisecond, the idle soft eviction duration accessor also returns one millisecond, and the minimum idle accessor returns the integer value one. Finally, call the string representation method on the configuration instance and assert that the resulting string is not empty to ensure the toString method executes without throwing exceptions. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the maximum instant comparison utility method within the pool implementation utilities. Initialize two instant constants representing different points in time, with one instant occurring before the other chronologically. Call the maximum utility method four times with different combinations of the two instant values: first with the earlier instant followed by the later instant, then with the later instant followed by the earlier instant, then with the later instant compared to itself, and finally with the earlier instant compared to itself. Assert that each call returns the expected maximum instant value, verifying that the utility correctly identifies the later of two instants in all parameter orderings and handles identical instant comparisons properly. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the client wait statistics tracking functionality of a generic keyed object pool by measuring borrow wait times under different scenarios. Initialize a simple factory with a make latency of 200 milliseconds to simulate object creation delay, then create a generic keyed object pool using this factory and default configuration. Borrow an object from the pool using the key "one", which will trigger object creation and introduce the configured latency. Assert that both the maximum and mean borrow wait time metrics are at least 100 milliseconds, accounting for the creation delay with some tolerance for clock precision. Return the borrowed object to the pool, then immediately borrow another object using the same key "one". Since the object already exists in the pool, this second borrow should not require creation time, so assert that the maximum borrow wait time remains above 100 milliseconds while the mean borrow wait time falls below 200 milliseconds but stays above 20 milliseconds, demonstrating that the pool correctly tracks and averages wait times across multiple borrow operations. The test uses a try-with-resources block to ensure proper cleanup of the pool. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that the multi-background initializer results component properly protects its initializer names collection from modification. Initialize a multi-background initializer and populate it with five child background initializers using sequential naming, then start the initialization process and retrieve the results object. Call the helper method to set up this state and verify that the correct number of initializers are present, their names are accessible, result objects are properly wrapped integers, no exceptions occurred, and child initializers are configured correctly. Once the results object is obtained, access its initializer names collection and retrieve an iterator from this set. Advance the iterator to the next element, then attempt to remove that element from the underlying collection through the iterator's remove method. Assert that this removal operation throws an UnsupportedOperationException, confirming that the initializer names collection is immutable and cannot be modified after initialization completion. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that an eviction configuration can be properly constructed with minimal duration and idle count values. Initialize an eviction configuration with one-millisecond durations for both idle eviction and soft idle eviction timeouts, along with a minimum idle count of one. Verify that the configuration correctly stores and returns the one-millisecond idle eviction duration, the one-millisecond soft idle eviction duration, and the minimum idle count of one through their respective accessor methods. Additionally, confirm that the string representation functionality operates without errors by ensuring the generated string output is not empty. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the constructor functionality of the EvictionConfig class to ensure proper initialization and field assignment when creating an eviction configuration object. The test constructs an EvictionConfig instance using the three-parameter constructor with Duration.ofMillis(1) for both idle eviction duration and idle soft eviction duration parameters, and the integer value 1 for the minimum idle parameter, then verifies that all three configuration values are correctly stored and retrievable through getter methods, and confirms the toString method produces non-empty output. Initialize a new EvictionConfig object by calling the constructor with Duration.ofMillis(1) as the first parameter representing the idle eviction duration, Duration.ofMillis(1) as the second parameter for the idle soft eviction duration, and the integer 1 as the third parameter for the minimum idle count. Assert that the getIdleEvictDuration method returns a Duration with toMillis equal to 1 to verify the idle eviction duration was properly set. Assert that the getIdleSoftEvictDuration method returns a Duration with toMillis equal to 1 to confirm the idle soft eviction duration was correctly assigned. Assert that the getMinIdle method returns the integer value 1 to validate the minimum idle count was stored accurately. Call the toString method on the EvictionConfig instance and assert that the returned string is not empty using assertFalse with isEmpty to ensure the string representation functionality works properly. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation and assertEquals and assertFalse assertion methods.

This test validates that an object pool's automatic eviction mechanism properly removes idle objects over time according to configured parameters. Initialize a pool with a factory and configure it to hold up to 500 objects with eviction settings that remove 100 objects per eviction run, mark objects for eviction after a short idle duration, run eviction checks every 500 milliseconds, and validate objects while idle. Borrow 500 objects from the pool and immediately return them all to create a full set of idle objects. Wait for the eviction process to run and assert that the number of idle objects progressively decreases below specific thresholds as time passes, eventually reaching zero idle objects. Repeat the entire borrowing and returning cycle a second time to verify that the eviction behavior remains consistent across multiple uses. Throughout the process, verify that the pool correctly reduces its idle count at each checkpoint, confirming that the eviction timer and validation mechanisms work as expected. After completion, clean up the pool resources and verify that no management beans remain registered and that the eviction timer has been properly shut down. This test uses JUnit for assertions and timeout management.

This test validates the hour-of-day rounding functionality of the DateUtils utility class, specifically testing that dates are correctly rounded to the nearest hour boundary when using the Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY field. Initialize a DateFormat field of the test class as a SimpleDateFormat with pattern "MMM dd, yyyy H:mm:ss.SSS" and English locale, then parse multiple Date fields including targetHourOfDayDate set to "June 1, 2008 8:00:00.000" and januaryOneDate set to "January 1, 2008 0:00:00.000", along with a Calendar field januaryOneCalendar configured with the januaryOneDate time. Set the calendar field constant to Calendar.HOUR_OF_DAY, then parse roundedUpDate to "June 1, 2008 9:00:00.000", assign roundedDownDate to the existing targetHourOfDayDate, and parse lastRoundedDownDate to "June 1, 2008 8:29:59.999". Call the helper method baseRoundTest with these dates and the calendar field, which internally tests DateUtils.round method behavior by adding one millisecond to the last round down date to create a first round up date, then asserting equality between expected rounded dates and actual results from DateUtils.round for both Date objects, Calendar objects, and generic Object parameters, validating that dates round down when closer to the lower boundary and round up when closer to the upper boundary. Parse minDate to "December 31, 2007 23:30:00.000" and maxDate to "January 1, 2008 0:29:59.999", then call the helper method roundToJanuaryFirst with these dates and the calendar field, which verifies that dates within the rounding range of January 1st correctly round to januaryOneDate and januaryOneCalendar, while dates outside this range by one millisecond do not equal the January 1st targets, using assertEquals for positive cases and assertNotEquals for boundary validation cases. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the hour-of-day rounding functionality of a date utility component by initializing a date formatter with English locale and creating various target dates representing different time scenarios including January 1st 2007, June 1st 2008 at different hours, minutes, seconds, and milliseconds, along with a January 1st 2008 reference date and corresponding calendar instance. Set the calendar field to represent hour-of-day and define expected rounded dates including a rounded-up date at 9:00 AM, a rounded-down date at 8:00 AM, and a last rounded-down date at 8:29:59.999 AM on June 1st 2008. Call the base round test helper which exercises the date utility's round method with both Date and Calendar objects, asserting that dates round correctly to the nearest hour boundary by comparing the results against expected rounded-up and rounded-down values, and also testing the round method when passed as generic objects. Additionally, define minimum and maximum dates around December 31st 2007 and January 1st 2008 to test edge cases, then call the January first rounding helper which validates that dates within the rounding boundary correctly round to January 1st 2008, while dates outside the boundary do not, using both Date and Calendar representations and asserting equality for valid cases and inequality for boundary violations. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that client wait time statistics are accurately tracked when borrowing objects from a keyed pool with artificial creation latency. Initialize a factory with a creation delay of 200 milliseconds to simulate slow object creation, then create a keyed object pool using this factory with default configuration. Borrow an object using a specific key, which will trigger object creation and introduce the configured latency, then verify that both the maximum and mean borrow wait times are at least 100 milliseconds to account for the creation delay with some tolerance for timing variations. Return the borrowed object to the pool, then immediately borrow another object with the same key, which should retrieve the existing object without creation delay. Assert that the maximum borrow wait time remains above 100 milliseconds from the first borrow, while the mean borrow wait time should be less than 200 milliseconds but greater than 20 milliseconds, reflecting the average of the slow first borrow and the fast second borrow. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the eviction behavior of a generic object pool by configuring eviction parameters and observing how idle objects are progressively removed over time. Initialize a simple factory and generic object pool during setup, then configure the pool with a maximum of 500 idle and total objects, 100 tests per eviction run, a minimum evictable idle duration of 250 milliseconds, eviction runs every 500 milliseconds, and enable testing while idle. Borrow 500 objects from the pool using an array to track active objects, then return all 500 objects back to the pool to make them idle. Sleep for 1000 milliseconds and assert that the number of idle objects is less than 500, then continue sleeping for 600 millisecond intervals while asserting that the idle count progressively decreases below 400, 300, 200, and 100 objects, finally reaching exactly zero idle objects. Repeat the entire borrowing and returning cycle with the same 500 objects, followed by the same series of sleep intervals and assertions to verify consistent eviction behavior across multiple cycles. During teardown, clear and close the object pool, unregister any remaining MBeans from the platform MBean server, assert that no pools remain registered, and verify that the eviction timer executor is properly shut down. This test uses the JUnit framework with a timeout annotation set to 60 seconds.

This test validates that the pool correctly handles concurrent access scenarios when validation failures occur during object invalidation without throwing null pointer exceptions. Initialize a pool with a simple factory, configure it to have a maximum of one total object, enable validation on object creation, and set the maximum wait time to indefinite. Borrow an object from the pool, then configure the factory to make validation fail which will cause subsequent object creation attempts to return null. Create and start a waiting test thread that will attempt to borrow from the pool with a specified pause duration, then allow some time for the thread to begin its borrowing attempt. Invalidate the previously borrowed object while the waiting thread is blocked, then restore the factory to allow successful validation so the waiting thread can be served with a valid object. The test verifies that the pool maintains proper state management and thread coordination when objects are invalidated concurrently with pending borrow requests, ensuring no null pointer exceptions occur during this complex interaction. This test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the automatic eviction functionality of an object pool system where idle objects are progressively removed over time based on configured eviction parameters. The test exercises the GenericObjectPool class's eviction mechanism by configuring specific timing and capacity parameters, then observing how idle objects are systematically removed through multiple eviction cycles, with assertions validating the decreasing idle object counts at each stage. Initialize a SimpleFactory instance and create a GenericObjectPool using this factory as a test class field, then configure the pool by calling setMaxIdle with 500, setMaxTotal with 500, setNumTestsPerEvictionRun with 100, setMinEvictableIdleDuration with a duration of 250 milliseconds, setDurationBetweenEvictionRuns with a duration of 500 milliseconds, and setTestWhileIdle with true to enable idle object validation during eviction. Create a String array of size 500 to hold active objects, then execute a loop 500 times calling borrowObject on the pool to obtain objects and store them in the array, followed by another loop 500 times calling returnObject to return all borrowed objects back to the pool, making them idle. Call sleepQuietly on the Waiter class with 1000 milliseconds to allow the first eviction cycle to complete, then assert using assertTrue that getNumIdle returns a value less than 500 with an appropriate failure message. Continue this pattern by calling sleepQuietly with 600 milliseconds followed by assertTrue assertions that getNumIdle is progressively less than 400, 300, 200, and 100, culminating in an assertEquals assertion that getNumIdle equals 0 to verify all idle objects have been evicted. Repeat the entire borrowing and returning cycle again with 500 objects, then perform the same sequence of sleep and assertion calls to validate that the eviction behavior is consistent across multiple test iterations. During teardown, retrieve the JMX name from the pool, clear and close the pool, nullify the pool and factory references, query the MBean server for any remaining registered pools, unregister any found pools while building a detailed error message, and assert that no pools remain registered with assertEquals expecting 0 registered pools, followed by yielding the current thread and sleeping for 1000 milliseconds if the EvictionTimer executor exists, then asserting with assertNull that the EvictionTimer executor is null. This test uses the JUnit testing framework with Test and Timeout annotations specifying a 60-second timeout with millisecond precision.

This test validates that client wait statistics are accurately tracked when borrowing objects from a keyed object pool, specifically testing the timing metrics for object creation latency and subsequent borrowing operations. Initialize a SimpleFactory with a makeLatency of 200 milliseconds to simulate object creation delay, then create a GenericKeyedObjectPool using this factory and a default GenericKeyedObjectPoolConfig. Call borrowObject with the key "one" to retrieve the first object, which will trigger object creation and introduce the configured latency. Assert that getMaxBorrowWaitTimeMillis returns a value of at least 100 milliseconds, allowing for clock timing variations, and similarly assert that getMeanBorrowWaitTimeMillis also returns at least 100 milliseconds, both validating that the initial borrow wait time reflects the object creation delay. Return the borrowed object to the pool using returnObject with the key "one" and the object instance. Call borrowObject again with the same key "one" to retrieve an object that should already exist in the pool, eliminating creation latency. Assert that getMaxBorrowWaitTimeMillis remains greater than 100 milliseconds from the first borrow operation, assert that getMeanBorrowWaitTimeMillis is now less than 200 milliseconds since the average includes both the slow first borrow and the fast second borrow, and assert that getMeanBorrowWaitTimeMillis is greater than 20 milliseconds to ensure the timing calculations are reasonable. The pool is automatically closed through the try-with-resources statement, ensuring proper cleanup. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates the utility method's ability to extract the correct generic type parameter from a factory class that implements a parameterized interface. The test specifically examines the PoolImplUtils class's getFactoryType method to ensure it correctly identifies and returns the Long class as the factory type when analyzing the NotSimpleFactory class. Call the getFactoryType method on the PoolImplUtils class, passing NotSimpleFactory class as the argument, and capture the returned Class object result. Assert that the result equals Long class using assertEquals, which validates that the utility method successfully extracted the Long type parameter from the NotSimpleFactory's generic interface implementation rather than returning a simple or default type. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that client wait time statistics are accurately tracked during object borrowing operations from a pool. Initialize a factory with a creation latency of 200 milliseconds to simulate object creation delays, then create a pool using this factory with default configuration settings. Borrow an object from the pool, which will trigger object creation and introduce the configured latency, then assert that both the maximum and mean borrow wait times are at least 100 milliseconds to account for the creation delay with some tolerance for timing variations. Return the borrowed object to the pool to make it available for subsequent operations. Borrow another object from the pool, which should now retrieve the previously created and returned object without requiring new object creation. Assert that the maximum borrow wait time remains above 100 milliseconds from the first operation, while the mean borrow wait time should be less than 200 milliseconds but greater than 20 milliseconds, reflecting the average of the two borrow operations where the second borrow had minimal wait time. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a utility can correctly determine the factory type for a non-simple factory implementation. Call the utility method to extract the factory type from a non-simple factory class, then assert that the returned type matches the expected Long class type. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the factory type resolution utility's ability to correctly identify the return type of a non-simple factory class. Call the utility method to get the factory type from a not-simple factory class, then assert that the returned class type equals the Long class type. The test uses JUnit as the testing framework.

This test verifies that a generic keyed object pool properly handles exceptions thrown during object passivation when returning borrowed objects. Initialize a simple factory and a generic keyed object pool using the factory during setup. Borrow a string object from the pool using the key "one". Configure the simple factory to throw exceptions during the passivation process by setting its throw exception on passivate flag to true. Return the borrowed object to the pool using the same key "one", which should trigger the passivation exception. Assert that the number of idle objects in the pool equals zero, confirming that the object was not successfully returned to the idle pool due to the passivation failure. Close the pool to complete the test. During teardown, clear and close the pool, nullify the pool and factory references, query the MBean server for any remaining registered pool instances, unregister any found pools, and assert that no pools remain registered. This test uses the JUnit testing framework with timeout annotations.

This test validates that when an exception occurs during object passivation while returning a borrowed object to the pool, the object is properly discarded rather than being added to the idle pool. Initialize a pool with a simple factory that can be configured to throw exceptions during passivation operations. Borrow an object from the pool to simulate normal usage, then configure the factory to throw an exception during the passivation phase. Return the borrowed object to the pool, which should trigger the passivation exception and cause the pool to discard the object rather than storing it as idle. Assert that the pool contains no idle objects, confirming that the problematic object was properly discarded when passivation failed. The test includes cleanup that verifies no pool instances remain registered and that background eviction timers are properly shut down. This test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates that date and time rounding functionality correctly rounds timestamps to the nearest hour of day boundary. Initialize a date formatter and create various target dates representing different time components including specific hour-of-day timestamps, along with boundary dates for January first scenarios.
