This test validates the error handling and time-based erosion behavior of the PoolUtils erodingPool method when applied to KeyedObjectPool instances, ensuring that null pool arguments and non-positive erosion factors are properly rejected while confirming that objects are automatically invalidated after a specified time period. Initialize a test by first asserting that IllegalArgumentException is thrown when calling PoolUtils erodingPool with null KeyedObjectPool arguments across three method overloads, then create an ArrayList called calledMethods to track method invocations and instantiate a MethodCallLogger InvocationHandler that overrides the invoke method to return Integer value 1 for any Integer return types to ensure getNumActive and getNumIdle methods return non-zero values. This test validates that a resilient factory wrapper correctly initializes with default configuration values when constructed with only a basic factory. This test validates the default constructor behavior of a resilient pooled object factory wrapper. This test validates the timing behavior of a pooled object within a generic object pool by examining how borrow and return operations affect various time-related metrics. The test constructs and verifies that a ResilientPooledObjectFactory properly initializes with default values when wrapping a FailingFactory, ensuring that monitoring and adding threads are not running initially and that all configuration parameters match their expected default values. Initialize a new FailingFactory instance to serve as the underlying object factory that will be wrapped by the resilient factory. Create a new ResilientPooledObjectFactory instance using the parameterized constructor that accepts the FailingFactory as the wrapped factory, which will initialize the resilient factory with default configuration values for monitoring behavior and object creation strategies. Call isMonitorRunning on the resilient factory instance and assert that it returns false to verify the monitoring thread is not automatically started upon construction. Call isAdderRunning on the resilient factory instance and assert that it returns false to confirm the adder thread responsible for proactively creating objects is not running initially. Call getLogSize on the resilient factory instance and assert that it equals the value returned by getDefaultLogSize to validate the makeObject event log size is set to the default value. Call getTimeBetweenChecks on the resilient factory instance and assert that it equals the value returned by getDefaultTimeBetweenChecks to verify the monitor thread check interval uses the default timing. Call getDelay on the resilient factory instance and assert that it equals the value returned by getDefaultDelay to confirm the delay between object creations by the adder thread is set to the default value. Call getLookBack on the resilient factory instance and assert that it equals the value returned by getDefaultLookBack to validate the time window for maintaining statistics uses the default duration. Call getMakeObjectLog on the resilient factory instance and assert that the returned list has a size of 0 to verify the makeObject event log is initially empty. Call setLogSize with the integer value 5 on the resilient factory instance to modify the log size configuration. Call getLogSize again on the resilient factory instance and assert that it returns 5 to confirm the log size setter properly updates the configuration. Call setTimeBetweenChecks with a Duration of 200 milliseconds on the resilient factory instance to modify the timing between monitor checks. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the Test annotation.

This test validates that timing information is accurately tracked and formatted for pooled objects throughout their lifecycle. Initialize a generic object pool with a simple factory, then capture the current system time and perform a series of operations with deliberate delays between each step: borrow an object from the pool, return it, and borrow it again, recording timestamps at key points. After completing these operations, retrieve information about all objects in the pool and verify that exactly one object exists. Extract the timing details for this object and validate that the creation time falls within the expected range between the first two timestamps, the last return time falls between the second and third timestamps, and the last borrow time falls between the third and fourth timestamps. Additionally, confirm that the formatted timestamp strings match the expected date format pattern for each timing event. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions and validation.

This test validates the timing information tracking capabilities of a generic object pool by creating a pool with a simple factory, then performing a sequence of borrow and return operations while capturing timestamps to verify that the pool correctly records creation, borrow, and return times for pooled objects. Initialize a generic object pool using a simple factory, capture the current system time in milliseconds, then sleep for 50 milliseconds before borrowing an object from the pool. Sleep again for 50 milliseconds, capture another timestamp, sleep once more for 50 milliseconds, then return the borrowed object to the pool. After another 50 millisecond sleep, capture a third timestamp, sleep again, borrow another object from the pool, sleep one final time, and capture a fourth timestamp. Retrieve all objects from the pool using the list all objects method and assert that exactly one object exists in the pool. Extract the pooled object information from the returned set and create a simple date formatter with the pattern "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss Z". Verify that the object's creation time falls between the first and second timestamps, assert that the formatted creation time string matches the expected date format, confirm that the last return time falls between the second and third timestamps with proper formatting, and validate that the last borrow time falls between the third and fourth timestamps with correct formatting. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a GenericObjectPool with a SimpleFactory instance using a try-with-resources statement to ensure automatic cleanup, then capture the current system time in milliseconds as the first timestamp and sleep for 50 milliseconds before borrowing a string object from the pool using the borrowObject method. Sleep for another 50 milliseconds and capture a second timestamp, then sleep again for 50 milliseconds before returning the borrowed object to the pool using the returnObject method. Sleep for 50 milliseconds and capture a third timestamp, then sleep for another 50 milliseconds before borrowing another object from the pool and sleeping for a final 50 milliseconds before capturing the fourth timestamp. Call the listAllObjects method on the GenericObjectPool to retrieve a Set of DefaultPooledObjectInfo objects and assert that the set contains exactly one element using assertEquals with the expected value of 1. Extract the single DefaultPooledObjectInfo object from the set using an iterator and create a SimpleDateFormat instance with the pattern "yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss Z" for timestamp formatting. Assert that the object's creation time retrieved via getCreateTime is greater than the first timestamp and less than the second timestamp using assertTrue assertions, and verify that the formatted creation time from getCreateTimeFormatted matches the SimpleDateFormat formatting of the creation time using assertEquals. Assert that the last return time from getLastReturnTime is greater than the second timestamp and less than the third timestamp, and verify its formatted representation matches the SimpleDateFormat output using assertEquals. Finally, assert that the last borrow time from getLastBorrowTime is greater than the third timestamp and less than the fourth timestamp, and confirm its formatted version matches the expected SimpleDateFormat output using assertEquals. This test validates the timing accuracy and formatting consistency of pooled object lifecycle timestamps including creation, borrowing, and return operations within a GenericObjectPool. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that a GenericObjectPool maintains its maximum total object count invariant under concurrent access with validation failures and destruction delays. The test configures a pool with specific validation and destruction behaviors, then exercises it with multiple concurrent threads to ensure the maximum total constraint is never violated. Initialize a SimpleFactory and GenericObjectPool in the setUp method, where the SimpleFactory is a field of the test class and the GenericObjectPool is parameterized with String and TestException types as a field of the test class. Configure the SimpleFactory by calling setEvenValid with false to make every other validation fail, setDestroyLatency with 100 to introduce a 100 millisecond delay during object destruction, setMaxTotal with 15 to bound the difference between makes and destroys, and setValidationEnabled with true to enable validation checks. Configure the GenericObjectPool by calling setMaxTotal with 15 to set the maximum total objects, setMaxIdle with -1 to allow unlimited idle objects, setTestOnReturn with true to validate objects when returned to the pool, and setMaxWait with a Duration of 1000 milliseconds to set the maximum wait time for borrowing objects. Execute the helper method runTestThreads with parameters 5 threads, 10 iterations, 50 millisecond delay, and the configured GenericObjectPool, which creates TestThread instances that concurrently borrow and return objects from the pool, starts each thread, waits for completion using Waiter sleepQuietly with 500 millisecond intervals, and fails the test if any thread encounters an error. In the tearDown method, retrieve the JMX name using getJmxName, clear and close the GenericObjectPool, nullify both pool and factory references, query the MBeanServer for any remaining registered pools using the pattern "org.apache.commoms.pool3:type=GenericObjectPool,*", unregister any found MBeans while building an error message with pool names and creation stack traces, assert that the registered pool count equals 0, yield the current thread, sleep for 1000 milliseconds if the EvictionTimer executor exists, and assert that the EvictionTimer getExecutor returns null. The test uses the Test and Timeout annotations with a 60 second limit and employs JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the constant utility methods in an object utilities class that return input values unchanged across all primitive data types and objects. Call the constant method with a boolean value of true and assert that it returns true, then call the constant method with numeric literals for each primitive type including byte value 3, character value 3, short value 3, integer value 3, long value 3, float value 3, and double value 3.0, asserting that each returns the exact same value passed in. Call the constant method with a string "abc" and assert it returns the same string. Create final variables using the constant methods with representative values such as boolean true, byte 127, character 'a', short 123, integer 123, long 123, float 1.0, and double 1.0, then assert each variable contains the expected value. Test the specialized byte constant method with an out-of-range value of negative 129 and assert it throws an IllegalArgumentException, then test with positive 128 and assert the same exception is thrown. Test the specialized short constant method with an out-of-range value of negative 32769 and assert it throws an IllegalArgumentException, then test with positive 32768 and assert the same exception is thrown. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a generic object pool maintains its maximum total object count invariant under concurrent access with validation failures and destruction delays. Initialize a simple factory and generic object pool during setup, then configure the factory to fail validation on every other attempt, introduce a 100 millisecond destruction latency, and enable validation while setting the maximum total objects to 15. Configure the pool with the same maximum total limit, unlimited maximum idle objects, return-time testing enabled, and a 1000 millisecond maximum wait duration. Execute concurrent operations by running 5 test threads that each perform 10 iterations with 50 millisecond delays, where each thread repeatedly borrows and returns objects from the pool while the factory's alternating validation failures and destruction delays stress the pool's ability to maintain its maximum object count constraint. After all threads complete, verify that no thread failures occurred and that the pool correctly enforced its maximum total invariant throughout the concurrent operations. During teardown, clear and close the pool, unregister any remaining JMX management beans, assert that no pools remain registered, and verify that the eviction timer executor has been properly shut down. This test uses JUnit 5 with a 60-second timeout annotation.

This test validates the thread safety and concurrent performance of a GenericKeyedObjectPool under high-load conditions with multiple threads simultaneously borrowing and returning objects. The test exercises the pool's ability to handle concurrent access patterns while maintaining proper resource management and thread synchronization, with assertions validating that all threads complete successfully without exceptions. Initialize a SimpleFactory instance and assign it to the simpleFactory field of the test class, then create a GenericKeyedObjectPool using this factory and assign it to the gkoPool field of the test class. Configure the pool by calling setMaxTotalPerKey with a value of 15 to limit the maximum number of objects per key, call setMaxIdlePerKey with a value of 15 to set the maximum idle objects per key, and call setMaxWait with a Duration of 1000 milliseconds to specify the maximum wait time for object borrowing. Execute the runTestThreads helper method with parameters 20 for the number of threads, 100 for iterations per thread, 50 for delay, and the configured gkoPool instance. The helper method creates 20 TestThread instances, each configured to perform 100 iterations with a 50-millisecond delay, starts each thread, and then monitors their completion by polling the complete method every 500 milliseconds using Waiter.sleepQuietly. For each completed thread, the helper method checks if the thread failed by calling the failed method, and if any thread failed, it calls fail with a detailed error message including the thread index and stack trace from the thread's exception field. During teardown, call the superclass tearDown method, retrieve the JMX name using getJmxName, clear the pool using clear, close the pool using close, nullify both gkoPool and simpleFactory fields, obtain the platform MBeanServer, query for any remaining registered GenericKeyedObjectPool MBeans, unregister each found MBean, and assert that the registered pool count equals 0 to ensure proper cleanup. This test uses the JUnit testing framework with Test and Timeout annotations specifying a 60-second timeout.

This test validates that a GenericKeyedObjectPool maintains its maximum total object count invariant under concurrent access with validation failures and object destruction delays. The test configures a pool with specific constraints and concurrent thread operations to ensure the pool correctly enforces its maximum total limit while handling validation failures and destruction latency. Initialize a SimpleFactory instance and a GenericKeyedObjectPool using the factory in the setUp method, storing them in the test class fields simpleFactory and gkoPool respectively. Configure the simpleFactory by calling setEvenValid with false to make every other validation fail, setDestroyLatency with 100 to introduce a 100 millisecond delay during object destruction, setMaxTotalPerKey with the maxTotal value of 15 to bound the difference between makes and destroys, and setValidationEnabled with true to enable validation. Configure the gkoPool by calling setMaxTotal with 15 to set the maximum total objects, setMaxIdlePerKey with -1 to allow unlimited idle objects per key, setTestOnReturn with true to validate objects when returned to the pool, and setMaxWait with a Duration of 10 seconds to set the maximum wait time for borrowing objects. Execute a helper method runTestThreads with parameters 5 threads, 10 iterations, 50 millisecond delay, and the configured gkoPool, which creates multiple TestThread instances that concurrently borrow and return objects from the pool, monitors their completion by sleeping for 500 milliseconds between checks, and fails the test if any thread encounters an exception. In the tearDownJmx method, retrieve the JMX name from gkoPool using getJmxName, clear and close the pool, set both pool and factory references to null, query the platform MBeanServer for any remaining registered GenericKeyedObjectPool MBeans, unregister any found MBeans while building a detailed message about their creation stack traces, and assert that the registered pool count equals 0 to ensure proper cleanup. This test uses the JUnit testing framework with Test and Timeout annotations, where the timeout is set to 60,000 milliseconds.

This test validates the append method's ability to handle Object type parameters by testing various object types and null values to ensure proper string concatenation behavior. Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and call appendNull to verify that appending null through this method results in an empty string when converted via toString. Call append with a null Object cast and assert that the result remains an empty string, demonstrating null handling consistency. Append the FOO constant (which represents the string "foo") and assert that toString returns "foo", confirming basic object-to-string conversion. Append a null StringBuffer cast and verify the result stays "foo", showing that null StringBuffer objects don't affect the builder content. Append a new StringBuffer containing "baz" and assert that toString returns "foobaz", validating StringBuffer content extraction. Append a new StrBuilder containing "yes" and assert the result becomes "foobazyes", confirming StrBuilder-to-StrBuilder concatenation. Append a CharSequence cast containing "Seq" and assert the final result is "foobazyesSeq", demonstrating CharSequence interface handling. Finally, append a new StringBuilder containing "bld" and assert the complete result is "foobazyesSeqbld", verifying StringBuilder integration and confirming that the append method supports StringBuilder objects as mentioned in the inline comment. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a string builder and append the text "barbaz", then verify the string representation equals "barbaz". Test the insert method's boundary validation by asserting that StringIndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown when attempting to insert an object at negative index -1 and at index 7 (beyond the current length). Insert a null object at index 0 and confirm the string remains "barbaz", then insert the string "foo" at index 0 and verify the result becomes "foobarbaz". Clear the builder and repeat this pattern for multiple data types: strings (testing null string insertion), character arrays (testing null arrays, empty arrays, and arrays with offset and length parameters), boolean values (true and false), single characters, integers, long values, float values, and double values. For each data type, verify boundary conditions by testing insertion at invalid negative and out-of-bounds positive indices, confirm null handling preserves the original string, and validate successful insertion at index 0 produces the expected concatenated result. The test uses JUnit framework with Test annotation.

This test validates the insertion functionality of a string builder across various data types and edge cases. Initialize a string builder and append an initial string value, then verify the content matches expectations. Test insertion behavior by attempting to insert at invalid negative and out-of-bounds indices, confirming that appropriate boundary exceptions are thrown for each data type including objects, strings, character arrays, booleans, characters, integers, longs, floats, and doubles. For valid insertions, insert null values and verify they do not change the builder content, then insert actual values at the beginning position and confirm the content reflects the prepended data. Clear the builder between different data type tests to reset the state. For character array insertions with offset and length parameters, validate that invalid offset and length values trigger boundary exceptions, while valid parameters successfully insert the specified portion. Repeat this pattern systematically for each supported data type, ensuring both the error handling for invalid indices and the successful insertion behavior for valid operations are properly validated. The testing uses JUnit framework.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and append the string "a b " to it, then call the asTokenizer method to create a StrTokenizer that tokenizes the builder's content using default whitespace delimiters. Call getTokenArray on the tokenizer to retrieve the initial token array and assert that it has a length of 2, with the first token being "a" and the second token being "b". Assert that the tokenizer's size method returns 2. Append "c d " to the original StrBuilder instance, then call getTokenArray again on the same tokenizer and assert that the returned array still has length 2 with tokens "a" and "b", demonstrating that the tokenizer does not automatically pick up changes to the builder after creation. Assert that the tokenizer size remains 2. Call the next method twice on the tokenizer to retrieve "a" and "b" sequentially. Call the reset method on the tokenizer to refresh it with the current builder content, then call getTokenArray again and assert that the array now has length 4 with tokens "a", "b", "c", and "d" in order. Assert that the tokenizer size is now 4. Call next four times to retrieve all tokens in sequence: "a", "b", "c", and "d". Finally, call getContent on the tokenizer and assert that it returns the complete string "a b c d ". This test validates that the StrBuilder asTokenizer method creates a linked tokenizer that can be reset to pick up builder changes, and that the tokenizer properly handles whitespace-delimited tokenization with default settings. The testing framework used is JUnit.

This test validates the constant utility methods in ObjectUtils that return the same values passed to them, ensuring proper handling of all primitive types and objects along with boundary condition validation for specialized byte and short constant methods. The test exercises the CONST method overloads for boolean, byte, char, short, int, long, float, double, and Object types, as well as the CONST_BYTE and CONST_SHORT methods, asserting that each method returns the exact input value and validating IllegalArgumentException throwing for out-of-range values. Call assertTrue on ObjectUtils CONST method with true as input and provide the assertion message "CONST(boolean)". Execute assertEquals assertions for each primitive type by calling ObjectUtils CONST method with specific literal values: byte 3, char 3, short 3, int 3, long 3L, float 3f, double 3.0, and string "abc", providing descriptive assertion messages for each type. Declare final variables using ObjectUtils CONST and CONST_BYTE/CONST_SHORT methods with various values including boolean true, byte 127, char 'a', short 123, int 123, long 123L and 3, float 1.0f, double 1.0, and string "abc", then assert each variable equals its expected value using assertEquals and assertTrue. Call assertIllegalArgumentException helper method to verify that ObjectUtils CONST_BYTE throws IllegalArgumentException when passed values -129 and 128, and ObjectUtils CONST_SHORT throws IllegalArgumentException when passed values -32769 and 32768, providing descriptive error messages for each boundary test. The test uses JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation and assertEquals, assertTrue assertion methods.

Initialize a string builder instance and call the method to append null text representation, then assert that the builder's string representation is empty. Next, append a null object cast explicitly to Object type and verify the builder remains empty. Append a string constant with value "foo" and confirm the builder's content equals "foo". Append a null StringBuffer object and assert the content remains "foo". Create and append a new StringBuffer containing "baz", then verify the builder content becomes "foobaz". Instantiate and append a new StrBuilder with content "yes", confirming the result is "foobazyes". Append a CharSequence cast string "Seq" and assert the final content equals "foobazyesSeq". Finally, create and append a new StringBuilder containing "bld" and verify the complete content becomes "foobazyesSeqbld". This test validates the string builder's append method behavior when handling various object types including null values, StringBuffer instances, StrBuilder instances, CharSequence objects, and StringBuilder instances, ensuring proper null handling and type-specific appending logic. The testing framework used is JUnit.

This test validates that string substitution functionality correctly handles templates containing unknown placeholder keys by leaving them unchanged in the output. Initialize a map containing key-value pairs for known substitution variables like animal and target identifiers. Create templates that include both known placeholders that should be replaced and unknown placeholders that should remain as-is in the final result. Execute the substitution process using multiple input formats including strings, character arrays, and various buffer types, testing both full template replacement and substring operations within specified boundaries. Verify that known placeholders are properly substituted with their corresponding values while unknown keys remain untouched in their original placeholder format. Confirm that in-place replacement operations return success indicators and that both complete and partial template processing produce the expected mixed results of substituted known values and preserved unknown placeholders. Clean up the test data after execution. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string substitution functionality when encountering unknown placeholder keys in template strings. Initialize a hash map containing key-value pairs for known variables like "animal" mapped to "quick brown fox" and "target" mapped to "lazy dog". Create a string substitutor instance using this map and test its behavior with template strings containing both known and unknown placeholder variables. Execute replacement operations on two test cases: first with a template containing an unknown "person" placeholder that should remain unchanged while the known "target" placeholder gets replaced, and second with a similar template that additionally includes an undefined number placeholder with a default value. For each test case, perform string substitution using multiple input types including strings, character arrays, string buffers, string builders, and custom string builder objects, testing both full string replacement and substring replacement operations. Assert that the substitutor correctly replaces known placeholders while leaving unknown ones untouched, and verify that in-place replacement methods return true to indicate successful processing. Clean up by nullifying the values map after test completion. This test uses JUnit framework.

This test validates that the alphabet converter properly rejects invalid character configurations when creating a converter with a do-not-encode list. Initialize three character arrays representing lowercase English letters, English letters combined with numbers, and numeric digits respectively. Call the alphabet converter's factory method to create a converter using the lowercase English array as the original alphabet, the English and numbers array as the target alphabet, and the numbers array as the do-not-encode list. Assert that this operation throws an IllegalArgumentException, then verify that the exception message indicates that the do-not-encode list cannot be used because the original alphabet does not contain the character '0'. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that XML numeric character references for supplementary Unicode characters are correctly converted back to their original character representations. Initialize test scenarios with XML strings containing numeric character references that represent supplementary characters, specifically using a high-value Unicode code point that requires surrogate pair representation. Call the XML unescaping functionality on a string containing only the numeric character reference to verify it produces the correct supplementary character. Assert that the result matches the expected surrogate pair representation of the character. Then call the same unescaping functionality on a mixed string containing both regular ASCII characters and the numeric character reference to ensure proper handling in combined contexts. Assert that the mixed content is processed correctly with the supplementary character properly decoded while preserving the surrounding text. The testing framework used is JUnit.

Initialize a string substitutor with an empty hash map for variable resolution, using identical prefix and suffix delimiters of "WV@i#y?N*[" and an asterisk escape character. Assert that the preserve escapes flag is disabled by default. Create a string buffer containing the same delimiter pattern "WV@i#y?N*[" and call the replace-in-place method on it, asserting that the method returns false indicating no substitutions were performed since no variables match the pattern. Finally, verify that the escape character is correctly set to asterisk by retrieving it from the substitutor. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the behavior of string substitution when encountering unknown placeholder keys, specifically testing that unknown keys remain unchanged in the output while known keys are properly replaced. Initialize a HashMap field of the test class containing key-value pairs with "animal" mapped to "quick brown fox" and "target" mapped to "lazy dog" during setup. Execute a helper method twice with different template strings that contain both known and unknown placeholder variables, where the first call uses a template "The ${person} jumps over the lazy dog." with expected result "The ${person} jumps over the ${target}." and substring processing enabled, and the second call uses template "The ${person} jumps over the lazy dog. 1234567890." with expected result "The ${person} jumps over the ${target}. ${undefined.number:-1234567890}." also with substring processing enabled. The helper method creates a StrSubstitutor instance initialized with the values map, then performs comprehensive testing by calling replace methods on multiple data types including String, char array, StringBuffer, StringBuilder, StrBuilder, and MutableObject, asserting that each returns the expected result where known keys like "target" are substituted while unknown keys like "person" and "undefined.number" remain as literal placeholder text. When substring processing is enabled, the helper method also tests substring replacement by calling replace methods with start index 1 and end index length minus 2, asserting the expected shortened result matches the substring of the full expected result. Additionally, the helper method tests in-place replacement using replaceIn methods on StringBuffer, StringBuilder, and StrBuilder objects, asserting that each returns true indicating replacement occurred and that the modified object's string representation matches the expected result. Clean up by setting the values field to null during teardown. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates that string substitution functionality correctly handles empty string templates without performing any replacements. Initialize a substitution engine with a map containing predefined variable mappings for animals and targets. Call the helper method with an empty string as the replacement template, which creates a string substitutor using the variable mappings and verifies that when given an empty string, the substitution process returns the original empty string unchanged across multiple input types including strings, character arrays, string buffers, and string builders, and confirms that in-place replacement operations return false indicating no modifications were made. Assert that the empty string remains unmodified and that no variable substitution occurs when the template contains no variable placeholders. Cleanup occurs by nullifying the variable mappings. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string substitution functionality of a string substitutor component when replacing variable placeholders with values from a map, specifically testing scenarios where template strings contain nested variable references without suffix delimiters. Initialize a hash map containing string key-value pairs representing template variables, such as "animal" mapped to "quick brown fox" and "target" mapped to "lazy dog". Create a string substitutor instance using this value map, then exercise the replacement functionality across multiple string representation types including String objects, character arrays, StringBuffer instances, StringBuilder instances, custom string builder objects, and mutable string objects. Test both full string replacement and substring replacement operations by calling the replace methods with templates containing nested variable syntax like "${animal}" and "${target}" placeholders. Assert that the substitutor correctly resolves these variable references to produce expected output strings, verifying that the "animal" placeholder becomes "quick brown fox" and "target" becomes "lazy dog" in the final result. Additionally, test in-place replacement operations on mutable string types, asserting that the replacement methods return true to indicate successful substitution and that the modified objects contain the expected resolved content. Clean up by nullifying the values map after test completion. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the behavior of string substitution functionality when performing in-place replacement operations on string buffers with specific delimiter configurations. Initialize a string substitution utility with an empty variable mapping and configure it to use identical custom prefix and suffix delimiters along with a specific escape character. Verify that the escape preservation feature is disabled by default. Create a string buffer containing only the delimiter pattern and attempt to perform an in-place replacement operation on it. Assert that the replacement operation returns false, indicating no substitutions were made since no variables were found within the delimiters. Finally, confirm that the escape character configuration remains unchanged after the operation. Cleanup occurs by nullifying the test data map. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the XML unescaping functionality for Unicode supplementary characters, specifically ensuring that numeric character references are correctly decoded into their corresponding UTF-16 surrogate pair representations. Initialize the test by calling the unescapeXml method from the StringEscapeUtils class with the input string containing the numeric character reference "𣎴" and assert that it equals the Unicode surrogate pair "\uD84C\uDFB4" using assertEquals, with the assertion message "Supplementary character must be represented using a single escape" to verify that supplementary characters are properly decoded from their numeric XML entity format. Next, call the unescapeXml method again with a more complex input string "a b c 𣎴" that mixes basic ASCII characters with the supplementary character reference, and assert that the result equals "a b c \uD84C\uDFB4" using assertEquals with the message "Supplementary characters mixed with basic characters should be decoded correctly" to ensure that the XML unescaping process correctly handles supplementary characters when they appear alongside regular characters in the same string. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the text capitalization functionality where the first letter of each word in a sentence is converted to uppercase while all other letters remain lowercase. The test specifically examines the capitalizeFully method from the WordUtils class when provided with an empty character array as a delimiter parameter, and asserts that the output matches the expected fully capitalized format. Initialize a test method annotated with @Test that calls the capitalizeFully method on the WordUtils class, passing the input string "i am fine now" as the first parameter and an empty character array as the second parameter which serves as the word delimiter specification. Assert using assertEquals that the method returns the string "I am fine now", validating that each word's first character has been capitalized to uppercase while maintaining lowercase for all subsequent characters in each word, demonstrating proper sentence case formatting when no custom delimiters are specified. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation and assertEquals assertion method.

This test validates the text capitalization functionality when provided with an empty delimiter array. Initialize a test that calls the word utility's full capitalization method with a lowercase input string and an empty character array as the delimiter parameter. Assert that the result transforms the entire input to proper case with the first letter of each word capitalized, demonstrating that when no specific delimiters are provided, the method defaults to standard word boundary detection for capitalization purposes. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the text capitalization functionality of a word utility component when provided with an empty character delimiter array. Initialize a test that calls the capitalize fully method on a lowercase input string such as "i am fine now" while passing an empty character array as the delimiter parameter. Assert that the method returns the expected result where each word's first letter is capitalized, producing output like "I Am Fine Now". This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that string substitution functionality correctly handles empty string templates by ensuring no replacement operations are performed. Initialize a map containing various key-value pairs including short single-character keys, longer multi-character keys, and semantic entries representing animals and targets. Create a string substitution component configured with this value map, then invoke the replacement process using an empty string as the template. Verify that the substitution mechanism properly recognizes empty strings as invalid templates and performs no replacement operations, maintaining the original empty input unchanged. Clean up the test data after execution. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the XML unescaping utility's ability to correctly decode supplementary Unicode characters from their numeric character reference format. Call the XML unescaping method with a numeric character reference representing a supplementary character (specifically Unicode code point 144308) and assert that it returns the correct UTF-16 surrogate pair representation. Then call the same unescaping method with a string containing basic ASCII characters mixed with the same supplementary character reference and assert that the result properly combines the unchanged ASCII characters with the correctly decoded supplementary character. Both assertions verify that supplementary characters are handled as single logical units rather than being split or corrupted during the unescaping process. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a string substitution utility correctly handles empty string templates without performing any replacements. Initialize a map containing various key-value pairs including short single-character keys like "a" mapped to "1", longer keys such as "aa" mapped to "11", and semantic keys like "animal" and "target" mapped to their respective actual values. Create a string substitutor instance using this populated map and pass an empty string as the replacement template to verify that no substitution operations are attempted when the input template is empty. Assert that the substitutor behaves correctly by not modifying or replacing any content when given an empty string input. Clean up by nullifying the values map after test completion. This test uses JUnit 5 testing framework.

This test validates the string substitution behavior when processing an empty string template. Initialize a string substitution component with a map containing animal and target key-value pairs representing a quick brown fox and lazy dog respectively. Create a string substitutor instance using the prepared values map, then call the replacement method with an empty string as the template. Assert that the result equals the original empty string input, demonstrating that no substitution occurs when there are no placeholder patterns to replace. Additionally, create a string builder with the empty template and verify that the in-place replacement operation returns false, indicating no modifications were made, and confirm the builder's content remains unchanged as the original empty string. After test completion, clean up the values map resource. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a string substitutor instance with default configuration, then verify its default string matcher implementations for both prefix and suffix matchers using helper assertion methods. This test validates that the longest common subsequence distance calculator properly handles null input by throwing an illegal argument exception. Call the assertStrMatcherSuffixImpl helper method from StrMatcherTest with "StringMatcher" and the substitutor to validate the suffix matcher implementation. This test validates that the longest common subsequence distance calculation properly handles null input by rejecting it with an appropriate error. This test validates the static replace functionality of a string substitution utility by verifying that variable placeholders in template strings are correctly replaced with corresponding values from a provided map. This test validates that string substitution functionality can replace variable placeholders within template text using a static utility method. Assert that the resulting string has the placeholder correctly replaced with the corresponding value from the mapping, producing the expected output text. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the creation and basic properties of a comma-matching string matcher through a factory. Confirm that the matcher can produce a string representation by checking that its string conversion is also not null. This test validates the functionality of a string matcher factory's comma matcher creation method. Assert that the returned comma matcher object is not null to verify successful instantiation. Assert that the matcher's string representation is not null to confirm the object has a valid string conversion method. This test validates the JSON escaping functionality for the delete control character to ensure proper string sanitization in JSON output. The test specifically examines the StringEscapeUtils class and its escapeJson method, asserting that the Unicode delete character is correctly escaped to its string representation. Assert that the returned escaped string equals "Delete: \\u007F" using assertEquals, which validates that the delete character has been properly escaped by converting the actual Unicode character to its escaped string representation with double backslashes. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the creation and basic properties of a comma character matcher through the StringMatcherFactory singleton instance. Initialize a StringMatcher by calling the commaMatcher method on the INSTANCE field of StringMatcherFactory, which is a public static final field of the test class that provides access to the singleton factory instance for creating various string matchers. The commaMatcher method returns a pre-configured CharMatcher that specifically matches comma characters in text processing operations. Assert that the returned StringMatcher is not null to verify successful instantiation. This test validates the static string substitution functionality where template strings with variable placeholders are replaced with actual values from a provided map. The test specifically examines the StringSubstitutor class's replace method and its ability to process variable substitution syntax, with assertions confirming the correct replacement output. Initialize a new HashMap with String keys and values, then populate it with a single entry where the key is "name" and the value is "commons". Call the static replace method on the StringSubstitutor class, passing a template string "Hi ${name}!" that contains a variable placeholder using dollar sign and curly brace syntax, along with the previously created map as the second argument. Use a helper method called assertEqualsCharSeq to validate that the result equals the expected string "Hi commons!", where this helper method internally performs an assertEquals assertion with a custom error message that includes the lengths of both the expected and actual character sequences using StringUtils length method. Initialize a string builder and append the text "a b " to it, then convert the builder to a tokenizer using the as tokenizer method. Retrieve the token array from the tokenizer and assert that it contains exactly 2 tokens with values "a" and "b", and verify the tokenizer size is 2. Append additional text "c d " to the original string builder, then retrieve the token array again from the same tokenizer and assert it still returns only the original 2 tokens "a" and "b" with size 2, demonstrating that the tokenizer maintains its original state. Use the tokenizer's next method to iterate through and assert the tokens "a" and "b" are returned in sequence. Reset the tokenizer to pick up the updated builder content, then retrieve the token array again and assert it now contains 4 tokens "a", "b", "c", "d" with size 4. Iterate through all tokens using the next method to verify they return "a", "b", "c", "d" in order, and finally assert that the tokenizer's content method returns the complete string "a b c d ". This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string builder's ability to append various object types while handling null values appropriately. Initialize an empty string builder, then call the null appending method and verify the result converts to an empty string. Append a null object cast explicitly and confirm it still produces an empty string. Append a simple string constant and assert the builder now contains that text. Append a null string buffer and verify no change occurs to the existing content. Append a non-null string buffer containing text and confirm it gets concatenated to the previous content. Append another string builder instance with different text and validate the combined result. Finally, append a character sequence and a string builder, checking that each addition properly concatenates to form the expected final string. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the tokenization capability that converts string content into individual tokens and maintains synchronization with the underlying string builder. Initialize a string builder and append some text content containing space-separated words. Convert the builder into a tokenizer using the tokenization conversion method. Retrieve the token array from the tokenizer and assert that it contains the expected number of tokens with the correct individual word values, then verify the tokenizer reports the correct size. Append additional text content to the original string builder and retrieve tokens again from the same tokenizer, asserting that the token count and values remain unchanged from the previous tokenization since the tokenizer has not been refreshed. Use the tokenizer's navigation methods to iterate through the available tokens and verify they return the expected word values. Reset the tokenizer to pick up the latest changes from the string builder, then retrieve the updated token array and assert it now contains all tokens from both the original and appended content with the correct count and individual values. Navigate through all tokens again using the iteration methods to confirm they return the expected sequence of words. Finally, retrieve the complete content from the tokenizer and assert it matches the full string representation of the builder. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string search functionality that locates substrings within a text builder starting from a specified position. Initialize a text builder with the content "abab" and perform multiple search operations to verify that the search method correctly finds substring occurrences from various starting positions. Test the search behavior with single character searches for "a" from different starting indices, including negative indices, boundary positions, and positions beyond the content length, asserting that the method returns the expected index or negative one when not found. Verify searches for longer substrings like "ab" and "ba" from specific positions, ensuring the results match the expected behavior of standard string searching. Test edge cases including searches for empty strings, substrings longer than the content, non-existent characters, and null inputs to confirm proper handling of boundary conditions. Create an additional text builder with different content "xyzabc" to test search functionality across varied character patterns and verify that all search operations return the correct indices or indicate when matches are not found. The testing framework used is JUnit.

This test validates the string representation functionality of a text string builder by initializing a builder with a predefined text value and confirming that the string conversion method returns the exact same content. Initialize a text string builder with the text content "abc", then call the string conversion method to retrieve the builder's current content as a string, and assert that the returned string equals "abc" to verify that the builder correctly maintains and outputs its internal text representation. The testing is performed using JUnit framework.

This test validates that character filters can be successfully removed from a random string generator configuration. Initialize a builder for random string generation with a character range from 'a' to 'z' and apply an initial character filter. Remove all filters by calling the filtering method with no arguments, then generate a string of 100 characters using the configured generator. Iterate through each character in the generated string and verify that characters other than 'a' are present, which would indicate the filter was successfully removed since the original filter would have restricted the output. If only 'a' characters are found throughout the entire string, fail the test as this suggests the filter remained active despite the removal attempt. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the custom variable resolution functionality when overriding the variable resolution method in a string substitution system. Initialize a text builder with a template string containing a variable placeholder with the name "name" surrounded by curly braces and preceded by a dollar sign. Create a map that associates the variable name "name" with the value "commons". Construct a string substitutor using this map but override the variable resolution method to perform custom validation and return a different value. In the overridden method, assert that the variable name parameter equals "name", verify that the buffer parameter is the same text builder instance, confirm the start position is 3, and validate the end position is 10, then return "jakarta" instead of the mapped value. Execute the substitution by calling the replace method on the text builder. Assert that the final result equals "Hi jakarta!" to confirm that the custom resolution method was invoked correctly and returned the expected replacement value rather than the value from the map. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a text string builder with the string content "abc", then call the toString method on the builder and assert that the returned string equals "abc". This test verifies that the toString method correctly converts the internal character buffer of the text string builder into a string representation, preserving the original content that was provided during construction. The test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the filter removal functionality of a random string generator builder by initializing a builder with a character range from 'a' to 'z' and applying an initial filter, then calling the filter method with no arguments to remove all filters, generating a string of 100 characters, and iterating through each character to verify that at least one character other than 'a' is present, which would indicate successful filter removal since the original filter would have restricted generation to only 'a' characters. If no non-'a' characters are found after checking all characters in the generated string, the test fails with an assertion indicating that the filter appears to have remained in place. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the insertion functionality of the StrBuilder class by testing various overloaded insert methods with different data types and edge cases. Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and append the string "barbaz" to establish a baseline state, then assert that the toString method returns "barbaz". Test boundary conditions by calling assertIndexOutOfBoundsException with lambda expressions that attempt to insert at invalid indices -1 and 7 using the insert method with an Object parameter, expecting StringIndexOutOfBoundsException to be thrown. Insert a null Object at index 0 and verify the builder content remains "barbaz", then insert the FOO constant at index 0 and assert the result is "foobarbaz". Clear the builder using the clear method and repeat the testing pattern for String insertion, including boundary validation with invalid indices, null string insertion, and valid string insertion at index 0. Continue this systematic approach for char array insertion, testing with null arrays, empty arrays, and arrays containing characters 'f', 'o', 'o', followed by testing the four-parameter insert method with char arrays, offset, and length parameters, validating boundary conditions for negative indices, out-of-bounds offsets, and invalid lengths. Test primitive data type insertion including boolean values (true and false), char values, int values, long values, float values, and double values, each time clearing the builder, appending "barbaz", validating boundary conditions with assertIndexOutOfBoundsException, and inserting values at index 0 to verify correct string conversion and concatenation. The test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a TextStringBuilder instance with the string literal "abc" as the constructor argument, which creates a mutable string builder containing the characters 'a', 'b', and 'c' in sequence. Call the toString method on this TextStringBuilder instance, which internally creates a new String object from the builder's character buffer using the current size to determine the substring bounds. Assert that the returned string equals the expected value "abc" using assertEquals, validating that the toString method correctly converts the builder's internal character array representation to a proper String object without any modifications or loss of data. This test verifies the fundamental string conversion functionality of the TextStringBuilder class, ensuring that the toString method accurately reflects the current contents of the builder's internal buffer. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation and assertEquals assertion method.

This test validates the capacity management behavior of a text string builder when handling various capacity requests, including edge cases that could trigger memory allocation errors. Initialize a new text string builder instance, then call the capacity management method with several different input values to verify proper handling: first with a negative value to ensure it doesn't cause unexpected exceptions, then with zero, and finally with a reasonable positive value like ten thousand to confirm normal operation. After these safe operations, assert that attempting to ensure capacity with the maximum integer value throws an out-of-memory error, demonstrating that the builder properly handles extreme capacity requests that would exceed available memory rather than causing system instability. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the user experience of removing character filters from a random string generator configuration, specifically testing that the Builder class's filteredBy method can clear previously set filters when called with no arguments, and asserting that the generator produces strings outside the original filter constraints. Initialize a RandomStringGenerator Builder instance by calling the builder method, then configure it with a character range from 'a' to 'z' using the withinRange method with character parameters, and apply a filter using the filteredBy method with the A_FILTER parameter. Next, call the filteredBy method again with no arguments to remove all previously applied filters, which should clear the inclusivePredicates field by setting it to null. Retrieve a RandomStringGenerator instance by calling the get method on the builder, then generate a string of 100 characters using the generate method with an integer parameter. Iterate through each character in the generated string using the toCharArray method, and for each character, check if it is not equal to 'a' - if any character other than 'a' is found, return from the test method as this indicates the filter was successfully removed. If the loop completes without finding any character other than 'a', call the fail method with the message "Filter appears to have remained in place" to indicate that the filter removal did not work correctly. This test uses the JUnit testing framework, identified by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and configure it to use the null text value "NULL" by calling setNullText, then append a null String with start index 0 and length 1 using the append method, and assert that the resulting string representation equals "NULL" to verify null handling with substring parameters. Create a second StrBuilder instance and append the string "foo" with start index 0 and length 3 using the append method, then assert that the string representation equals "foo" to confirm basic substring appending functionality. Create a final StrBuilder variable reference and use the assertIndexOutOfBoundsException helper method to verify that calling append with invalid parameter combinations throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, testing scenarios including negative start index with append("bar", -1, 1), start index beyond string length with append("bar", 3, 1), negative length with append("bar", 1, -1), length extending beyond string bounds with append("bar", 1, 3), both negative start index and valid length with append("bar", -1, 3), and start index at string length with positive length append("bar", 4, 0). Verify that appending with valid boundary conditions works correctly by calling append("bar", 3, 0) and asserting the string remains "foo", then append a substring "bar" from the string "abcbardef" starting at index 3 with length 3 and assert the result equals "foobar". Finally, append a CharSequence cast of "abcbardef" starting at index 4 with length 3 and assert the final result equals "foobarard" to test CharSequence parameter handling. The testing framework used is identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the functionality of a single quote character matching utility by verifying that it correctly identifies single quote characters at specific positions within a character buffer. Initialize a single quote matcher using the factory method and confirm that subsequent calls to the same factory method return the identical matcher reference. Create a character buffer containing various characters including a single quote, then test the matcher's ability to detect matches at different positions by calling the matching method with the buffer and specific position indices. Assert that the matcher returns zero when checking positions that do not contain a single quote character, and returns one when checking the position that contains the single quote character, confirming that the matcher correctly identifies single quotes and returns the appropriate match length. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the single quote matcher functionality within a string matching utility. Initialize a string matcher by calling the single quote matcher factory method, then verify that subsequent calls to the same factory method return the identical matcher instance using reference equality assertion. Create a character buffer and test the matcher's behavior at different positions by calling the match method with position indices 10, 11, and 12, asserting that the matcher returns 0 for non-matching positions and 1 when a single quote character is found at the specified location. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a test to verify the custom variable resolution behavior in StringSubstitutor by creating a TextStringBuilder with the content "Hi ${name}!" where the variable placeholder contains whitespace formatting. Create a HashMap and populate it with the key-value pair "name" mapped to "commons". Instantiate a StringSubstitutor with this map and override its resolveVariable method to perform custom assertions and return a different value than what's in the map. Within the overridden resolveVariable method, assert that the variable name parameter equals "name", assert that the buffer parameter is the same instance as the original TextStringBuilder using assertSame, assert that the start position parameter equals 3, and assert that the end position parameter equals 10, then return the string "jakarta" instead of the mapped value. Call the replaceIn method on the StringSubstitutor instance, passing the TextStringBuilder to perform in-place substitution. After substitution, use the helper method assertEqualsCharSeq to verify that the builder's toString output equals "Hi jakarta!" rather than "Hi commons!", confirming that the custom resolveVariable implementation was invoked and its return value was used. The helper method assertEqualsCharSeq compares two CharSequence objects for equality and provides detailed length information in case of assertion failure. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a new TextStringBuilder instance with the default constructor to create an empty string builder. Call the ensureCapacity method on the TextStringBuilder instance with the argument Integer.MIN_VALUE to test that it does not throw a NegativeArraySizeException when given the minimum integer value. Call ensureCapacity again with the argument -1 to verify proper handling of negative capacity values. Call ensureCapacity with the argument 0 to test zero capacity handling. Call ensureCapacity with the argument 10000 to test a reasonable positive capacity value that should succeed without issues. Finally, use assertThrows to verify that calling ensureCapacity with Integer.MAX_VALUE throws an OutOfMemoryError, confirming that the method properly handles capacity requests that exceed available memory limits. The ensureCapacity method programmatically ensures the internal character buffer has at least the specified capacity by reallocating if necessary, supporting the user experience of pre-allocating buffer space to minimize memory reallocations during string building operations. This test validates that the TextStringBuilder class correctly handles edge cases for capacity management including negative values, zero, reasonable positive values, and memory overflow conditions, with the assertion confirming that attempting to allocate maximum integer capacity results in the expected OutOfMemoryError exception. The testing framework used is JUnit 5, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the functionality of a single quote character matcher within a string matching utility, specifically testing that the StrMatcher class correctly identifies and matches single quote characters at specific positions within a character buffer. Initialize a StrMatcher instance by calling the singleQuoteMatcher method on the StrMatcher class, which returns a pre-configured matcher designed to identify single quote characters in text processing scenarios. Assert that subsequent calls to singleQuoteMatcher return the same singleton instance using assertSame to verify proper object reuse and memory efficiency. Call the isMatch method on the matcher instance with a character buffer named BUFFER1 and position 10, then assert that the return value equals 0 using assertEquals, indicating no match at that position. Call isMatch again with the same buffer at position 11 and assert that the return value equals 1, confirming that a single quote character is successfully detected at that location and that exactly one character matches. Finally, call isMatch with position 12 and assert the return value equals 0, verifying that no match occurs at the subsequent position, thus demonstrating the matcher's precision in identifying single quotes only at their exact locations within the character array. The testing framework used is JUnit, as indicated by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a test that validates the custom variable resolution behavior of a string substitutor by creating a text string builder containing a template with a variable placeholder "name" surrounded by curly braces and preceded by a dollar sign, then construct a hash map that associates the key "name" with the value "commons". Create an anonymous subclass of string substitutor that overrides the resolve variable method to perform assertions on the variable name parameter (expecting "name"), the buffer parameter (expecting it to be the same instance as the original builder), the start position parameter (expecting 3), and the end position parameter (expecting 10), while returning the hardcoded value "jakarta" instead of using the map lookup. Call the replace in method on the substitutor instance passing the text string builder, then assert that the final string content equals "Hi jakarta!" using a character sequence equality assertion helper method. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that the readFrom method of TextStringBuilder correctly appends content from a Reader to the end of an existing string buffer. Initialize a new TextStringBuilder instance with the initial string value "Test", then call the readFrom method passing a StringReader constructed with the string " 123" as the input source, which programmatically reads all available characters from the Reader and appends them to the current buffer contents without replacing the existing data. After the readFrom operation completes, assert that the toString method returns the expected concatenated result "Test 123" using assertEquals, verifying that the original content "Test" remains intact and the new content " 123" from the Reader has been properly appended to form the complete string. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation and assertEquals assertion method.

Initialize a text string builder with the content "abab" and systematically test the indexOf method that searches for a string starting from a specified index position. Call the indexOf method with the search string "a" and various starting indices including negative values like -1, valid positions 0 through 5, and verify that it returns the correct first occurrence index or -1 when not found. Test edge cases by searching for a non-existent substring "abcdef" which should return -1, and search for empty strings which should return the starting index. Verify the method behaves consistently with Java's String indexOf by testing searches for "ab", "b", and "ba" substrings with different starting positions. Create a second text string builder with content "xyzabc" to test additional scenarios including searching for "za" from different starting positions. Test null string input to ensure it returns -1. Assert that each indexOf call returns the expected index value, confirming the method correctly finds substring positions or indicates absence with -1. The testing framework used is JUnit.

Initialize a text string builder with the initial content "Test", then call the read from reader method with a string reader containing " 123" to append the reader's content to the existing builder content. Assert that the resulting string representation equals "Test 123" to verify that the read operation correctly appends the input to the end of the existing content rather than replacing it. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that reading content from a character stream appends the new data to the end of an existing string builder rather than replacing it. Initialize a text string builder with an initial string value, then invoke the read operation using a string reader containing additional characters including whitespace and numbers. Verify that the final string representation contains both the original content and the newly read content concatenated together, confirming that the read functionality preserves existing data while extending the builder's contents. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a new TextStringBuilder instance using the default constructor, which creates an empty string builder with an initial capacity of 32 characters. Call the startsWith method on the empty builder with the string literal "a" and assert that it returns false, validating that an empty builder does not start with any non-empty string. Call startsWith with a null argument and assert that it returns false, confirming that the method handles null input by returning false rather than throwing an exception. Call startsWith with an empty string literal and assert that it returns true, verifying that an empty builder starts with an empty string. Use the append method to add the string "abc" to the builder, which internally copies the characters into the builder's internal buffer and updates the size. Call startsWith with "a" and assert it returns true, confirming the builder now starts with the single character. Call startsWith with "ab" and assert it returns true, validating that the builder starts with the two-character prefix. Call startsWith with "abc" and assert it returns true, verifying that the builder starts with the complete string content. Finally, call startsWith with "cba" and assert it returns false, confirming that the method correctly identifies when the builder does not start with the specified string. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a text string builder instance and verify its starts-with behavior across various scenarios. Assert that the empty builder returns false when checked against the string "a", false when checked against null, and true when checked against an empty string. Append the string "abc" to the builder to establish content for further testing. Verify that the builder now correctly identifies strings it starts with by asserting true for "a", "ab", and "abc", while asserting false for the non-matching string "cba" which represents characters in reverse order. The testing framework used is JUnit.

Initialize a text string builder instance and assert that its initial size is zero. Append the string "Hello" to the builder and assert that the size method now returns five, which matches the length of the appended string. This test validates that the size method correctly tracks the number of characters contained in the builder as content is added, ensuring the internal size field is properly maintained during append operations. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the prefix matching functionality of a text string builder by checking various scenarios with different input strings. Initialize an empty text string builder and verify that it correctly returns false when checking if it starts with a single character or null value, while confirming it returns true for an empty string prefix. Append a three-character string to the builder and assert that the prefix matching correctly identifies single character, two-character, and full string matches as true, while rejecting a string that does not match the beginning sequence. The test ensures proper handling of edge cases including null inputs and empty string comparisons, validating that the prefix detection behaves consistently across different string lengths and content scenarios. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance without any constructor arguments to create an empty string builder, then call the assertEquals method to verify that the toStringBuilder method returns a StringBuilder with the same string representation as a new empty StringBuilder by comparing their toString outputs. Next, call the append method on the StrBuilder instance with the string literal "junit" to add content to the builder, then again use assertEquals to verify that the toStringBuilder method now returns a StringBuilder containing "junit" by comparing its toString output with that of a new StringBuilder constructed with "junit" as its initial value. The test validates that the toStringBuilder method correctly converts the internal character buffer of the StrBuilder into a StringBuilder instance that maintains the same string content, testing both empty and non-empty states of the builder. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the size tracking functionality of a text string builder by verifying that the size correctly reflects the number of characters contained. Initialize a new text string builder instance, then assert that its initial size equals zero to confirm it starts empty. Append a simple text string to the builder, then assert that the size now equals the length of the appended text to verify that the size accurately tracks content additions. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that an alphabet converter correctly implements equality comparison by rejecting non-converter types. Initialize a character array with two elements, create two identical character variables with the plus symbol, populate the array with these characters where both positions contain the same character, then create an alphabet converter using the factory method that accepts three identical character arrays as parameters for original alphabet, encoding alphabet, and characters not to encode. This test validates URL validation functionality with case-insensitive scheme handling and custom scheme configuration by testing the UrlValidator class's isValid method across different URL formats and validator configurations. This test validates that a specialized hash map can be properly duplicated while preserving both its contents and performance optimization settings. This test validates the ISSN extraction functionality from EAN-13 barcodes, specifically testing the ISSNValidator class's ability to correctly parse and extract ISSN numbers from their EAN-13 encoded representations. Initialize the test by accessing the VALIDATOR field, which is a private static final field of the test class configured as an ISSNValidator instance. Execute four sequential assertions by calling the extractFromEAN13 method on the VALIDATOR instance with different EAN-13 barcode strings as input parameters. Third, assert that calling extractFromEAN13 with "9770317847001" returns "03178471", verifying another standard ISSN extraction case. Finally, assert that calling extractFromEAN13 with "9771144875007" returns "1144875X", confirming proper handling of ISSN numbers that end with the check digit 'X'. Each assertion uses assertEquals to validate that the extracted ISSN matches the expected eight-character string format, ensuring the method correctly strips the EAN-13 prefix and suffix while preserving the core ISSN identifier including any alphabetic check digits. This test validates the copy functionality of a fast hash map utility method. This test validates that the flag checking functionality correctly returns false when not all specified flags are active within a Flags object, specifically testing the bitwise AND operation behavior for composite flag values. This test validates that the ISSN validator properly rejects invalid EAN13 codes that cannot be converted to valid ISSN format by ensuring IllegalArgumentException is thrown for incompatible input formats.
