This test validates that domain validator configuration overrides work correctly at both the class and instance levels for top-level domain validation. Begin by updating the global TLD override tables to add a custom generic TLD and remove a standard one, then add a custom country code TLD and remove a standard one. Create a validator instance with local addresses disabled and verify that it correctly validates the added custom TLDs as valid while rejecting the removed standard TLDs for both generic and country code categories. Next, create a new validator instance with the same local address setting but provide custom override items that clear the minus tables, effectively restoring the previously removed TLDs. Verify that this new instance validates both the custom added TLDs and the previously removed standard TLDs as valid. Finally, create another validator instance without custom overrides to confirm that the global class-level overrides remain unchanged and still enforce the original restrictions. Assert throughout that the validation results match the expected behavior for each configuration scenario. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the range checking functionality for byte values by testing boundary conditions and edge cases. Initialize a strict byte validator and use it to parse several string representations of numbers with a simple pattern, creating byte values for the numbers 9, 10, 11, 19, 20, and 21. Similarly, validate the maximum value checking to ensure it accepts values at or below the maximum threshold while rejecting those that exceed it. Assert that all boundary conditions behave as expected, with values exactly at the boundaries being considered valid and values outside the range being rejected. The testing is performed using JUnit framework.

This test validates email address formatting rules by checking various email strings against validation logic to ensure proper acceptance and rejection of different character combinations. Initialize a value container and set it with an email containing an invalid Unicode character in the domain portion, then verify through validation that it correctly fails the email format check. This test validates the domain validator's ability to handle static TLD override configurations and instance-specific overrides. Begin by calling the static update method on the domain validator to configure TLD overrides at the class level, adding "gp" to the generic plus list, removing "com" from the generic minus list, adding "cp" to the country code plus list, and removing "ch" from the country code minus list. Finally, create another domain validator instance with local validation disabled to verify that the original class-level overrides remain unchanged, asserting that "gp" is valid, "com" is invalid, "cp" is valid, and "ch" is invalid. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that a validator can successfully process a single field with date validation rules and return appropriate results. This test validates the required field validation functionality by ensuring that empty or null fields are properly identified as validation failures when processed through the Apache Commons Validator framework. Initialize a NameBean instance without setting any values for its firstName and lastName properties, then construct a Validator instance using the ValidatorResources field of the test class and a FORM_KEY constant. Set the NameBean as a parameter on the validator using the BEAN_PARAM constant from the Validator class, then call the validate method to execute the validation rules and obtain a ValidatorResults object. Perform identical assertions for the lastName field result, checking that it is not null with the message "First Name ValidatorResult should not be null.", contains the ACTION with the message "Last Name ValidatorResult should contain the '" + ACTION + "' action.", and that isValid returns false with the message "Last Name ValidatorResult for the '" + ACTION + "' action should have failed." The test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the range checking functionality of a byte validator component by exercising its minimum, maximum, and range validation methods. Initialize a strict byte validator instance and use it to validate several string representations of numbers including "9", "10", "11", "19", "20", and "21" with a simple hash pattern, converting each to byte objects. Invoke the maximum value validation method to ensure that values at or below the maximum return true while values above the maximum return false. Assert that each validation result matches the expected boolean outcome using true and false assertions with descriptive messages indicating the boundary condition being tested. Initialize a name bean object and set its last name property to an empty string, then construct a validator instance using the loaded validator resources and a form key. This test validates that required field validation properly fails when a last name field is set to a blank string. This test validates the range checking functionality of the ByteValidator class by testing whether byte values fall within, below, or above specified minimum and maximum boundaries. Initialize a ByteValidator instance by casting the strictValidator field of the test class to ByteValidator, then call the validate method five times with string inputs "9", "10", "11", "19", and "20" along with the pattern "#" to convert these strings into Byte objects representing the values 9, 10, 11, 19, and 20 respectively. Set up local byte variables for minimum value 10 and maximum value 20 to define the range boundaries for testing. Call the isInRange method to verify range validation by asserting that value 9 returns false since it is below the minimum, values 10, 11, and 20 return true since they are within or at the boundaries, and value 21 returns false since it exceeds the maximum. Call the minValue method to test minimum boundary validation by asserting that value 9 returns false for being below the minimum, while values 10 and 11 return true for meeting or exceeding the minimum threshold. Call the maxValue method to test maximum boundary validation by asserting that values 19 and 20 return true for being below or at the maximum, while value 21 returns false for exceeding the maximum threshold. The isInRange method programmatically checks if a byte value falls between inclusive minimum and maximum bounds, the minValue method verifies a value meets or exceeds a minimum threshold, and the maxValue method confirms a value does not exceed a maximum threshold, all supporting user scenarios where numeric input validation requires range constraints. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation and assertion methods.

This test validates the retrieval and verification of variable configurations associated with form fields in a validation framework. Initialize the test by calling setUp which loads resources from a configuration file named VarTest-config.xml using the loadResources method. Retrieve a Form object by calling getForm on the resources field of the test class with the default locale and a constant FORM_KEY. Extract the first field by calling getField with the string field-1 on the form object, then assert that the field is not null and verify its property equals field-1 using assertEquals. Verify that the variable's isResource method returns false using assertFalse and that getBundle returns null using assertNull. Extract the second field by calling getField with field-2 on the form, assert it is not null, and confirm its property equals field-2. Retrieve the first variable from the second field using getVar with var-2-1, assert it is not null, and validate its name equals var-2-1, value equals value-2-1, and JavaScript type equals jstype-2-1. Verify that isResource returns true using assertTrue and that getBundle equals bundle-2-1. Finally, obtain the second variable from the second field using getVar with var-2-2, assert it is not null, validate its name equals var-2-2 and value equals value-2-2, confirm that getJsType returns null, verify that isResource returns false, and check that getBundle equals bundle-2-2. The test method uses the @Test annotation and employs JUnit testing framework for assertions.

This test validates that a validator configuration system can successfully merge multiple configuration files and access forms and their validation constants across different locales. Initialize a validator resources component by loading two separate XML configuration files containing form definitions and validation rules, then close the input streams after loading. Retrieve forms from both configuration files using empty locale parameters and specific form names, asserting that each form exists and is properly accessible. Extract fields from each form and verify that their associated validation constants are correctly stored and retrievable by checking specific variable values against expected constant values. Repeat the same validation process for a French locale by retrieving locale-specific forms with French naming conventions and verifying their field constants contain the expected French-localized values. The test framework used is JUnit.

This test validates the merging functionality of validator resources when multiple XML configuration files are loaded together. Initialize a validator resources object by loading two separate XML configuration streams from the classpath, then close the input streams after loading. Retrieve forms from both configuration files using empty locale parameters and specific form names like "testForm1" and "testForm2", asserting that both forms exist and are not null. Extract fields from each form using property names such as "testProperty1" and "testProperty2", then verify that variable values are correctly accessible through the field's variable retrieval method with keys like "var11", "var12", "var21", and "var22", asserting that each returns expected constant values like "testConstValue1" and "testConstValue2". Repeat the same validation process for French locale forms by retrieving forms with "fr" locale parameter and form names ending with "_fr", extracting their corresponding fields with French-specific property names, and verifying their variable values contain French-specific constant values ending with "_fr". Assert that all forms, fields, and variable values are properly merged and accessible from the combined validator resources configuration. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the field-specific validation functionality of the validator framework by setting up a date validation scenario and verifying that a single field can be validated independently. Initialize validator resources by creating a validator action with the name "date" that references a date formatting method, then construct a form set containing a test form with a single field property named "date" that depends on the date validation action, and process the resources to make them ready for validation. Create a test bean instance and set its date property to a valid date string like "2/3/1999". Instantiate a validator with the prepared resources, specifying "testForm" as the form name and "date" as the specific field to validate, then configure the validator by setting the bean parameter to the test bean instance. Execute the validation by calling the validate method, which returns a validator results object containing the outcomes of the validation process. Assert that the results object is not null to confirm validation executed successfully, then verify that the results contain the validated field by checking that the property names collection includes the "date" property, demonstrating that the field was processed and included in the validation results regardless of whether it passed or failed. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the domain validator's top-level domain override functionality by configuring conflicting generic TLD overrides and verifying that exclusion rules take precedence over inclusion rules. First, update the domain validator's generic TLD override tables by adding a specific country code TLD like "ch" to both the generic plus override array and the generic minus override array using the TLD override update method with the appropriate array type enumerations. Next, obtain a singleton instance of the domain validator using the standard factory method. Then, validate that the TLD is not considered a valid generic TLD by calling the generic TLD validation method with the country code and asserting that it returns false, demonstrating that the minus override successfully excludes the TLD despite its presence in the plus override. Finally, verify that a standard generic TLD like "com" remains valid by calling the same validation method and asserting that it returns true, confirming that the override mechanism only affects the specifically configured TLD. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that type conversion validation works correctly with French locale formatting conventions. Initialize a data container and populate it with string representations of various numeric types and a date using French formatting, including a float with comma as decimal separator, a double with comma as decimal separator, and a date in day/month/year format. Execute locale-specific validation processing using French locale settings, which should convert the string inputs to their appropriate numeric and date types according to French formatting rules. Verify that the validation results contain properly typed values by checking that each result is of the expected type, then specifically assert that the float and double values were correctly parsed from their comma-separated French format to their numeric equivalents. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the domain validator's ability to handle static TLD override configurations and instance-specific override behaviors for both generic and country code top-level domains. The test verifies that static overrides applied through the updateTLDOverride method affect new validator instances, while instance-specific overrides can selectively restore or modify validation behavior without affecting the global static configuration. Begin by calling the DomainValidator updateTLDOverride method four times to establish static overrides: first with ArrayType.GENERIC_PLUS and the string "gp" to add a custom generic TLD, second with ArrayType.GENERIC_MINUS and "com" to remove the standard com TLD, third with ArrayType.COUNTRY_CODE_PLUS and "cp" to add a custom country code TLD, and fourth with ArrayType.COUNTRY_CODE_MINUS and "ch" to remove the standard ch country code TLD. Create a DomainValidator instance by calling getInstance with false as the parameter to disable local domain validation. Assert that the isValidGenericTld method returns true when passed "gp" to verify the custom generic TLD addition, assert that isValidGenericTld returns false when passed "com" to confirm the standard TLD removal, assert that isValidCountryCodeTld returns true for "cp" to validate the custom country code addition, and assert that isValidCountryCodeTld returns false for "ch" to confirm the country code removal. Create a new ArrayList of DomainValidator.Item objects and add two items: one Item constructed with ArrayType.GENERIC_MINUS and an empty string, and another Item with ArrayType.COUNTRY_CODE_MINUS and an empty string, which effectively clears the minus overrides for this instance. Create a new validator instance by calling getInstance with false and the items list to apply instance-specific overrides. Assert that isValidGenericTld returns true for both "gp" and "com" to verify that the instance override restored "com" validation while preserving the "gp" addition, and assert that isValidCountryCodeTld returns true for both "cp" and "ch" to confirm that the instance override restored "ch" validation while preserving the "cp" addition. Finally, create another validator instance using getInstance with false and no items list to demonstrate that the static class-level overrides remain unchanged, then assert that isValidGenericTld returns true for "gp" and false for "com", and assert that isValidCountryCodeTld returns true for "cp" and false for "ch" to confirm the static overrides persist independently of instance-specific configurations. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the format and check digit validation capabilities for American Express credit card numbers. Initialize an American Express credit card validator and extract its regular expression component to test the format requirements. Verify that the regular expression correctly rejects card numbers with lengths other than fifteen digits, accepts only numbers starting with prefixes thirty-four or thirty-seven while rejecting other prefixes, and rejects numbers containing invalid characters. Test the complete validator functionality by confirming it accepts valid American Express numbers while rejecting numbers from other credit card types like Diners, Discover, Mastercard, and Visa, and verify that validation returns the original number for valid inputs but returns null for invalid ones including those that pass format checks but fail check digit validation. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the required field validation functionality when a last name field is set to a blank string, ensuring that both first name and last name fields fail validation as expected when empty values are provided. Initialize a NameBean instance and set its last name property to an empty string using the setLastName method, leaving the first name unset which defaults to null. Load validator resources from the ExtensionTest-config.xml file in the setUp method using ValidatorResources constructor with an InputStream from the test class resource. Create a Validator instance using the loaded resources and a FORM_KEY constant, then configure it by calling setParameter with BEAN_PARAM and the name bean to specify the object to validate. Assert that the results object is not null with the message "Results are null." Retrieve individual ValidatorResult objects for both "firstName" and "lastName" fields using getValidatorResult method. Assert that the first name result is not null with message "First Name ValidatorResult should not be null." Verify that the first name result contains the specified ACTION using containsAction method and assert it with message "First Name ValidatorResult should contain the 'ACTION' action." Confirm that the first name validation failed by calling isValid with ACTION parameter and asserting false with message "First Name ValidatorResult for the 'ACTION' action should have failed." Assert that the last name result is not null with message "First Name ValidatorResult should not be null." Verify that the last name result contains the ACTION using containsAction and assert it with message "Last Name ValidatorResult should contain the 'ACTION' action." Confirm that the last name validation failed by calling isValid with ACTION parameter and asserting false with message "Last Name ValidatorResult for the 'ACTION' action should have failed." The test uses JUnit framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that a validation framework correctly identifies when a required field fails validation due to being blank. Initialize a name data structure and populate it with a valid first name and an empty string for the last name. Load validation configuration resources and construct a validator using those resources along with a specific form identifier. Confirm that the first name validation passes since it contains a valid value, while asserting that the last name validation fails because it violates the required field constraint by being empty. This test validates the type conversion functionality of a validator framework when processing numeric and date values using French locale formatting conventions. Initialize a type bean object and populate its properties with string representations of various data types including a byte value of "12", a short value of "-129", an integer of "1443", a long of "88000", a float using French decimal notation "12,1555", a double with French formatting "129,1551511111", and a date in European format "21/12/2010". This test uses JUnit framework with standard assertion methods.

This test validates the American Express credit card validator component by exercising both its regular expression pattern matching and overall validation logic. Initialize a code validator instance specifically configured for American Express cards and extract its underlying regex validator component. Test the regular expression validation by asserting that card numbers with lengths of 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, and 18 digits are rejected while a 15-digit number is accepted, then verify that numbers starting with prefixes 33, 35, 36, 38, and 41 are rejected while those beginning with 34 and 37 are accepted, and confirm that numbers containing invalid characters like letters are also rejected. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the American Express credit card number validation functionality by testing both the regular expression pattern matching and the complete validation logic of the AMEX_VALIDATOR. Initialize a CodeValidator instance by accessing the AMEX_VALIDATOR static field from CreditCardValidator, then retrieve its RegexValidator component using the getRegexValidator method to test the underlying regular expression pattern that enforces American Express card format requirements of exactly 15 digits starting with either "34" or "37". Test character validation by passing a string containing an invalid character 'x' and asserting false. Proceed to test the complete CodeValidator functionality by first verifying that a malformed card number passes regex validation but fails the full validator's isValid method and returns null from the validate method, then assert that a valid American Express number returns itself when passed to validate and returns true from isValid. Validate exclusivity by confirming the AMEX validator rejects valid card numbers from other providers including Diners, Discover, Mastercard, Visa, and short Visa formats, expecting false for each. Finally, assert that several specific valid American Express test numbers including "371449635398431", "340000000000009", "370000000000002", and "378734493671000" all return true when passed to the isValid method. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that domain validation override configurations properly handle conflicting rules where exclusion takes precedence over inclusion. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions.

This test validates the user experience of loading and merging multiple validator configuration files to ensure forms and their validation rules are properly combined and accessible across different locales. Initialize a ValidatorResources object by loading two XML configuration files named MultipleConfigFilesTest-1-config.xml and MultipleConfigFilesTest-2-config.xml from the classpath using getResourceAsStream, then close both input streams after the ValidatorResources constructor processes them. Call the getForm method on the ValidatorResources instance with empty strings for the first three parameters and testForm1 as the form name to retrieve the first form, then assert it is not null with the message Form 'testForm1' not found. For the first form, call getField with testProperty1 to retrieve a Field object, then call getVarValue with var11 on that field and assert it equals testConstValue1 with the message testProperty1 - const 1, followed by calling getVarValue with var12 and asserting it equals testConstValue2 with the message testProperty1 - const 2. For the second form, call getField with testProperty2 to retrieve another Field object, then call getVarValue with var21 and assert it equals testConstValue1 with the message testProperty2 - const 1, followed by calling getVarValue with var22 and asserting it equals testConstValue2 with the message testProperty2 - const 2. Repeat the entire validation process for the French locale by calling getForm with fr as the first parameter and testForm1_fr as the form name, asserting it is not null with the message Form 'testForm1_fr' not found, then calling getForm with fr and testForm2_fr, asserting it is not null with the message Form 'testForm2_fr' not found. For the French forms, call getField with testProperty1_fr on the first form and validate its variable values var11_fr equals testConstValue1_fr and var12_fr equals testConstValue2_fr with corresponding assertion messages, then call getField with testProperty2_fr on the second form and validate its variable values var21_fr equals testConstValue1_fr and var22_fr equals testConstValue2_fr with corresponding assertion messages. The testing framework used is JUnit 5, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that email addresses with top-level domains as the entire domain portion are properly handled by the validation system. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the domain validation behavior when TLD override configurations demonstrate that minus overrides take precedence over plus overrides for country code top-level domains. The test configures the DomainValidator class by calling updateTLDOverride twice with ArrayType.COUNTRY_CODE_PLUS and ArrayType.COUNTRY_CODE_MINUS enum values, both specifying the string literal "com" as the TLD to modify, which adds "com" to the plus override array and then to the minus override array for country code validation. Call isValidCountryCodeTld with the string literal "com" and assert that the method returns false using assertFalse, which validates that the minus override configuration correctly excludes "com" from being recognized as a valid country code TLD despite its presence in the plus override array, demonstrating that exclusion rules take precedence over inclusion rules in the TLD validation logic. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the required field validation functionality of the Apache Commons Validator framework by setting up a name bean with a valid first name and an empty last name, then verifying that the validator correctly identifies the missing required field. Initialize a name bean object and populate it with a first name value of "Joe" and set the last name to an empty string. First, update the domain validator's country code plus override array to include the TLD "com", which would normally make it a valid country code TLD. Obtain a domain validator instance using the singleton pattern, then validate that the TLD "com" is not considered a valid country code TLD by calling the country code validation method and asserting that it returns false. The test uses JUnit framework for assertions.

This test validates the required field validation functionality of the Apache Commons Validator framework by testing a name bean with both first and last name fields populated. Initialize a name bean object and set both the first name and last name properties to the value "Test". Load validation resources from a configuration file during setup, then construct a validator instance using these resources and a form key. Configure the validator by setting the name bean as a parameter using the bean parameter constant. Execute the validation process by calling the validate method, which returns a validator results object containing the outcomes for each validated field. For each field result, assert that the result object is not null, verify that it contains the expected validation action, and confirm that the validation passed for that action by checking the validity status. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the required field validation functionality when a last name field is left blank while a first name is provided, ensuring that the validation framework correctly identifies missing required fields and passes validation for properly filled fields. This test validates the required field validation functionality for a name bean containing both first and last name fields, ensuring that when both required fields are populated, the validation passes and returns appropriate ValidatorResult objects indicating successful validation. This test validates that the Apache Commons Validator framework correctly performs locale-specific type conversion and validation for French locale formatting, specifically testing that numeric values with French decimal separators are properly converted to their corresponding Java primitive wrapper types. Initialize a new TypeBean instance and populate it with string representations of various data types using French locale formatting conventions, setting the byte field to "12", short field to "-129", integer field to "1443", long field to "88000", float field to "12,1555" with comma as decimal separator, double field to "129,1551511111" with comma as decimal separator, and date field to "21/12/2010" in day/month/year format. After the helper method returns the result map, assert that the float value converted from "12,1555" equals 12 when cast to Float and converted to integer with the message "float value not correct", and assert that the double value converted from "129,1551511111" equals 129 when cast to Double and converted to integer with the message "double value not correct". The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation and assertion methods like assertEquals, assertNotNull, and assertInstanceOf.

This test validates the null value handling behavior of the RegexValidator class when provided with null input across its three primary validation methods. Call the isValid method on the validator instance passing null as the argument, then assert that the result is false using assertFalse with the message "Instance isValid()" to verify that null input is correctly identified as invalid. The RegexValidator's isValid method programmatically returns false for null values without attempting pattern matching, the validate method returns null for null input without processing regex groups, and the match method returns null for null input without extracting capture groups, ensuring consistent null-safe behavior across all validation operations for users attempting to validate potentially null string values. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the behavior of a validator when the first dependent validation rule fails, ensuring that subsequent dependent validations are not executed. This test validates that a big integer validator can correctly parse and validate numeric strings across different locales and formatting patterns. This test validates that an alphabet converter correctly implements reflexive equality when compared to itself. This test validates the string builder's append line functionality for character values. Initialize a new string builder instance and define a character variable with the value 'c'. This test validates the equals method implementation of an alphabet converter by verifying that an object returns true when compared to itself. Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and assign the character literal 'c' to a variable, then call the appendln method on the StrBuilder instance with the character as an argument and immediately invoke toString on the returned StrBuilder to convert it to a String representation. Assert that the resulting string equals the concatenation of the character 'c' with the system line separator obtained from System.lineSeparator using assertEquals. The assertion validates that the appendln method correctly appends both the character and the appropriate line separator to produce the expected string output. This test validates the reflexive property of the equals method implementation in the AlphabetConverter class, ensuring that an object is equal to itself when compared using the equals method. Assert that the equals method returns true using assertTrue, which validates that the equals implementation correctly handles the case where an object is compared to itself by checking reference equality before proceeding to field-by-field comparison of originalToEncoded, encodedToOriginal, and encodedLetterLength fields. This test validates the string substitution functionality for system properties by comparing two different approaches to variable replacement. Initialize a system property with key "test_key" and value "test_value" using the system property setter. Assert that both the expected and actual results are equal, confirming that the system property replacement method produces the same output as the general replacement approach when using system properties as the variable source. After test completion, cleanup occurs by nullifying the values map. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the system property substitution functionality to ensure that the StringSubstitutor class correctly handles variable replacement using system properties as the variable source. The test specifically examines the replaceSystemProperties method's ability to substitute variables with values from system properties and compares its output against the general replace method when provided with the same system properties map. Initialize a string tokenizer with the input "a b c d e" and create an anonymous subclass that overrides the tokenize method to ignore the original input parameters and instead tokenize the character array "w x y z" starting at offset 2 with a count of 5 characters. Call the next method twice on the tokenizer instance and assert that the first returned token equals "x" and the second returned token equals "y", verifying that the subclass successfully redirects the tokenization to process a different substring than the original input. This test validates that a string tokenizer subclass can override the tokenization behavior to process different input than what was originally provided. This test validates that string substitution functionality correctly handles system properties when processing templates with variable placeholders. This test validates the functionality of a tab character matcher by verifying its singleton behavior and character matching capabilities. Using a character buffer containing various characters, verify that the matcher correctly identifies tab characters by testing it at multiple positions within the buffer, asserting that it returns zero when positioned at non-tab characters and returns one when positioned at a tab character, demonstrating proper character recognition and match length reporting. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the tab matcher functionality of a string matching utility by verifying that the tab matcher factory method returns a singleton instance and correctly identifies tab characters at specific positions within a character buffer. Create or reference a character buffer containing various characters including at least one tab character, then invoke the matcher's position-checking method at multiple buffer positions such as index 2, 3, and 4, asserting that the method returns 0 for non-tab positions and 1 for positions containing tab characters, demonstrating that the matcher correctly identifies tab characters and returns the appropriate match length. This test validates the behavior of a StringTokenizer subclass that overrides the tokenize method to substitute different input parameters during tokenization processing. Initialize a StringTokenizer instance with the input string "a b c d e" and create an anonymous subclass that overrides the protected tokenize method to ignore the provided character array, offset, and count parameters and instead call the superclass tokenize method with a hardcoded character array from "w x y z", an offset of 2, and a count of 5, effectively tokenizing the substring "x y z". Call the next method on the tokenizer instance and assert that it returns the string "x", validating that the overridden tokenize method successfully substituted the input and returned the first token from the modified input. This test uses the JUnit testing framework, identified by the @Test annotation and assertEquals assertion methods.

This test validates the functionality of a tab character matcher in string processing operations, specifically testing the StrMatcher class's tabMatcher method and its ability to correctly identify tab characters within character arrays through match validation assertions. Initialize a StrMatcher instance by calling the tabMatcher method on the StrMatcher class, which returns a singleton matcher specifically designed to identify tab characters in text content. Verify that the tabMatcher method returns the same singleton instance by asserting that subsequent calls to tabMatcher return the identical object reference using assertSame. Test the matcher's character matching behavior by calling the isMatch method with a character array buffer named BUFFER1 and various position indices, where the method returns an integer indicating the number of matching characters or zero for no match. Assert that calling isMatch with BUFFER1 at position 2 returns 0, indicating no tab character match at that position. Assert that calling isMatch with BUFFER1 at position 3 returns 1, confirming a successful tab character match that consumes one character. Assert that calling isMatch with BUFFER1 at position 4 returns 0, verifying no tab character exists at that position. The test method uses the Test annotation and operates within a deprecated test class that contains multiple StrMatcher field declarations for various character matching scenarios. This test validates the functionality of a double quote character matching utility by verifying both singleton behavior and character position matching capabilities. Using a predefined character buffer, verify that the matcher correctly identifies the absence of a double quote character at one specific position by asserting a zero match result, then confirm the presence of a double quote character at the next position by asserting a single character match result. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the double quote matcher functionality within the string matcher utility. Initialize a double quote matcher by calling the factory method that returns a matcher specifically designed to identify double quote characters. This test validates the singleton behavior and character matching functionality of the double quote matcher factory method in the StrMatcher class, which provides string matching utilities for text processing applications. This test validates the string matching functionality when checking for pattern matches at specific positions within a text buffer with custom boundary constraints. Execute multiple match operations against a predefined input text, testing the matcher's ability to identify the pattern at a specific starting position while respecting different buffer boundary parameters, including scenarios with varying start and end positions within the text. Assert that the matcher returns the correct number of matching characters for successful matches and zero for cases where the pattern cannot be found within the specified constraints. The validation confirms that the matching logic properly handles position-based searches with custom buffer boundaries and accurately reports match lengths. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string matcher functionality by creating a string matcher for the pattern "bc" using the string matcher factory instance, then verifying its size and match behavior against various input positions and boundaries. Execute the matcher's isMatch method against a predefined input string at position 1 with different boundary parameters, first testing with start position 1 and end position matching the input length, expecting a return value of 2 indicating a successful match. This test validates the functionality of extracting character arrays from specific ranges within a text builder. Initialize an empty text builder and verify that extracting a character array from an empty range returns an array of zero length. Append the text "junit" to the builder, then extract a character array from the beginning with a length parameter that exceeds the actual content size, confirming that the returned array matches the full content "junit" and has the correct length. The testing uses JUnit framework.

This test validates the string matching functionality for substring pattern matching within character arrays, specifically testing the isMatch method's ability to correctly identify pattern positions and return match lengths with various buffer boundaries. Initialize a StringMatcher instance by calling the stringMatcher method on the INSTANCE field of StringMatcherFactory with the literal string "bc" as the pattern to match. Assert that the size method returns 2, which represents the length of the pattern string being matched. Call the isMatch method on the matcher with INPUT2 as the character array buffer, position 1 as the start index, position 1 as the buffer start, and INPUT2_LENGTH as the buffer end, then assert that it returns 2 indicating a successful match of length 2. Call isMatch again with INPUT2, position 1, buffer start 0, and buffer end 3, asserting the return value equals 2 to verify the match succeeds within these broader buffer boundaries. The StringMatcher class provides the core pattern matching logic through its abstract isMatch method that returns the number of matching characters or zero for no match, while the StringMatcherFactory creates matcher instances for specific patterns, and this test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

Initialize a TextStringBuilder instance with the string literal "abcbccba" to create a mutable string buffer for character replacement operations. Call the replaceFirst method with character 'x' as the search parameter and character 'y' as the replacement parameter, which searches for the first occurrence of 'x' in the buffer and replaces it with 'y', then assert that the toString method returns "abcbccba" since no 'x' character exists in the original string. Call replaceFirst again with character 'a' as the search parameter and character 'd' as the replacement parameter to replace the first occurrence of 'a' with 'd', then assert that toString returns "dbcbccba" to verify that only the first 'a' at index 0 was replaced. Call replaceFirst with character 'b' as the search parameter and character 'e' as the replacement parameter to replace the first occurrence of 'b' with 'e', then assert that toString returns "decbccba" to confirm that only the first 'b' at index 1 was replaced. Call replaceFirst with character 'c' as the search parameter and character 'f' as the replacement parameter to replace the first occurrence of 'c' with 'f', then assert that toString returns "defbccba" to validate that only the first 'c' at index 2 was replaced. Finally, call replaceFirst with character 'd' as both the search and replacement parameters to test replacing a character with itself, then assert that toString returns "defbccba" to confirm that the string remains unchanged when replacing a character with the same character. This test validates that the TextStringBuilder replaceFirst method correctly identifies and replaces only the first occurrence of a specified character in the buffer, handles cases where the search character does not exist, and properly handles self-replacement scenarios. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the functionality of replacing the first occurrence of a specific character within a text string builder. Next, replace the first occurrence of the character 'a' with 'd' and confirm the result is "dbcbccba". Continue by replacing the first occurrence of 'b' with 'e' to produce "decbccba", then replace the first occurrence of 'c' with 'f' to yield "defbccba". Finally, replace the first occurrence of 'd' with itself and verify the content remains "defbccba", demonstrating that self-replacement operations work correctly. Each replacement operation should only affect the first matching character found when scanning from left to right, leaving subsequent occurrences unchanged. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of finding string patterns within a mutable string buffer using pattern matching capabilities with starting position parameters. Extend the buffer with additional text containing alphanumeric characters and test pattern matching for more complex patterns including space characters and custom pattern matchers, verifying that the search correctly identifies pattern locations when starting from different positions within the extended buffer. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

After each initialization, verify that the capacity, length, and size properties return the expected values according to the constructor's behavior - default constructors should provide a standard capacity with zero content length, capacity-based constructors should respect minimum capacity requirements while maintaining zero content, and string-based constructors should allocate appropriate capacity while setting content length to match the input string length. This test validates the tokenization of a complex string containing semicolon delimiters, quoted sections, and empty tokens. The testing is performed using JUnit framework.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance using the default constructor, then immediately call the minimizeCapacity method on this empty builder and assert that the capacity method returns 0, verifying that an empty builder's capacity is minimized to zero. Next, call the append method with the string literal "HelloWorld" to add content to the builder, then invoke minimizeCapacity again to resize the internal buffer to match the current content length, and assert that the capacity method now returns 10, confirming that the capacity has been reduced to exactly match the length of the appended string. The test validates that the minimizeCapacity method correctly adjusts the internal character array buffer size to eliminate unused capacity, first ensuring an empty builder has zero capacity and then verifying that a builder with content has its capacity minimized to the exact content length. This test uses the JUnit testing framework with the @Test annotation.

Initialize a string tokenizer with a multi-line input string containing semicolon-delimited tokens, some of which are quoted with double quotes and include escaped quotes and whitespace. Configure the tokenizer by setting the delimiter character to semicolon, the quote character to double quote, the ignored matcher to a none matcher from the string matcher factory, and disable the ignore empty tokens setting to ensure all tokens including empty ones are preserved. The test validates that the string tokenizer correctly handles complex parsing scenarios with mixed quoted and unquoted content, escaped characters, and preserves empty tokens when configured to do so. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the behavior of appending null string builder references to a string builder. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of appending a character followed by a line separator to a string builder. Initialize an empty string builder and define a character value. Call the append-with-line method using the character as input, then convert the result to a string representation. Assert that the resulting string equals the character concatenated with the system's line separator value. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a new TextStringBuilder instance without any constructor arguments to create an empty string builder, then assert that calling toStringBuilder on this empty instance and converting the result to a string using toString equals the string representation of a new empty StringBuilder created with the default constructor. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a string builder instance and append the text "Hello" to it, then invoke the clear method to reset the builder's content. Assert that the length of the builder is zero after clearing, confirming that the size has been properly reset. Additionally, verify that the internal character buffer capacity remains at least 5 characters, ensuring that the buffer array itself retains its allocated space even though the logical size has been cleared. This test validates that the clear operation properly resets the string builder's size while preserving the underlying buffer capacity for potential reuse. The testing is performed using JUnit framework.

Initialize multiple StrBuilder instances using different constructor variations to test the proper initialization of capacity, length, and size properties across various input scenarios. Create a default StrBuilder instance with no arguments and assert that its capacity method returns 32, its length method returns 0, and its size method returns 0. Instantiate a StrBuilder with an integer capacity of 32 and verify the same capacity, length, and size values. Create a StrBuilder with a capacity of 0 and assert that it defaults to a capacity of 32 while maintaining zero length and size. This test validates the StrBuilder constructor behavior for handling default initialization, capacity specification, null and empty string inputs, and string content initialization, ensuring proper internal state management across all scenarios. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the conditional separator appending functionality when provided with a loop index parameter. Initialize a string builder and call the separator appending method with a comma character and an index of zero, then verify the builder remains empty since no separator should be added when the index is zero. Append the text "foo" to the builder and confirm it contains only "foo". Next, call the separator appending method again with a comma and an index of one, then assert the builder now contains "foo," as the separator should be appended when the index is greater than zero. Finally, call the separator appending method with a comma and a negative index of negative one, and verify the builder content remains unchanged at "foo," since no separator should be added for negative indices. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and assign a null StringBuilder reference, then call the append method with the null StringBuilder and assert that the resulting string representation equals an empty string. Create a second StrBuilder instance and call the append method with the null StringBuilder reference along with start index 0 and length 0, then assert that the resulting string representation also equals an empty string. The test validates that the StrBuilder class properly handles null StringBuilder inputs by checking that both the single-parameter append method and the three-parameter append method (with start index and length) return empty strings when given null StringBuilder arguments, ensuring consistent null handling behavior across different append method overloads. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance using the default constructor, then call the append method with the string literal "Hello" to add content to the builder, followed by invoking the clear method on the StrBuilder instance to reset its internal state. Assert that the length method returns 0 to verify the builder's content has been cleared, then assert that the buffer field of the StrBuilder instance has a length greater than or equal to 5 to confirm that the internal character array capacity remains allocated despite the content being cleared. This test validates that the clear operation properly resets the builder's logical content while maintaining the physical buffer capacity for performance optimization. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance without any constructor arguments to create an empty string builder. Call the appendSeparator method on this StrBuilder instance with a comma character and the integer value 0 as arguments, which should have no effect since the loop index is not greater than zero. Assert that the toString method on the StrBuilder returns an empty string to verify no separator was added. Next, call the append method with the string "foo" to add content to the builder. Assert that toString now returns "foo" to confirm the content was properly appended. Finally, call appendSeparator once more with a comma character and the integer value -1, which should have no effect since negative loop indices do not trigger separator addition. Assert that toString still returns "foo," to confirm no additional separator was appended. This test validates the conditional separator appending behavior of the appendSeparator method in the StrBuilder class, specifically testing that separators are only added when the loop index parameter is greater than zero, and uses the JUnit testing framework with the @Test annotation.

This test validates that the clear functionality properly resets the string builder's content while preserving its underlying buffer capacity. Assert that the length of the builder returns zero, confirming that the content has been removed. Additionally, verify that the internal buffer capacity remains at least as large as the original content size, ensuring that the clear operation only resets the content without deallocating the underlying storage space. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of appending a string buffer followed by a new line to a string builder. Initialize a string builder with custom behavior that tracks method invocations by overriding the append method for string buffers and the append new line method, using counters to monitor how many times each method is called. Create a string buffer containing a simple text value and call the append-with-newline method on the string builder, passing the string buffer as an argument. Verify that the resulting string content matches the original text followed by the system line separator, and confirm that both the string buffer append method and the new line append method were each invoked exactly once by checking the counter values. This test validates the behavior of a string builder's append method when handling null StringBuilder objects. Call the append method on the first string builder instance passing the null StringBuilder reference, and assert that converting the result to a string produces an empty string. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of appending string builder content with specified start and length parameters, including proper handling of null values and boundary conditions. Initialize a string builder and configure it to display a custom null text representation, then attempt to append a null string with valid indices to verify the null text is properly rendered. Create a fresh string builder and append a portion of another string builder containing sample text, specifying the full range to confirm the entire content is copied correctly. Execute multiple boundary violation scenarios by attempting to append with invalid start indices that are negative or exceed the source length, invalid lengths that are negative or extend beyond available content, and combinations of invalid parameters, ensuring each attempt triggers the appropriate index out of bounds exception. Verify that edge cases like appending zero-length content and appending partial content from various positions within the source work correctly without errors. Confirm the final string builder state matches expected content after valid append operations. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a string builder instance and configure it to set a null text representation to "NULL", then append a null string with start index 0 and length 1, asserting that the resulting string equals "NULL". Create a new string builder instance and append a StringBuilder containing "foo" with start index 0 and length 3, verifying the output equals "foo". Test boundary conditions by attempting to append a StringBuilder with "bar" using invalid index combinations: negative start index (-1) with length 1, start index (3) beyond the string length with length 1, valid start index (1) with negative length (-1), start index (1) with length (3) that exceeds remaining characters, negative start index (-1) with length (3) that would exceed bounds, and start index (4) beyond string length with zero length, expecting IndexOutOfBoundsException for each invalid case. Verify that valid edge cases work correctly by appending with start index 3 and length 0 (no change to "foo"), then appending substring "bar" from "abcbardef" with start index 3 and length 3 to produce "foobar", and finally appending substring "ard" from "abcbardef" with start index 4 and length 3 to produce "foobarard". The test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and configure it to use the string "NULL" as the null text representation by calling setNullText, then append a null String value with start index 0 and length 1 using the append method, and assert that the resulting string equals "NULL" using assertEquals and toString. Create a second StrBuilder instance and append a StringBuilder containing "foo" with start index 0 and length 3 using the append method, then assert that the resulting string equals "foo". Test boundary conditions by attempting to append a StringBuilder containing "bar" with invalid parameters: first with start index -1 and length 1, expecting an IndexOutOfBoundsException to be thrown and using a try-catch block with fail to ensure the exception occurs. Repeat this pattern for additional invalid parameter combinations including start index 3 with length 1, start index 1 with length -1, start index 1 with length 3, start index -1 with length 3, and start index 4 with length 0, each time expecting IndexOutOfBoundsException and using try-catch blocks with fail statements. Test valid edge cases by appending a StringBuilder containing "bar" with start index 3 and length 0, asserting the result still equals "foo", then append a StringBuilder containing "abcbardef" with start index 3 and length 3, asserting the result equals "foobar", and finally append a StringBuilder containing "abcbardef" with start index 4 and length 3, asserting the final result equals "foobarard". The test uses the JUnit testing framework with @Test annotation.

Initialize a string builder instance and call the minimize capacity method to verify it correctly adjusts the internal buffer size to match the current content length. This test validates that alphabet converters created from different mapping configurations are properly distinguished through equality comparison. Verify that the first converter reports an encoded character length of one, confirming its internal configuration remains consistent with the empty mapping used during its creation. This test validates the alphabet converter's factory method and equality comparison behavior by initializing an empty hash map, creating an alphabet converter from it using the static factory method, then modifying the original map by adding an integer key with value zero mapped to a string value, creating a second alphabet converter from the modified map, and asserting that the two converters are not equal to demonstrate that converters created from different map states produce distinct instances. Initialize a string builder with a custom anonymous subclass that overrides the append method for string buffers and the append new line method, both incrementing counters in an integer array to track invocations. This test validates the capacity minimization functionality of a string builder by creating an empty string builder and calling the minimize capacity operation to verify it reduces the internal buffer to match the actual content size. This test validates the equality comparison behavior of AlphabetConverter instances created from maps with different contents, specifically testing that converters with different mappings are not equal while verifying the encoded character length property. Assert that the equals method returns false when comparing the first converter (created from the empty map) with the second converter (created from the populated map), validating that AlphabetConverter instances with different originalToEncoded mappings are correctly identified as unequal through the equals method's comparison of the originalToEncoded, encodedToOriginal, and encodedLetterLength fields. Initialize a string builder instance and call the append separator method with a comma character, then assert that the builder's string representation is empty since no content has been added yet. Append the string "foo" to the builder and verify that the string representation equals "foo" without any separator. Initialize a test to verify the behavior of the appendln method when called with a StringBuffer argument on a StrBuilder instance, ensuring that both the append and appendNewLine methods are invoked correctly during the operation. Initialize a new TextStringBuilder instance and test the appendFixedWidthPadLeft method with integer values by calling appendFixedWidthPadLeft with the integer value 123, various width parameters, and the dash character as the padding character, then assert the expected string output and clear the builder between each test case. Begin by calling appendFixedWidthPadLeft with 123, width -1, and dash padding, then assert that toString returns an empty string since negative widths have no effect. Clear the builder and call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with 123, width 0, and dash padding, then assert toString returns an empty string since zero width has no effect. Clear the builder and call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with 123, width 1, and dash padding, then assert toString returns "3" since the width is smaller than the string representation and only the rightmost character is kept. Clear the builder and call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with 123, width 2, and dash padding, then assert toString returns "23" showing the rightmost two characters. Clear the builder and call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with 123, width 3, and dash padding, then assert toString returns "123" since the width exactly matches the string length. Clear the builder and call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with 123, width 4, and dash padding, then assert toString returns "-123" showing left padding with the dash character. Clear the builder and call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with 123, width 10, and dash padding, then assert the length equals 10 to verify the builder contains exactly 10 characters with appropriate left padding. The appendFixedWidthPadLeft method converts the integer to its string representation using String.valueOf and then applies fixed-width formatting with left padding, truncating from the left if the value is longer than the specified width or padding on the left with the specified character if shorter. This test validates the method's behavior across edge cases including negative widths, zero width, exact width matches, and scenarios requiring padding or truncation. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

Initialize a text string builder instance and append the string "Hello" to establish an initial state with content. Call the set length method with a value of 2 to shorten the builder, then assert that the string representation equals "He" to verify truncation behavior. Call set length again with the same value of 2 to test that no change occurs when the length is already at the target size, and assert the string representation still equals "He". This test validates that plain number formatting produces output equivalent to standard locale-specific decimal patterns across different locales. Initialize a plain formatter builder with a minimum decimal exponent of negative three and configure it to use format symbols from each available system locale, then verify the resulting formatter produces strings matching the expected decimal pattern with optional fractional digits. Repeat this validation using the same configuration but with thousands grouping enabled, ensuring the formatter output matches the expected pattern that includes comma separators for thousands groups. The test iterates through all available locales to ensure consistent formatting behavior regardless of regional number formatting conventions. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the plain double format functionality by comparing its output against expected decimal format patterns across different locales. Initialize a test that calls a helper method twice to check localized formats, first with the pattern "0.0##" using a plain double format builder configured with a minimum decimal exponent of -3 and format symbols for each locale, then with the pattern "#,##0.0##" using the same configuration but with thousands grouping enabled. The helper method iterates through all available system locales and validates that the plain format produces output consistent with the expected decimal format patterns for each locale's formatting symbols. Assert that the formatted output matches the expected localized decimal representations across all tested locales. This test uses JUnit as the testing framework.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and call the appendSeparator method with a comma character to test the conditional separator functionality that only appends when the builder is not empty. Assert that the builder's string representation equals an empty string since no separator should be appended to an empty builder. Call the append method with the string "foo" to add content to the builder, then assert that the toString method returns "foo" to verify the content was properly added. Call appendSeparator again with the same comma character, which should now append the separator since the builder contains content, and assert that toString returns "foo," to confirm the separator was correctly appended after the existing content. The appendSeparator method programmatically checks if the builder is not empty using the isNotEmpty method and conditionally appends the separator character only when content exists, providing a convenient way to add separators between elements without manually checking the builder's state. This test validates the core user experience of building comma-separated lists where separators should only appear between elements, not before the first element. The testing is performed using the Test annotation from a testing framework.

This test validates the string representation functionality of detailed edit distance calculations between character sequences. Initialize a default distance calculator and apply it to compute detailed edit distance results between three pairs of character sequences: short dissimilar words, longer dissimilar words, and an empty string compared to a single character. For each computation, create expected result data containing the total distance and counts of insert, delete, and substitute operations, then assert that the string representations of the actual and expected results are identical. The string representation format includes the total distance followed by the individual operation counts in a structured text format. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates that the PLAIN double format type produces localized output equivalent to specific DecimalFormat patterns across all available system locales. The test constructs DoubleFormat instances using the PLAIN builder with various configurations and compares their output against DecimalFormat patterns to ensure consistent localized formatting behavior. Initialize the test by calling the helper method checkLocalizedFormats twice with different pattern and factory function combinations. For the first call, pass the pattern "0.0##" along with a lambda function that creates a PLAIN DoubleFormat builder, sets the minDecimalExponent to -3, configures formatSymbols using DecimalFormatSymbols getInstance for the provided locale, and calls get to build the formatter. For the second call, use the pattern "#,##0.0##" with a similar lambda that additionally calls groupThousands with true to enable thousands grouping. The helper method checkLocalizedFormats iterates through all available locales from Locale getAvailableLocales and delegates to another helper method checkLocalizedFormat for each locale, passing the locale, pattern, and factory function to validate that the DoubleFormat output matches the expected DecimalFormat pattern output for that specific locale's formatting symbols. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the string representation functionality of the Levenshtein detailed distance calculator by comparing the string output of actual and expected results objects. Initialize a default instance of the Levenshtein detailed distance calculator, then apply it to compute the edit distance between three pairs of character sequences: "fly" and "ant", "hippo" and "elephant", and an empty string and "a". For each computation, create an expected results object with the anticipated distance value and operation counts (insertions, deletions, substitutions), then assert that the string representation of the actual result matches the string representation of the expected result. The string representation format includes the total distance and counts for each type of edit operation. The test uses representative string pairs that demonstrate different edit distance scenarios: complete character replacement, mixed operations with longer strings, and insertion into an empty string. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

Initialize a text string builder instance and test the appendFixedWidthPadLeft method with integer values across various width scenarios. Call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with the integer 123, a negative width of -1, and dash padding character, then assert the resulting string is empty and clear the builder. Repeat this process with width 0, asserting an empty result again. Test with width 1, verifying the result is "3" (rightmost digit only), then with width 2 expecting "23" (two rightmost digits). When the width equals the number's length at 3, assert the full "123" appears. Test padding behavior with width 4, confirming the result is "-123" (one dash pad character followed by the number). Finally, test with width 10 and verify the builder's length equals 10, demonstrating that the method pads the integer representation to the specified width by truncating from the left when the width is smaller than the number's string length, or padding with the specified character when the width is larger. The testing framework used is JUnit.

Initialize a new TextStringBuilder instance without any constructor arguments, then call the append method with the string literal "Hello" to add initial content to the builder. Next, call the setLength method with the integer value 2 to truncate the builder's content, which programmatically reduces the internal size field and effectively shortens the string representation to the first two characters. Assert that calling toString on the builder returns the string "He" to validate the truncation behavior. Call setLength again with the same value 2 to test that setting the length to the current length has no effect, then assert that toString still returns "He" to confirm no change occurred. Call setLength with the integer value 3 to extend the builder beyond its current content length, which programmatically increases the internal size field and fills the new position with null character '\0' using Arrays.fill. Assert that toString returns "He\0" to validate that the builder correctly pads with null characters when lengthened. Finally, use assertThrows to verify that calling setLength with the negative integer value -1 throws an IndexOutOfBoundsException, confirming that the setLength method properly validates input parameters and rejects negative length values. This test validates the TextStringBuilder setLength method's ability to both shorten existing content by adjusting the internal size, extend content by padding with null characters, maintain state when setting to current length, and enforce proper bounds checking for invalid negative inputs. The testing framework used is JUnit 5, identified by the @Test annotation and assertThrows method.

This test validates the string representation functionality of Levenshtein distance calculation results by comparing the output of the toString method across multiple character sequence pairs. Initialize a LevenshteinDetailedDistance instance by calling the getDefaultInstance method to obtain the default configuration without threshold limitations. Execute the apply method on this instance with the string literals "fly" and "ant" to compute the detailed Levenshtein distance, which calculates the edit operations needed to transform one string into another. Create an expected LevenshteinResults object with constructor parameters 3, 0, 0, 3 representing total distance, insert count, delete count, and substitute count respectively. Assert that the toString method output of the actual result equals the toString method output of the expected result using assertEquals, which validates that both objects produce identical string representations containing the distance metrics. Repeat this process by calling apply again with "hippo" and "elephant" strings, creating a new expected LevenshteinResults with values 7, 3, 0, 4, and asserting the toString equality. Execute a final iteration using apply with an empty string and "a", constructing an expected LevenshteinResults with parameters 1, 1, 0, 0, and performing the same toString comparison assertion. The toString method in LevenshteinResults formats the output as "Distance: [distance], Insert: [insertCount], Delete: [deleteCount], Substitute: [substituteCount]" providing a human-readable representation of the edit distance analysis. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the reset functionality when providing character array input to a string tokenizer. Initialize a string tokenizer with a sample input containing space-separated tokens, then create a character array with specific letter values. Call the reset method with this character array to replace the tokenizer's content, then retrieve the next token and verify it matches the expected concatenated string from the array. Confirm that no additional tokens remain available. Next, call the reset method again but pass a null character array, and verify that the tokenizer correctly indicates no tokens are available for processing. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the conditional separator appending functionality when using a character separator.
