Next, append the text "foo" to the builder and verify the content is "foo". Finally, append the comma separator again, which should now add the comma since the builder is no longer empty, resulting in "foo," as the final string representation. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the reset functionality of a string tokenizer when provided with a character array input. Initialize a string tokenizer with the input "x x x" which contains space-delimited tokens, then create a character array containing the letters 'a', 'b', and 'c'. Call the reset method on the tokenizer with this character array to replace its internal content, then invoke the next method to retrieve the first token and assert that it equals "abc" as a single concatenated string. Verify that the hasNext method returns false, indicating no additional tokens are available after the reset operation. Subsequently, call the reset method again with a null character array parameter, and assert that hasNext returns false, confirming that resetting with null input results in an empty tokenizer state with no available tokens. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the length adjustment functionality of a text string builder by exercising various scenarios of setting the builder's length. Initialize an empty text string builder and append a simple text value to establish initial content. Set the length to a smaller value than the current content to verify truncation behavior, then confirm the content has been shortened appropriately. Set the length to the same value again to ensure no changes occur when the length remains constant, and verify the content stays unchanged. Increase the length beyond the current content size to test expansion behavior, then validate that the content has been extended with null characters as padding. Finally, attempt to set the length to a negative value and verify that an appropriate bounds exception is thrown to handle invalid input. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of resetting a StringTokenizer with character array input and handling null input scenarios. Initialize a StringTokenizer instance with the string "x x x" which contains three space-separated tokens. Create a character array containing the characters 'a', 'b', and 'c' in sequence. Call the reset method on the StringTokenizer instance, passing the character array as the argument, which internally clones the input array and assigns it to the chars field while clearing any existing tokenization state. Invoke the next method to retrieve the first token and assert that it equals "abc", validating that the tokenizer correctly processes the character array as a single concatenated string. Call the hasNext method and assert that it returns false, confirming that only one token was produced from the character array input. Execute the reset method again, this time passing a null character array cast explicitly to char array type, which should set the internal chars field to null and clear the tokenization state. Finally, call the hasNext method and assert that it returns false, verifying that the tokenizer correctly handles null input by producing no tokens. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation and assertEquals and assertFalse assertion methods.

This test validates that engineering string formatting produces correct output with default configuration settings across various numeric inputs. Initialize a format options configuration with default values, then verify the engineering string conversion functionality by testing it against a comprehensive set of numeric values including zero, negative zero, positive integers, decimal numbers, very small negative numbers, large positive numbers, mathematical constants, and extreme boundary values like maximum and minimum representable doubles. For each test case, confirm that the generated engineering string matches the expected format and that the exponent values are properly constrained to multiples of three as required by engineering notation standards. The validation covers both positive and negative versions of each input to ensure consistent formatting behavior across the numeric spectrum. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the engineering string conversion functionality of a parsed decimal formatter using default format options. Initialize a format options implementation instance with default settings to control the string formatting behavior. Execute a series of validation checks by calling the engineering string conversion helper method with various double precision floating point inputs including zero, negative zero, positive integers like 1 and 10, decimal values such as 1.5, very small negative numbers like -0.000000123, large positive numbers such as 12300000, mathematical constants including pi and e, and extreme boundary values like the maximum double value, minimum double value, and minimum normal double value, along with their expected engineering notation string representations such as "0.0", "-0.0", "1.0", "1.5", "10.0", "-123.0E-9", "12.3E6", "3.141592653589793", "2.718281828459045", "-179.76931348623157E306", "4.9E-324", and "22.250738585072014E-309" respectively. The helper method validates that the parsed decimal's engineering string output matches the expected format and additionally asserts that the exponent values in both positive and negative versions of each number are multiples of three, which is a fundamental requirement of engineering notation. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the tokenization of a string containing quoted content with trimming enabled. Initialize a string tokenizer with an input string that has a colon-delimited structure where one token is wrapped in single quotes, configure it with a colon delimiter and single quote character for quoting, then enable trimming functionality to remove whitespace around tokens and configure it to preserve empty tokens while treating them as null values. Execute the tokenization process by retrieving tokens sequentially and verify that the first token is the unquoted text before the delimiter, the second token is the content from within the quotes with whitespace trimmed, and the third token is null due to the trailing delimiter creating an empty token that gets converted to null. Confirm that no additional tokens remain after processing the complete input. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string tokenizer's ability to parse quoted tokens with trimming enabled. Initialize a string tokenizer with an input string containing "a: 'b' :" where the colon serves as the delimiter and single quote as the quote character. Configure the tokenizer to use a trimmer matcher for whitespace removal, disable the ignoring of empty tokens, and enable the conversion of empty tokens to null values. Execute the tokenization process by calling the next method three times in sequence, asserting that the first token equals "a", the second token equals "b" (with quotes removed and whitespace trimmed), and the third token is null due to the empty string after the final colon being converted to null. Verify that no additional tokens remain by asserting that the has-next method returns false. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the maximum precision limiting functionality for decimal number representations. Initialize a decimal value with multiple fractional digits, then systematically apply different maximum precision constraints ranging from high to low values, including edge cases with zero precision. For each precision level, verify that the decimal representation correctly truncates or rounds the significant digits according to the specified limit, ensuring the resulting digit string and exponent values match expected outcomes for progressively reduced precision requirements. The validation spans multiple precision inputs to confirm consistent behavior across the full range of precision constraints. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the tokenization of a quoted string with trimming enabled, specifically testing that the StrTokenizer class correctly parses a colon-delimited input containing a quoted token and handles whitespace trimming and empty token processing. Initialize a StrTokenizer instance with the input string "a: 'b' :" using a colon character as the delimiter and a single quote character as the quote matcher. Configure the tokenizer by calling setTrimmerMatcher with StrMatcher.trimMatcher to enable whitespace trimming, setIgnoreEmptyTokens with false to retain empty tokens, and setEmptyTokenAsNull with true to convert empty tokens to null values. Execute the tokenization by calling next three times in sequence, asserting that the first call returns "a" using assertEquals, the second call returns "b" using assertEquals, and the third call returns null using assertNull to verify the empty token after the final colon is properly converted to null. Finally, call hasNext and assert it returns false using assertFalse to confirm no additional tokens remain in the tokenizer. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the maximum precision functionality of a parsed decimal component by exercising precision truncation behavior across various precision levels. Initialize a double value representing approximately 1.026 and systematically call the precision assertion helper with different maximum precision parameters ranging from 10 down to 0, along with a boolean flag set to false, expected digit strings, and corresponding exponent values. The helper method creates a parsed decimal object from the input double, applies the specified maximum precision constraint, and then validates the resulting decimal representation. Assert that when higher precision values like 10 or 9 are applied, the full digit string "102576552" is preserved with an exponent of -8, while progressively lower precision values like 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, and 3 result in truncated digit strings such as "10257655", "1025766", "102577", "10258", "1026", and "103" respectively, with correspondingly adjusted exponents. Verify that very low precision values of 2 and 1 both produce a single digit "1" with zero exponent, and that a precision of 0 reverts to the original full precision representation. The testing framework used is JUnit.

This test validates the ability to reset a string tokenizer with a character array input and handle null array inputs appropriately. Initialize a string tokenizer with an initial text containing space-separated characters, then create a character array containing three consecutive letters. Reset the tokenizer with this character array and verify that retrieving the next token returns the entire array content as a single concatenated string, and confirm that no additional tokens are available. Subsequently, reset the tokenizer again using a null character array and verify that no tokens are available for iteration. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the engineering string formatting functionality of ParsedDecimal with default format options by verifying that various double values are correctly converted to their engineering notation representations. Initialize a FormatOptionsImpl instance with default configuration settings, which serves as the formatting options object for controlling the string output behavior. Execute a series of calls to the helper method checkToEngineeringString, passing specific double values alongside their expected engineering string representations and the format options instance, starting with zero represented as "0.0", negative zero as "-0.0", simple values like 1.0 as "1.0" and 1.5 as "1.5", ten as "10.0", a small negative scientific value -0.000000123 as "-123.0E-9", a large value 12300000 as "12.3E6", mathematical constants Math.PI as "3.141592653589793" and Math.E as "2.718281828459045", the maximum double value negated as "-179.76931348623157E306", the minimum positive double value as "4.9E-324", and the minimum normal double value as "22.250738585072014E-309". The helper method validates each conversion by calling checkToStringMethod with the ParsedDecimal toEngineeringString method reference and the provided format options, then performs additional assertions to ensure the exponent values in both positive and negative versions of each number are multiples of three, which is a fundamental requirement of engineering notation where exponents must be divisible by three to align with standard engineering prefixes. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates the string tokenizer's ability to reset its input source using a character array and handle null input scenarios. Initialize a string tokenizer with the initial input "x x x", then create a character array containing the letters 'a', 'b', and 'c'. Call the reset method on the tokenizer with this character array to replace the original input, then invoke the next method to retrieve the first token and assert that it equals "abc" as a single concatenated string. Verify that the hasNext method returns false, indicating no additional tokens are available. Subsequently, call the reset method again with a null character array parameter, and assert that hasNext returns false, confirming the tokenizer properly handles null input by having no tokens to iterate over. This test validates the wrapping functionality of a text string builder when initialized with a character array and a specific length parameter. Initialize a character array containing a simple text sequence, then create a text string builder by wrapping this array with a length value of one. Verify that the builder's internal buffer matches the original input array and that both the length and size properties return the expected length value of one. Confirm that the builder has not been reallocated at this point. Force the builder to expand its capacity by requesting double the current capacity, then assert that the internal buffer no longer equals the original input array and that the builder now reports as having been reallocated. This test uses JUnit as the testing framework.

This test validates the functionality of resetting a StrTokenizer instance with character array input, ensuring proper tokenization behavior and null handling. Initialize a StrTokenizer instance with the string "x x x" which will be tokenized into three separate tokens when processed. Create a character array containing the values 'a', 'b', and 'c' in sequence. Call the reset method on the StrTokenizer instance, passing the character array as input, which internally clones the array and assigns it to the chars field while clearing any existing tokens. Invoke the next method to retrieve the first token and assert that it equals "abc", validating that the character array was properly converted to a single concatenated string token. Call the hasNext method and assert that it returns false, confirming that only one token was generated from the character array input. Reset the tokenizer again by calling the reset method with a null character array parameter, which should set the internal chars field to null and clear any existing tokens. Finally, call hasNext and assert that it returns false, verifying that the tokenizer correctly handles null input by having no tokens available for iteration. This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the precision truncation functionality of a decimal parsing system by verifying that a parsed decimal value can be accurately reduced to various precision levels while maintaining correct digit representation and exponent values. The test focuses on the maxPrecision method of the ParsedDecimal class and uses assertion validation to confirm proper truncation behavior across multiple precision scenarios. Initialize a double variable with the value 1.02576552 to serve as the test input for all precision operations. Execute a series of assertions using a helper method called assertMaxPrecision, passing the double value along with varying precision levels from 10 down to 0, a boolean false value, expected digit strings, and corresponding exponent values. The helper method creates a ParsedDecimal instance from the input double using the from method, applies the specified maximum precision using the maxPrecision method, and validates the result through assertSimpleDecimal with the expected negative flag, digit string, and exponent. Verify that precision level 10 and 9 both produce the digit string "102576552" with exponent -8, precision 8 yields "10257655" with exponent -7, precision 7 results in "1025766" with exponent -6, precision 6 gives "102577" with exponent -5, precision 5 produces "10258" with exponent -4, precision 4 yields "1026" with exponent -3, precision 3 results in "103" with exponent -2, and both precision 2 and 1 produce "1" with exponent 0, while precision 0 returns to the full representation "102576552" with exponent -8. The testing framework used is JUnit, as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the wrapping functionality of a text string builder when initialized with a character array and a specific length parameter. Initialize a character array containing the string "abc" and create a text string builder by wrapping this array with an expected length of 1. Assert that the builder's internal buffer matches the original input array, and verify that both the length and size methods return the expected length value of 1. Confirm that the builder has not been reallocated by checking the reallocation status returns false. Force the builder to expand its capacity by calling ensure capacity with double the current capacity, then assert that the internal buffer no longer equals the original input array and verify that the reallocation status now returns true, indicating the builder has created a new internal buffer. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the character array wrapping functionality of TextStringBuilder when initialized with a specific length parameter, ensuring proper buffer management and reallocation behavior. The test exercises the TextStringBuilder wrap method with a character array and length parameter, asserting that the builder correctly maintains the wrapped array reference, tracks length and size properties, and handles capacity expansion with proper reallocation detection. Initialize the test by calling a helper method with the string literal "abc" and the integer value 1 as arguments. Within the helper method, create a character array by converting the string "abc" to a character array, then invoke the TextStringBuilder wrap method with this character array and the expected length parameter to create a new builder instance. Assert that the builder's buffer matches the original input character array using assertArrayEquals, verify that both the length and size methods return the expected length value using assertEquals, and confirm that the isReallocated method returns false initially. Trigger a capacity expansion by calling ensureCapacity with double the current capacity, then assert that the buffer no longer equals the original input array and verify that isReallocated now returns true, demonstrating that the builder properly detects when the underlying buffer has been reallocated during capacity changes. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string tokenizer's ability to process input with ignored patterns and trimming while handling empty tokens. Initialize a string tokenizer with a colon delimiter using an input string containing the pattern "IGNORE" interspersed with characters like "IGNOREaIGNORE: IGNORE bIGNOREc IGNORE : IGNORE ". Configure the tokenizer to ignore occurrences of the literal string "IGNORE" by setting an ignored matcher, enable trimming of whitespace characters with a trimmer matcher, disable the ignoring of empty tokens, and enable the conversion of empty tokens to null values. Invoke the tokenizer's next method to retrieve the first token and assert it equals "a", then call next again to retrieve the second token and assert it equals "bc". Call next a third time to get the next token and assert it returns null, representing an empty token converted to null. Finally, verify that the tokenizer reports no more tokens are available by asserting that hasNext returns false. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string tokenization functionality when both character ignoring and trimming are applied simultaneously. Initialize a string tokenizer with a colon delimiter and configure it to ignore occurrences of a specific substring pattern and to trim whitespace characters from tokens. Set the tokenizer to preserve empty tokens but convert them to null values rather than empty strings. Process an input string that contains the ignored substring pattern interspersed with actual token content and whitespace, where the delimiters separate tokens that should result in cleaned content after ignoring and trimming operations. Verify that the first token returns the expected cleaned character, the second token returns the expected concatenated characters, the third token is null due to being empty after processing, and confirm no additional tokens remain. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the string tokenization functionality when both ignored characters and trimming are applied simultaneously to extract meaningful tokens from a delimited string. Initialize a StrTokenizer instance with the input string "IGNOREaIGNORE: IGNORE bIGNOREc IGNORE : IGNORE " and configure it to use a colon as the delimiter by passing ':' to the constructor. Configure the tokenizer to ignore all occurrences of the literal string "IGNORE" by calling setIgnoredMatcher with StrMatcher.stringMatcher("IGNORE"), which will remove these substrings during tokenization. Set up trimming behavior by calling setTrimmerMatcher with StrMatcher.trimMatcher() to remove whitespace characters from token boundaries. Configure the tokenizer to preserve empty tokens by calling setIgnoreEmptyTokens with false, ensuring empty tokens are included in the results. Enable null representation for empty tokens by calling setEmptyTokenAsNull with true, which converts empty strings to null values. Execute the tokenization process and validate the results by calling next() three times in sequence, asserting that the first call returns "a" using assertEquals, the second call returns "bc" using assertEquals, and the third call returns null using assertNull. Finally, verify that no additional tokens remain by calling hasNext() and asserting it returns false using assertFalse. The test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the @Test annotation.

This test validates that an alphabet conversion utility can properly encode and decode Hebrew text using different target character sets. Initialize predefined character arrays representing Hebrew characters, binary digits, numeric digits, and lowercase English letters that serve as the source and target alphabets for conversion operations. Execute conversion testing by creating converters that transform Hebrew text to binary representation and Hebrew text to numeric representation, then verify bidirectional conversion accuracy using sample Hebrew Unicode strings. Test the reverse scenario by converting numeric strings to Hebrew representation and English text to Hebrew representation using empty exclusion character arrays. For each conversion scenario, create a converter from the specified character mappings, reconstruct an equivalent converter from the generated mapping, and validate that both converters are functionally identical through equality and hash code comparisons. Verify that encoding operations only produce characters from the target alphabet, decoding operations only produce characters from the source alphabet, and the round-trip conversion preserves the original input exactly. Assert that null inputs are handled appropriately and that the conversion process maintains data integrity across multiple test strings containing various Hebrew phrases and numeric sequences. This test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the alphabet converter's ability to handle Hebrew character encoding and decoding operations across different character set combinations. Execute the helper test method four times with different parameter combinations: first convert Hebrew characters to binary representation using an empty exclusion array and Hebrew Unicode strings as test data, then convert Hebrew to numeric representation with the same test strings, followed by converting numeric characters to Hebrew representation using numeric test strings, and finally convert lowercase English to Hebrew using an English test string. Within each test execution, create an alphabet converter from the provided character arrays, reconstruct a second converter from the first converter's character mapping, and assert that both converters are equal in value, hash code, and string representation. Verify that encoding null input returns null and that encoding operations only produce characters from the target encoding set while decoding operations only produce characters from the original character set. Assert that the decode operation on encoded strings returns the original input string exactly, ensuring bidirectional conversion accuracy. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the behavior of appending integer values with fixed-width left padding functionality. Initialize a text string builder and repeatedly test the fixed-width left padding operation with an integer value, various width specifications, and a dash character as the padding character, clearing the builder between each test. Call the fixed-width left padding method with the integer 123, testing with negative width to verify empty output, zero width to confirm empty result, and positive widths of 1, 2, and 3 to validate truncation from the right side when the value exceeds the specified width. Test with width 4 to ensure proper left padding with the dash character, and verify with width 10 that the resulting length matches the specified width and contains the expected padded content. Assert that each operation produces the expected string representation, including empty strings for invalid widths, truncated digits for insufficient width, the full number for exact width matches, and properly padded results for larger widths. The testing framework used is JUnit.

Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and test the appendFixedWidthPadLeft method with an integer value of 123 across various width scenarios to validate its left-padding behavior with truncation and padding logic. Call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with the integer 123, a width of -1, and the pad character '-', then assert that the resulting string via toString is empty, followed by calling clear to reset the builder. Repeat this pattern by calling appendFixedWidthPadLeft with width 0 and asserting an empty string result, then clear again. Next, call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with width 1 and assert the result equals "3" to verify right-most character extraction when the value exceeds the specified width, then clear. Continue by calling appendFixedWidthPadLeft with width 2 and assert the result equals "23" to confirm extraction of the two rightmost characters, then clear. Call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with width 3 and assert the result equals "123" to validate that when the width matches the value length, the full value is returned without padding, then clear. Call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with width 4 and assert the result equals "-123" to verify left-padding with the specified pad character when the width exceeds the value length, then clear. Finally, call appendFixedWidthPadLeft with width 10 and assert that the length method returns 10 to confirm the builder contains exactly 10 characters when significant padding is applied. The test validates that appendFixedWidthPadLeft correctly handles edge cases with negative and zero widths, truncates from the right when the value exceeds the width, preserves the full value when widths match, and applies left-padding with the specified character when the width is greater than the value length. This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the Hebrew character encoding and decoding functionality of an alphabet converter system by testing bidirectional conversion between Hebrew characters and other character sets. The test exercises the AlphabetConverter class through multiple conversion scenarios and verifies that encoding and decoding operations maintain data integrity across different alphabets. Initialize the test by calling the helper method test four times with different parameter combinations, where the first call converts from the HEBREW field (a Character array test class field containing Hebrew characters) to the BINARY field (a Character array test class field containing binary characters) using ArrayUtils.EMPTY_CHARACTER_OBJECT_ARRAY as the do-not-encode parameter and Hebrew Unicode strings including "\u05d0", "\u05e2", and a longer Hebrew text sequence. Execute the second test call converting from HEBREW to NUMBERS field (a Character array test class field containing numeric characters) with the same empty character array and Hebrew string parameters. Perform the third test call converting from NUMBERS to HEBREW using the empty character array parameter and numeric strings "123456789", "1", and "5". Complete the fourth test call converting from LOWER_CASE_ENGLISH field (a Character array test class field containing lowercase English characters) to HEBREW using the empty character array parameter and the English string "this is a test". This test uses the JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the character set matching functionality that determines if characters at specific positions within a buffer match any character from a predefined set. Initialize a string builder instance and test the behavior of the fixed-width left-padding method for integer values with various width parameters and a dash padding character. Repeat this process with a width of 0, asserting an empty result again. Test with width 1, asserting the result is "3" (the rightmost digit), then with width 2 asserting "23", and width 3 asserting the full "123". For width 4, assert the result is "-123" showing left padding with the dash character. Finally, test with width 10 and assert the length is 10 characters, demonstrating proper padding behavior when the width exceeds the integer's string representation length. The testing framework used is JUnit.

This test validates the character set matcher functionality of the string matcher utility by creating a matcher for a specific set of characters and verifying its matching behavior against a character buffer. Initialize a character set matcher using a character array containing the letters 'a', 'c', and 'e', then test the matcher's ability to identify matches at various positions within a predefined character buffer by calling the match method with different position indices. Assert that the matcher returns 1 for positions where the buffer contains characters from the target set and 0 for positions where it does not, specifically testing positions 0 through 5 to verify correct matching behavior. This test validates the engineering format functionality with custom configuration settings. Initialize an engineering format builder and configure it with a maximum precision of three digits, a minimum decimal exponent of negative three, disabled signed zero formatting, disabled fraction placeholders, a comma as the decimal separator, lowercase 'e' as the exponent separator, 'inf' for infinity representation, 'nan' for not-a-number values, and an exclamation mark as the minus sign, then build the formatter. This test validates the behavior of a string builder's fixed-width left-padding functionality for integer values across various width scenarios. Initialize a string builder and repeatedly test the fixed-width left-padding method with an integer value, different width parameters, and a dash character as the padding character, clearing the builder between each test. Call the method with negative and zero widths to verify it produces empty results, then test with widths of one through four to confirm it truncates the integer representation from the right when the width is smaller than the value's string length, displays the full value when widths match, and adds left padding when the width exceeds the value's length. Assert that each operation produces the expected string output, including verifying the final test case produces a string of exactly ten characters in length. The testing is performed using JUnit.

This test validates the character set matching functionality of the StrMatcher class, specifically testing how the charSetMatcher method creates matchers that can identify characters from a specified set within a character buffer. Initialize a StrMatcher by calling the charSetMatcher method on the StrMatcher class, passing a character array created by converting the string "ace" to a character array using toCharArray, which creates a matcher that will identify any of the characters 'a', 'c', or 'e' in a target buffer. Execute six sequential isMatch calls on the matcher, passing the test class field BUFFER2 of type char array and position indices 0 through 5, asserting that the method returns 1 for positions 0, 2, and 4 (indicating matches) and 0 for positions 1, 3, and 5 (indicating no matches), which validates that the matcher correctly identifies characters from the specified set at the expected buffer positions. Verify edge case behavior by calling charSetMatcher with no arguments and asserting using assertSame that it returns the same instance as noneMatcher, then call charSetMatcher with a null character array cast and assert using assertSame that it also returns the same instance as noneMatcher, confirming that empty or null inputs produce the non-matching matcher. Use a helper method assertStrMatcherImpl to validate the internal implementation by passing the string "CharMatcher" and a StrMatcher created by calling charSetMatcher with a single character 'a' converted to a character array, which verifies that the returned matcher has the expected internal class name structure. The testing framework used is JUnit, identified by the @Test annotation.

This test validates the engineering format functionality of a double formatting utility by constructing a custom engineering formatter with specific configuration settings and verifying its output against various numeric inputs. Initialize an engineering format builder and configure it with a maximum precision of 3 digits, a minimum decimal exponent of -3, disabled signed zero representation, disabled fraction placeholders, a comma as the decimal separator, lowercase 'e' as the exponent separator, 'inf' for infinity representation, 'nan' for NaN representation, and an exclamation mark as the minus sign, then build the formatter function. Execute the formatter against a comprehensive set of test cases including special values like NaN which should produce "nan", positive infinity which should produce "inf", and negative infinity which should produce "!inf". Test various numeric ranges including very small values like 0.00001 and -0.0001 which should format as "0", small decimal values like 0.001 and -0.01 which should produce "1e!3" and "!10e!3" respectively, standard values like -1.0 and 10.0 which should format as "!1" and "10", larger values like 1000.0 and -10000.0 which should produce "1e3" and "!10e3", and edge cases including maximum double values, minimum values, and mathematical constants like pi and e which should format as "3,14" and "2,72" respectively. Assert that each formatted result exactly matches the expected string output using a helper method that applies the formatter to the input value and compares the result. The test uses JUnit 5 framework as indicated by the Test annotation and Assertions class.

This test validates the string tokenization functionality when processing text with semicolon delimiters, double quote characters, and whitespace handling. This test validates the custom configuration capabilities of the engineering number format by ensuring that a formatter with specific customizations produces expected string representations for various double values. Verify that the custom decimal separator appears in formatted numbers like 12345 producing "12,3e3" and mathematical constants like Pi producing "3,14" and E producing "2,72". This test uses the JUnit testing framework as indicated by the Test annotation.

This test validates that scientific notation formatting works correctly with customized formatting options and alternative symbols. Verify that each conversion produces the expected string representation using the custom formatting symbols, ensuring that commas replace decimal points, exclamation marks replace minus signs, the custom exponent separator appears correctly, and exponents are always displayed even for values that would normally omit them. The testing uses JUnit framework.

Initialize a string tokenizer with a multi-line input string containing semicolon-delimited tokens, some of which are quoted with double quotes and include escaped quotes and semicolons within the quoted sections. The test uses JUnit testing framework.

This test validates the scientific string formatting functionality of a parsed decimal component with customized formatting options. Initialize a format options implementation and configure it to disable fraction placeholders and signed zero display, set the decimal separator to a comma, change the minus sign to an exclamation mark, use a custom exponent separator of "x10^", and enable always including the exponent. Execute the scientific string conversion method through a helper function that validates the output against expected strings for various double values including zero, negative zero, positive numbers like 1.0 and 1.5, negative scientific notation values like -0.000123, large integers such as 12301, mathematical constants including pi and e, and edge cases like maximum double value, minimum double value, and minimum normal double value. Assert that each conversion produces the correctly formatted scientific notation string with the custom formatting applied, such as using commas for decimal separation, exclamation marks for negative signs, and the custom exponent separator throughout all test cases. This test validates that a string tokenizer can properly parse comma-separated values using a simple CSV data fixture. This test validates the scientific string formatting functionality with customized format options by verifying that various double values are correctly converted to scientific notation using non-standard formatting characters and settings. Execute a series of assertions by calling the helper method checkToScientificString with various double inputs and their expected scientific string representations: validate that 0.0 produces "0x10^0", negative 0.0 also produces "0x10^0", 1.0 produces "1x10^0", 1.5 produces "1,5x10^0" demonstrating the comma decimal separator, -0.000123 produces "!1,23x10^!4" showing both the exclamation mark minus sign and negative exponent, 12301 produces "1,2301x10^4", Math.PI produces "3,141592653589793x10^0", Math.E produces "2,718281828459045x10^0", negative Double.MAX_VALUE produces "!1,7976931348623157x10^308", Double.MIN_VALUE produces "4,9x10^!324", and Double.MIN_NORMAL produces "2,2250738585072014x10^!308". This test validates the string tokenization functionality when processing a complex input containing semicolon delimiters, quoted sections, and empty tokens. This test validates the string tokenizer's ability to parse a complex input string containing semicolon delimiters, quoted content, and empty tokens. This test validates the tokenization of a complex string containing semicolon delimiters, quoted sections, and empty tokens to ensure proper parsing and null handling behavior. Initialize a StrTokenizer instance with a multi-line input string containing semicolons as delimiters, quoted text with embedded semicolons and quotes, and trailing empty sections, then configure the tokenizer by calling setDelimiterChar with a semicolon character, setQuoteChar with a double quote character, setIgnoredMatcher with StrMatcher.trimMatcher to ignore whitespace, setIgnoreEmptyTokens with false to retain empty tokens, and setEmptyTokenAsNull with true to convert empty tokens to null values. Initialize a new StrBuilder instance and append the string "a b " to it, then call the asTokenizer method to create a StrTokenizer that uses the builder's internal character buffer as its source. Verify the configuration transfer by asserting that target returns true when calling isEnableSubstitutionInVariables to confirm substitution in variable names is enabled, assert that target returns true when calling isEnableUndefinedVariableException to verify exception throwing for undefined variables is enabled, assert that target returns the character 'e' when calling getEscapeChar to confirm the escape character was copied, assert that the string representation of target's value delimiter matcher ends with "['d']" by calling getValueDelimiterMatcher followed by toString and checking the suffix, assert that the string representation of target's variable prefix matcher ends with "['p']" by calling getVariablePrefixMatcher followed by toString and checking the suffix, and assert that the string representation of target's variable suffix matcher ends with "['s']" by calling getVariableSuffixMatcher followed by toString and checking the suffix. The test uses the Test annotation and employs the JUnit testing framework for assertions.

Initialize a new TextStringBuilder instance and append the string "barbaz" to it, then assert that calling toString returns "barbaz". Test boundary conditions by asserting that calling insert with index -1 and the FOO field throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, and similarly assert that calling insert with index 7 and FOO throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.
